t: A multi-resolution imaging and analysis pipeline for comparative circuit reconstruction in insects
sum: Mapping insect brains is usually too expensive for small labs. This team images the same brain at two zoom levels and finds that a navigation circuit looks largely the same across six insect species, with some local tweaks.

t: Beyond Agreement: Standardizing Crowdsourced Synapse Annotations through Proofreading in EM Connectomics
sum: People often disagree about whether a tiny blob in a brain image is a synapse. This team trains raters, combines their votes with a statistical model, and reports how sure the group is, so the labels can be used more honestly.

t: ConnectoFM: A Foundation Model for Learning the Language of the Connectome
sum: Computers that trace neurons from electron-microscope pictures usually have to be retrained for every new dataset. This team pretrains one model on a huge mix of unlabeled brain images and shows it can learn new tracing jobs with far fewer hand-drawn labels.

t: Learning the wiring rules of a mammalian cortical column
sum: Instead of starting from known cell labels, this study lets a model invent a compact description of each neuron and the simple rules that wire them together in mouse visual cortex. Two of those invented axes turn out to be depth and whether the cell is excitatory or inhibitory.

t: Brain rewiring during development: A comparative analysis of larval and adult Drosophila melanogaster connectomes
sum: Fruit-fly brains are rewired as the animal grows from larva to adult. This paper compares the two wiring diagrams and finds that the adult network is sparser and more hub-like, and that the most central cells change from a learning center to an odor center.

t: Cascades and convergence: dynamic signal flow in a synapse-level brain network
sum: A wiring diagram shows which cells touch, not how a signal would actually travel. This team runs simple spreading simulations on the fly brain map to guess which cells light up together for different senses.

t: CAVE: Connectome Annotation Versioning Engine
sum: When many people correct a giant brain map at once, cell names and synapse lists keep changing. CAVE is software that versions those edits so scientists can still run analyses and get the same answer later.

t: Inhibitory specificity from a connectomic census of mouse visual cortex
sum: Inhibitory cells in the cortex come in many kinds, but it has been unclear exactly whom each kind talks to. This team mapped inhibition across a column of mouse visual cortex and found that inhibitory cells are choosier than a random mix would suggest.

t: NEURD offers automated proofreading and feature extraction for connectomics
sum: Computers can now outline cells in huge electron-microscope volumes, but the outlines still have mistakes and are hard to measure. NEURD turns each cell’s 3D shape into a simpler labeled graph so corrections and measurements can be automated.

t: Synaptic-resolution connectomics: towards large brains and connectomic screening
sum: Scientists can now map tiny pieces of brain at the level of individual connections, about a thousand times larger than twenty years ago. This review explains what that makes possible next—and why a whole mouse brain at that detail is still a huge leap.

t: The unique synaptic circuitry of specialized olfactory glomeruli in Drosophila melanogaster
sum: Fruit flies smell some odors with many glomeruli at once and other special odors with just one. This paper compares the wiring inside one “generalist” and one “specialist” glomerulus and lists connection patterns that may go with each job.

t: Whole-body connectome of a segmented annelid larva
sum: This team mapped the cells and connections of an entire young marine worm, not just its brain. The map shows how segments share cell types and how senses can reach muscles, cilia, and glands across the body.

t: A petavoxel fragment of human cerebral cortex reconstructed at nanoscale resolution
sum: Researchers reconstructed a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex at very high detail and posted the data for anyone to explore. They found more support cells than neurons, and a few unusually strong connections mixed in with many weak ones.

t: Combined topological and spatial constraints are required to capture the structure of neural connectomes
sum: Brain wiring is shaped both by which cells sit near each other and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows you need both kinds of rules to copy the structure of fly, mouse, and human connection maps.

t: Comparative connectomics of the descending and ascending neurons of the Drosophila nervous system: stereotypy and sexual dimorphism
sum: Messages between a fly’s brain and its body travel through a narrow neck. This team finished mapping those up and down neurons in a female fly, compared them with a male, and tied many types to genetic tools.

t: Comparative prospects of imaging methods for whole-brain mammalian connectomics
sum: Scientists want maps of entire mammal brains at the level of connections, starting with the mouse. This paper compares electron microscopes and expansion light-sheet methods to see which could finish that job, and on what timescale.

t: Connectomic reconstruction of a female Drosophila ventral nerve cord
sum: A fruit fly’s “spinal cord” contains the cells that move legs and wings. This team automatically traced that cord, matched motor neurons to muscles, and spotted circuits that help the fly take off.

t: Diverging network architecture of the C. elegans connectome and signaling network
sum: Knowing which worm neurons are wired together is not the same as knowing which ones actually pass signals. This study measures signal spread and finds that the functional groups only partly match the wiring groups.

t: Driver lines for studying associative learning in Drosophila
sum: To test what each cell type does in fly learning, scientists need genetic on-switches for those cells. This paper releases hundreds of such switches and notices that one pair of output cells looks surprisingly different from fly to fly.

t: Global Neuron Shape Reasoning with Point Affinity Transformers
sum: Computers that trace neurons usually look at small patches of the image. This method looks at the whole sketched shape of a cell as a cloud of points, which helps it fix tracing mistakes and guess the cell’s type.

t: Hierarchical communities in the larval Drosophila connectome: Links to cellular annotations and network topology
sum: This paper groups larval fruit-fly neurons into nested communities using only the wiring, then checks those groups against known cell types. Most groups stay among similar cells, but a small hub club of in-between cells helps messages travel across the brain.

t: Network statistics of the whole-brain connectome of Drosophila
sum: With a whole fruit-fly brain wiring diagram in hand, this paper counts common connection patterns and finds a large club of well-connected cells. About three in ten neurons sit in that highly connected group.

t: Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain
sum: This paper releases a wiring diagram of an entire adult fruit-fly brain: which cells connect, what kinds they are, and roughly what chemical they use. The map is public so others can follow paths from the eyes to the cells that drive movement.

t: Predicting modular functions and neural coding of behavior from a synaptic wiring diagram
sum: Researchers mapped connections in a young zebrafish’s brainstem, then asked whether the wiring could predict how cells encode eye position. The predictions matched calcium-imaging measurements.

t: The fly connectome reveals a path to the effectome
sum: A fly brain map shows possible routes, not how strongly one cell actually pushes another. This paper argues you can learn those strengths with clever light-based perturbations, because the brain seems to be made of many small, mostly separate circuits.

t: Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila
sum: Scientists named the cell types in a whole fruit-fly brain so it can be compared with another fly’s brain. Many types match, but some do not, so they propose a stricter rule: a real type should look more like its partners in another brain than like other cells in the same brain.

t: A Connectome of the Male Drosophila Ventral Nerve Cord
sum: To understand movement, you have to map the nerve cord that talks to the muscles, not only the brain. This team built a detailed connection map of a male fruit fly’s ventral nerve cord.

t: A consensus cell type atlas from multiple connectomes reveals principles of circuit stereotypy and variation
sum: This preprint names the cell types in a whole fly brain and checks them against an earlier partial map. Strong connections tend to match, weaker ones vary, and the authors suggest a type should look more like the same cells in another brain than like other cells in its own brain.

t: Cell-type-specific inhibitory circuitry from a connectomic census of mouse visual cortex
sum: This preprint maps how inhibitory cells connect inside a column of mouse visual cortex. It finds that inhibition is organized into repeating targeting patterns, not a uniform blanket, and that even neurons in the same layer can sit in different inhibitory networks.

t: Connectome-constrained deep mechanistic networks predict neural responses across the fly visual system at single-neuron resolution
sum: We can map every connection in a circuit and still not know how each cell fires. This team freezes the fly visual system’s wiring, tunes the unknown cell and synapse knobs so the network detects motion, and finds that the predicted activity matches many published experiments.

t: Immersion fixation and staining of multi-cubic millimeter volumes for electron microscopy-based connectomics of human brain biopsies
sum: Human brain samples for electron microscopy usually cannot be perfused with fixative the way animal brains can. This team shows how to dunk fresh surgical biopsies in cold fixative and stain them so large chunks stay well preserved for mapping synapses.

t: Joint Learning Neuronal Skeleton and Brain Circuit Topology with Permutation Invariant Encoders for Neuron Classification
sum: A neuron’s identity is written both in its 3D shape and in who it talks to. This paper trains a computer to use both the stick-figure skeleton and the wiring diagram to guess each cell’s type.

t: mEMbrain: an interactive deep learning MATLAB tool for connectomic segmentation on commodity desktops
sum: Tracing neurons in electron-microscope pictures usually needs expert programmers and big computers. This free MATLAB add-on lets a lab label examples, train a network, and check predictions on an ordinary desktop, using software many biologists already know.

t: Multiplexed volumetric CLEM enabled by antibody derivatives provides new insights into the cytology of the mouse cerebellar cortex
sum: Electron-microscope maps show every wire but not which molecular “name tags” a cell carries. This team makes tiny fluorescent antibody pieces that soak into tissue without soap, so the same mouse cerebellum chunk can be seen in color and then in EM detail.

t: SynapseCLR: Uncovering features of synapses in primary visual cortex through contrastive representation learning
sum: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged in 3D contains far too many synapses for people to label one by one. This method teaches a computer to compare synapse snapshots with no labels, then uses a tiny handful of human tags to fill in the rest and to flag broken reconstructions.

t: The structure and function of neural connectomes are shaped by a small number of design principles
sum: Brain wiring looks complicated, but much of it may follow a few simple local rules. This study builds statistical models of three very different circuits and finds that those simple ingredients already predict both the wiring and, in one case, the circuit’s job.

t: The XPRESS Challenge: Xray Projectomic Reconstruction - Extracting Segmentation with Skeletons
sum: Electron microscopes can see every synapse locally but cannot yet photograph a whole mouse brain. This contest shares X-ray nanotomography pictures of white-matter cables and asks computers to trace those axons, using stick-figure drawings as the main teaching signal.

t: ViMO - Visual Analysis of Neuronal Connectivity Motifs
sum: When a wiring diagram has tens of thousands of cells, looking for a repeating little circuit is like finding a pattern in a huge subway map. This software lets scientists draw the pattern, jump to every match, and peel the 3D cells apart so the connections are easier to see.

t: A set of hub neurons and non-local connectivity features support global brain dynamics in C. elegans.
sum: In a tiny worm, scientists can compare the full wiring diagram with how cells fire together across the whole brain. This paper finds that a few well-connected hub cells, and patterns that reach beyond simple neighbor links, help explain those brain-wide activity partnerships.

t: A Survey of Visualization and Analysis in High‐Resolution Connectomics
sum: Brain maps from electron microscopes are so big that scientists need clever pictures and interactive tools just to work with them. This review walks through those tools from the moment images are taken to the moment circuits are analyzed, and lists free datasets and software.

t: Automated Synapse Detection Method for Cerebellar Connectomics
sum: Finding every synapse in a 3D brain picture is still harder than tracing the cells. This method looks at touching pieces of known cerebellar cell types and asks two computer networks whether each touch is a real synapse, and whether it is excitatory or inhibitory.

t: Automated synapse-level reconstruction of neural circuits in the larval zebrafish brain
sum: The baby zebrafish brain is small enough to photograph entirely in an electron microscope, and the same fish can first be watched while it sees motion. This resource traces cells and synapses in that whole brain and works out a motion-processing circuit whose activity had already been recorded.

t: Connectomic comparison of mouse and human cortex
sum: Mouse and human cortices are built from similar parts, but the human version is far larger and has more inhibitory cells. This comparison of 3D electron-microscope wiring finds that pyramidal cells still get a similar mix of excitation and inhibition; what grows instead is a network of inhibitory cells talking mainly t

t: Connectomics and the neural basis of behaviour
sum: Fruit-fly brain maps are now being finished fast enough that biologists can look up a cell, see who it connects to, and tie that wiring to smell, navigation, or courtship. This review explains how those maps are made, what you can do with a reconstructed neuron, and why comparing several brains is the next step.

t: Connectomics of the Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe provides insight into conserved and novel principles of a memory acquisition network
sum: Octopuses learn using a brain area called the vertical lobe, whose wiring had never been mapped in detail. Electron-microscope reconstruction shows two kinds of small cells: a huge crowd that each hear from just one incoming cable, and a rarer type that listens more broadly and may sharpen the memory signal.

t: How innovations in methodology offer new prospects for volume electron microscopy
sum: Electron microscopes can show tissue in three dimensions at nanometer detail, but they used to be too slow for whole organs. This review explains newer, faster microscopes and warns that preparing samples, analyzing the pictures, and storing the data become the new traffic jams.

t: Multi-layered maps of neuropil with segmentation-guided contrastive learning
sum: Once a computer has colored in the cells in a 3D brain picture, it still does not know what part of a cell it is looking at or what cell type it is. This method learns a compact description of each snippet from the pictures themselves, so a few human labels can name parts and types even on very short broken pieces.

t: neuPrint: An open access tool for EM connectomics
sum: A wiring diagram with tens of millions of connections is useless to most scientists if they have to download a giant file. neuPrint is a website and programming interface that lets anyone ask ordinary biology questions of a connectome in a web browser.

t: Rapid reconstruction of neural circuits using tissue expansion and light sheet microscopy
sum: Electron microscopes map every synapse but too slowly to compare many animals. This method swells the tissue, photographs it with a light-sheet microscope, and counts synapses in chosen fly circuits fast enough to compare sex, experience, and behavior.

t: RoboEM: automated 3D flight tracing for synaptic-resolution connectomics
sum: Computers still lose thin axons in 3D electron-microscope volumes, so people spend huge effort correcting maps. RoboEM is a virtual pilot that flies along those axons from the pictures alone, fixing breaks cheaply enough that much of that human proofreading can be skipped.

t: The connectome of an insect brain
sum: This paper maps every neuron and synapse in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain. The wiring is highly recurrent, mixes the senses, and uses extra connection styles beyond the usual axon-to-dendrite pattern, especially in the learning center.

t: The neuropeptidergic connectome of C. elegans
sum: Worms—and likely all brains—send many messages not across tight synapses but as chemical broadcasts. This paper draws a first whole-animal map of those peptide signals and finds a dense, less hub-dominated network than the classic synaptic wiring diagram.

t: A connectomic study of a petascale fragment of human cerebral cortex
sum: A cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex was sliced thousands of times, photographed with a fast electron microscope, and reconstructed into a digital tissue with tens of thousands of cells and more than a hundred million synapses. Among many findings, glia outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many cont

t: A multiscale brain map derived from whole-brain volumetric reconstructions
sum: The worm’s central nerve bundle was thought to be a packed tangle of wires. Reconstructing it in 3D in two animals shows orderly neighborhoods, a shared core circuit, and extra connections that differ between individuals.

t: AxonEM Dataset: 3D Axon Instance Segmentation of Brain Cortical Regions
sum: Thin axons in cortex are among the hardest objects to color in automatically, and there was no big public test set. AxonEM hands the community two cubes of human and mouse cortex with more than 18,000 carefully checked axons so algorithms can be scored fairly.

t: Connectomes across development reveal principles of brain maturation
sum: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.

t: Connectomic features underlying diverse synaptic connection strengths and subcellular computation
sum: A wiring diagram says how many synapses two cells share, but not how strong the message feels. In the fly olfactory system, counting synapses and noting whether they sit on the dendrite or the axon predicts the electrical bump recorded at the cell body after one spike.

t: Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex
sum: A mouse watched movies while thousands of its visual-cortex cells lit up, and the same cubic millimeter was later reconstructed in an electron microscope with hundreds of millions of synapses. The public dataset lets anyone match those firing patterns to actual wiring.

t: Partial connectomes of labeled dopaminergic circuits reveal non-synaptic communication and axonal remodeling after exposure to cocaine
sum: Dopamine cables in the mouse reward center almost never make textbook synapses. They more often interleave with neighbors and, after a short cocaine exposure, sprout extra branches and swollen, mitochondria-packed endings.

t: Petascale neural circuit reconstruction: automated methods
sum: Photographing a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex on thousands of slices creates a mountain of images full of cracks and folds. This paper is the factory software that lines the slices up, finds cell borders and synapses, and glues fragments together in the cloud so people can browse an automated reconstruction.

t: PyTorch Connectomics: A Scalable and Flexible Segmentation Framework for EM Connectomics
sum: Computers must paint every pixel of a brain microscope volume before anyone can follow the wiring. This paper shares an open toolbox, PyTorch Connectomics, that trains those painting models on big three-dimensional images without rewriting code for each new dataset.

t: Structure and function of axo-axonic inhibition
sum: Some inhibitory cells grab the axon of a neighbor right where it starts its output spike. This paper maps those chandelier connections onto many visual-cortex pyramids in a mouse and shows the cells fire together when the animal is aroused.

t: A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain
sum: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.

t: A Connectome of the Adult Drosophila Central Brain
sum: This preprint announces a public wiring map of a large part of the adult fruit-fly central brain. It is the methods-and-data release that later companion papers analyze in more biological depth.

t: A connectome of the Drosophila central complex reveals network motifs suitable for flexible navigation and context-dependent action selection
sum: Flies steer, sleep, and navigate using a deep midline brain region called the central complex. This paper maps every neuron and chemical synapse in that region so the loops that could hold a heading and pick an action can be read from the wiring.

t: Combined membrane potential imaging and connectome of behavioral circuits in an annelid worm
sum: One leech motor neuron helps swimming, crawling, and a local escape bend without changing its wiring. This paper records the ganglion's activity, then traces that cell's incoming synapses in the electron microscope to see how the same anatomy supports different jobs.

t: Comparative Connectomics Reveals How Partner Identity, Location, and Activity Specify Synaptic Connectivity in Drosophila
sum: Developing fly neurons can still find their partners even if those partners sit in the wrong place or are quiet. This paper shows that getting the right number of connections, and therefore the right behavior, still depends on location and on activity during development.

t: Complete Connectomic Reconstruction of Olfactory Projection Neurons in the Fly Brain
sum: Smell information leaves the fly's antennal lobe on projection neurons headed for higher brain centers. This paper traces all of those cells in an electron-microscope whole brain and finds about twice as many as light microscopy had suggested.

t: Connectomics Analysis Reveals First-, Second-, and Third-Order Thermosensory and Hygrosensory Neurons in the Adult Drosophila Brain
sum: Flies sense heat, cold, and humidity with antenna cells that look a lot like smell cells. This paper traces those pathways through the brain and finds a temperature hub that even talks to the circadian clock.

t: FlyWire: Online community for whole-brain connectomics
sum: A whole fly brain is too big for one lab to correct by hand. FlyWire is a website where people anywhere can jointly fix an automated tracing and see one another's edits.

t: Information flow, cell types and stereotypy in a full olfactory connectome
sum: This paper turns the fly hemibrain wiring map into a full tour of the smell system, from sensors to cells that leave the brain. It also checks how similar those cells are in a second fly.

t: Massive Data Management and Sharing Module for Connectome Reconstruction
sum: Connectomics volumes are so large that just storing and fetching the pictures becomes its own problem. This paper describes a server and browser cache built so researchers can jump around huge electron-microscope stacks without waiting.

t: neuPrint: Analysis Tools for EM Connectomics
sum: A fly connectome is a huge list of cells and the synapses between them. neuPrint is a database and website that lets biologists ask graph questions of that list without writing a custom pipeline.

t: Neurotransmitter classification from electron microscopy images at synaptic sites in Drosophila melanogaster
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of fly synapses carry clues to which chemical a cell uses. This paper trains a network to guess six transmitters so wiring diagrams can be given plus and minus signs.

t: Permeabilization-free en bloc immunohistochemistry for correlative microscopy
sum: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot tell you which proteins a cell or synapse contains. This paper stains thick mouse brain slices without punching holes in membranes, so the same tissue can still be imaged in the electron microscope.

t: Reconstruction of motor control circuits in adult Drosophila using automated transmission electron microscopy
sum: The fly's ventral nerve cord is the analog of a spinal cord, running the legs and wings. This paper describes a tape-based electron-microscope pipeline that imaged a whole female cord and found a direct sensory shortcut onto big motor axons.

t: Recurrent architecture for adaptive regulation of learning in the insect brain
sum: Learning in the fly larva depends on dopamine cells that tell the mushroom body what was good or bad. This paper maps every neuron that talks to those dopamine cells and finds a thick web of feedback from the memory outputs themselves.

t: Structured sampling of olfactory input by the fly mushroom body
sum: Fly memory cells were thought to sample smells at random. This electron-microscope map finds that food-related smell channels share Kenyon cells more often than chance, as if the memory center spends extra resolution on meals.

t: Synaptic counts approximate synaptic contact area in Drosophila
sum: Connectome papers usually count synapses and treat bigger counts as stronger connections. This study checks that shortcut in the fly larva and finds that contact number does predict total contact area.

t: The connectome of the adult Drosophila mushroom body provides insights into function
sum: The fly mushroom body is the brain's famous learning center. This paper reads its complete wiring map and finds extra visual input, shortcuts to descending neurons, and feedback that could tell dopamine cells what has already been learned.

t: The connectome of the adult Drosophila mushroom body: implications for function
sum: This preprint is the mushroom-body wiring analysis later published in eLife: a complete look at how the fly learning center is hooked up, including vision, dopamine, and paths out to behavior.

t: The connectome predicts resting state functional connectivity across the Drosophila brain
sum: Does the fly's wiring diagram predict which brain regions rise and fall together at rest? This paper says yes, and that learning centers are even more in sync than their direct cables would suggest.

t: The Mind of a Mouse.
sum: Some scientific maps are valuable because they let people ask new questions for years. This Cell commentary argues that a synapse-level wiring diagram of a mouse brain would be that kind of map.

t: The natverse, a versatile toolbox for combining and analysing neuroanatomical data
sum: Fly brain maps now live in many different atlases and file formats. The natverse is a set of R tools that read those data, put them in one space, and compare shapes and connections without starting from scratch.

t: Whitening of odor representations by the wiring diagram of the olfactory bulb
sum: The olfactory bulb cleans up overlapping smell patterns so they are easier to tell apart—a step called whitening. This zebrafish study pairs recordings with a complete electron-microscope wiring map and finds the trick in extra inhibition between cells that like the same odors.

t: Whole-animal connectome and cell-type complement of the three-segmented Platynereis dumerilii larva
sum: This paper maps every cell in a three-segment marine worm larva, nerves and non-nerves alike. The wiring shows how sensors can reach cilia, glands, pigment, and muscle throughout the body.

t: A Genetic Model of the Connectome
sum: If genes tell neurons whom to connect to, the wiring diagram should contain a telltale pattern: two groups of cells in which everyone on one side talks to everyone on the other. This paper finds those patterns in worm, sea squirt, and fly-larva maps.

t: A petascale automated imaging pipeline for mapping neuronal circuits with high-throughput transmission electron microscopy
sum: Taking electron-microscope pictures of a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex used to be out of reach. This team ran six automated transmission microscopes around the clock and finished that volume in under six months.

t: Big data in nanoscale connectomics, and the greed for training labels.
sum: Brain electron-microscope datasets are enormous, yet the computers that trace them still need people to label lots of examples. This review says that mismatch is a central obstacle on the way to a human connectome.

t: Constraining computational models using electron microscopy wiring diagrams.
sum: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as having a working theory of what the circuit computes. This review asks how to put electron-microscope connection maps into the models theorists already use.

t: Convolutional nets for reconstructing neural circuits from brain images acquired by serial section electron microscopy
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are still often pieced into circuits by people, a slow job. This review explains how convolutional neural networks now trace cells, find synapses, and line up serial images—and why messy images remain hard.

t: DVID: Distributed Versioned Image-Oriented Dataservice
sum: Huge electron-microscope brain maps are hard to share and edit as a team. This paper describes DVID, software that versions those maps like git versions code, so people can branch, proofread, and merge changes.

t: En bloc preparation of Drosophila brains enables high-throughput FIB-SEM connectomics
sum: To map an entire fruit-fly nervous system, the brain and cord must be dissected, stained, and imaged as one piece. This methods paper shows how to prepare that specimen so a FIB-SEM microscope can collect synapse-ready images much faster than before.

t: Large Scale Image Segmentation with Structured Loss Based Deep Learning for Connectome Reconstruction
sum: Mapping neurons in electron-microscope volumes means deciding which voxels belong to which cell. This paper trains a 3D neural net to score how voxels should stick together, then groups them with a simple rule, and reports large accuracy gains on several datasets.

t: Structure and function of a neocortical synapse
sum: Connectomes show which nerve cells touch, but not how strong each contact is. This study records from connected mouse cortical cells and then images those same synapses, finding that bigger contacts are stronger and that each synapse likely has several release sites.

t: Synaptic Partner Assignment Using Attentional Voxel Association Networks
sum: After a synapse’s gap is found in an electron-microscope image, a computer still has to say which two cells meet there. This paper trains a network that, given the gap, paints the voxels of the sending and receiving partners.

t: UNI-EM: An Environment for Deep Neural Network-Based Automated Segmentation of Neuronal Electron Microscopic Images
sum: Cutting-edge neuron-tracing networks are usually locked behind Python and specialist software. UNI-EM packages those tools into a desktop environment so biologists can train and check segmentations without writing code.

t: Whole-animal connectomes of both Caenorhabditis elegans sexes
sum: The roundworm C. elegans has a tiny nervous system that can be mapped cell by cell in both sexes. This paper updates those maps and shows that males and hermaphrodites share many cells but wire them differently.

t: A Pipeline for Volume Electron Microscopy of the Caenorhabditis elegans Nervous System
sum: The first complete wiring diagram of an animal was traced by hand in a tiny worm decades ago. This methods paper explains a modern volume-electron-microscopy pipeline for making new worm maps faster and for asking how wiring changes with age, sex, and experience.

t: Cross-Classification Clustering: An Efficient Multi-Object Tracking Technique for 3-D Instance Segmentation in Connectomics
sum: Following every nerve fiber through a stack of microscope images usually means chasing one cell at a time. This computer-vision paper instead classifies all cells at once with a clever combination of a few labels, which is much cheaper to compute.

t: Dense connectomic reconstruction in layer 4 of the somatosensory cortex
sum: Mammalian cortex is packed so tightly that mapping every wire and synapse in even a small block has been nearly impossible. This study reconstructs a much larger piece of mouse barrel cortex than before and reads cell types and possible learning traces from the wiring alone.

t: Multi-Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy for High-Throughput Imaging in Connectomics Research
sum: Scanning electron microscopes usually look at one tiny patch at a time, which makes big brain volumes slow to image. This short review explains multi-beam SEM and related volume methods that are meant to photograph much larger pieces of tissue.

t: NeuTu: Software for Collaborative, Large-Scale, Segmentation-Based Connectome Reconstruction
sum: After a computer carves an electron-microscope volume into candidate neurons, people still have to fix mistakes in objects that can be enormous. NeuTu is a collaborative 3D editor, built on the DVID database, for doing that on whole fly-brain datasets.

t: Of what use is connectomics? A personal perspective on the Drosophila connectome
sum: Fruit flies are small enough that every synapse in the brain can, in principle, be listed. This essay argues why that list is worth the remaining proofreading grind: it lets us turn identified cells on and off and watch behavior change.

t: Synaptic Cleft Segmentation in Non-Isotropic Volume Electron Microscopy of the Complete Drosophila Brain
sum: Finding every synapse in a fruit-fly brain imaged as thin, stretched slices is harder than in cube-shaped vertebrate volumes. This paper trains a 3D network on the shape of synaptic clefts and runs it over an entire adult fly brain in days.

t: VAST (Volume Annotation and Segmentation Tool): Efficient Manual and Semi-Automatic Labeling of Large 3D Image Stacks
sum: Giant electron-microscope stacks are useless if you cannot paint and correct labels inside them. VAST is a relatively simple desktop tool for coloring cells in very large 3D images, including using a computer’s draft segmentation as a stencil.

t: Verifying, Challenging, and Discovering New Synapses Among Fully EM-Reconstructed Neurons in the Leech Ganglion
sum: Leeches have repeating packets of identified neurons whose connections were first mapped with electrodes. This study images a whole ganglion in the electron microscope, checks those old connections, and uses the map to find a new synapse that still works when recorded in another animal.

t: A Complete Electron Microscopy Volume of the Brain of Adult Drosophila melanogaster
sum: A fruit-fly brain is small enough to photograph entirely in the electron microscope, but that had not been done. This paper releases that whole-brain volume and uses the mushroom body—the fly’s learning center—to show that new cell types and tighter input clusters appear once synapses are visible.

t: A connectome of a learning and memory center in the adult Drosophila brain
sum: Flies store associations in a brain region called the mushroom body. This paper traces every neuron in part of that region and finds extra synapse types—including from teaching cells straight onto output cells—that textbooks had not drawn.

t: An Error Detection and Correction Framework for Connectomics
sum: Once a computer has drawn draft neurons in an electron-microscope volume, someone still has to find the remaining cuts and accidental joins. This paper trains networks that both highlight those mistakes and propose a cleaned-up cell shape.

t: Automated synaptic connectivity inference for volume electron microscopy
sum: Electron-microscope volumes are now huge, but turning traced cells into a table of synapses, cell parts, and cell types still eats years. SyConn is software that fills in those labels automatically and is used here to read wiring in a songbird brain region.

t: Conserved neural circuit structure across Drosophila larval development revealed by comparative connectomics
sum: A maggot’s body grows enormously, yet its nerve cells must keep reporting touch and pain in the right place. This study compares the same identified circuit in a young and an older larva and finds the wiring pattern stays the same even as cells get much larger.

t: EM connectomics reveals axonal target variation in a sequence-generating network
sum: Songbirds sing with clock-like timing from a brain area called HVC. This study follows the timing cells’ axons in the electron microscope and finds they inhibit neighbors locally but excite other timing cells farther away—wiring that could carry a wave of song.

t: Enhanced FIB-SEM systems for large-volume 3D imaging
sum: A focused ion beam can shave a sample one thin layer at a time while a scanning electron microscope photographs each new face, giving sharp 3D pictures. This paper shows how to keep that process running for months so the pictures cover volumes useful for tracing neurons.

t: High-precision automated reconstruction of neurons with flood-filling networks
sum: Computers that trace neurons in electron-microscope images usually still make enough mistakes that people spend months fixing them. Flood-filling networks follow one fiber at a time and, in songbird tissue, go more than a millimeter between mistakes.

t: Learning from connectomics on the fly.
sum: Fruit-fly neuroscience suddenly has both genetic remote controls and electron-microscope wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together—and how long a full adult-brain connectome will take if computers, not only people, do the tracing.

t: SynEM, automated synapse detection for connectomics
sum: A speck of cortex contains enormous numbers of synapses, too many to click by hand once the wires are traced. SynEM is a program that looks at each place two processes touch and decides whether it is a real synapse, without a person in the loop.

t: The complete connectome of a learning and memory centre in an insect brain
sum: Young fruit-fly maggots already learn to like or avoid odors using a brain structure called the mushroom body. This paper traces every synapse in that structure and finds both random mixing of odor inputs and extra loops among the cells that teach and remember.

t: webKnossos: efficient online 3D data annotation for connectomics
sum: Tracing nerve fibers in 3D microscope data is usually done with clunky desktop software. webKnossos lets people fly through the volume in a browser, and trained tracers move several times faster than with earlier tools.

t: 3-dimensional electron microscopic imaging of the zebrafish olfactory bulb and dense reconstruction of neurons
sum: The nose-brain of a baby zebrafish is small enough that almost every neuron can be traced in an electron-microscope stack. This data paper releases those pictures and 1,022 cell skeletons, plus software to browse them.

t: Anatomy and function of an excitatory network in the visual cortex
sum: In mouse visual cortex, nerve cells that like the same line orientation tend to talk to each other. This team imaged those cells while they were alive, then used electron microscopy to show that the preference is built into the wiring, not just into which axons happen to pass nearby.

t: Fully-Automatic Synapse Prediction and Validation on a Large Data Set
sum: After computers learned to outline fly neurons in electron-microscope images, finding the actual synapses became the slow step. This paper automates that step for fruit-fly connections, where one sending site often talks to several partners at once.

t: Patterns and distribution of presynaptic and postsynaptic elements within serial electron microscopic reconstructions of neuronal arbors from the medicinal leech Hirudo verbana
sum: Leech nerve cells were long too tangled to map in full with electron microscopy. This team imaged adult and juvenile ganglia in 3D and found that some cells keep incoming and outgoing contacts in separate neighborhoods, while others mix them, and none were outgoing-only.

t: Progress Towards Mammalian Whole-Brain Cellular Connectomics
sum: We still do not have a complete wiring diagram of any mammal’s brain. This perspective argues that sample preparation and electron microscopy have improved enough to try mapping a small mammalian brain end to end.

t: The CNS connectome of a tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis (L.) highlights sidedness in the brain of a chordate sibling
sum: A sea-squirt tadpole has a tiny chordate brain that is visibly lopsided. This paper maps every chemical and electrical connection among its 177 central neurons and shows that the two sides are not mirror images, even when cell counts match.

t: The wiring diagram of a glomerular olfactory system
sum: Fruit-fly larvae smell with a miniature version of the same glomerular layout used in our olfactory bulb. This preprint maps every connection in that first smell center and suggests two parallel paths: one that copies each odor channel onward, and another that mixes channels and can switch how strongly they compete.

t: Challenges of microtome‐based serial block‐face scanning electron microscopy in neuroscience
sum: To map every connection in a tangle of brain cells you need 3D electron microscopy, not ordinary light pictures. This review explains how a diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope can shave and image a tissue block, and why the resulting data piles are so hard to analyze.

t: Extracellular space preservation aids the connectomic analysis of neural circuits
sum: Brain tissue usually collapses when it is chemically fixed, so nerve-cell membranes stick together and computers merge the wrong cells. This paper keeps a little space between cells on purpose, which makes automatic tracing easier and also helps antibodies and gap-junction synapses show up.

t: Large-volume en-bloc staining for electron microscopy-based connectomics
sum: Electron-microscope stains often fail to reach the middle of a large piece of brain, so only tiny blocks could be mapped. This paper describes a faster way to stain mouse cortex all the way through a millimeter-wide chunk so every wire can be seen.

t: Quantitative neuroanatomy for connectomics in Drosophila
sum: When people trace fly neurons in electron-microscope stacks, most mistakes are missing tiny side branches, not the main trunk. This paper shows that strong connections usually use many of those twigs, so a careful, anatomy-aware tracing method can skip doing the same cell three times.

t: Saturated Reconstruction of a Volume of Neocortex
sum: This team used a tape-collection electron-microscope pipeline to catalog every cell process and 1,700 synapses in a bit of mouse cortex. They show that an axon sitting next to a spine is not enough to predict a connection—cells seem choosier than that.

t: Ultrastructurally-smooth thick partitioning and volume stitching for larger-scale connectomics
sum: The best 3D electron microscopes can shave tissue only a few nanometers at a time, so big samples have to be cut into slabs first. This paper shows how to make those slabs about 20 micrometers thick with a heated knife and then digitally glue the pictures back into one volume.

t: A mesoscale connectome of the mouse brain
sum: This project traces outgoing axons from many starting points in the mouse brain and lines all the experiments up in one 3D map. The result is a public wiring atlas of regional connections, not a synapse-by-synapse diagram.

t: Neuronal connectome of a sensory-motor circuit for visual navigation
sum: A marine worm larva has four simple eyes and can swim toward or away from light. This paper maps the 71 nerve cells from those eyes to the swimming muscles and shows the animal compares brightness on the two sides of its body.

t: Space-time wiring specificity supports direction selectivity in the retina
sum: How the eye spots movement has been a puzzle for decades. Volunteers on EyeWire helped trace starburst cells and bipolar cells, and the wiring pattern looks like a delay line: some inputs arrive farther out on the branch and earlier in time, which can make the branch prefer motion away from the cell body.

t: The natverse: a versatile computational toolbox to combine and analyse neuroanatomical data
sum: Fly brain maps now come from many labs and many microscopes, which makes comparing neurons a hassle. This software collection in R lines those maps up in shared templates so you can analyze shape and connections together.

t: A visual motion detection circuit suggested by Drosophila connectomics
sum: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.

t: Cellular-resolution connectomics: challenges of dense neural circuit reconstruction
sum: Taking the pictures for a brain wiring map is getting easier; turning those pictures into a list of who talks to whom is the hard part. This perspective explains why tracing densely packed neurons at cellular resolution is so demanding and how crowds and machine learning were being used to catch up.

t: Connectomic reconstruction of the inner plexiform layer in the mouse retina
sum: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.

t: From the connectome to brain function
sum: A complete list of who is connected to whom is not enough to know what a nervous system will do. This perspective uses well-mapped small animal circuits—and the retina—to argue that timing, chemical modulators, and spare parallel pathways also matter.

t: The Rich Club of the C. elegans Neuronal Connectome
sum: In the worm’s tiny nervous system, a handful of highly connected cells form a “rich club” that other cells use as a shortcut. Those club members are mostly the command cells for crawling, and they appear early in development.

t: TrakEM2 Software for Neural Circuit Reconstruction
sum: Huge stacks of electron-microscope pictures are useless until someone traces the cells. TrakEM2 is a free program that stitches those pictures, lets people draw neurons and synapses, and exports a 3D wiring sketch.

t: Volume electron microscopy for neuronal circuit reconstruction.
sum: Scientists now have several ways to take 3D electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue, each with different speed and sharpness. This review says those pictures can give a wiring diagram, but you still need other tools—genes, light, and electrical recordings—to understand what the circuit does.

t: High-accuracy neurite reconstruction for high-throughput neuroanatomy
sum: When every nerve fiber is stained, even experts mix up branches. This paper has people quickly draw stick-figure traces of the same cell several times, then a statistical method (RESCOP) votes out the mistakes much faster than painting every voxel.

t: Network anatomy and in vivo physiology of visual cortical neurons
sum: Researchers first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to oriented bars, then traced some of their connections in electron-microscope slices. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors that preferred many different orientations, which may help explain why those inhibitory cells are less picky.

t: Wiring specificity in the direction-selectivity circuit of the retina
sum: Some retinal cells fire only when a spot moves one way. This paper shows that starburst cells wire most strongly onto those motion cells along the opposite, “null” direction, which can shut them down when motion goes the wrong way.

t: Ultrastructural analysis of hippocampal neuropil from the connectomics perspective
sum: In a bit of rat hippocampus, this team outlined every nearby axon and dendrite in electron-microscope slices. Simply sitting next to each other does not mean two cells are connected; you still need the synapse’s fine structure to tell a real contact from a near miss.

t: Structural Properties of the Caenorhabditis elegans Neuronal Network
sum: The worm’s wiring list had gaps and inconsistencies. This paper rebuilds a coherent map of chemical synapses and gap junctions for the hermaphrodite and then asks what the network’s shape can tell us about signal flow and behavior.

t: Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy to Reconstruct Three-Dimensional Tissue Nanostructure
sum: This paper shows how to put a tiny diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope so the machine can shave a stained tissue block and photograph each new face automatically. The resulting 3D stack is sharp enough to follow the thinnest nerve fibers and see synapses.

t: The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: This classic monograph maps every nerve cell in a tiny roundworm—302 of them—and lists how they connect with chemical synapses, muscle junctions, and electrical gap junctions. It is the original whole-animal wiring diagram.

t: ConnectomeBench2: A Unified Benchmark for Automated Connectomic Proofreading
sum: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps still takes huge amounts of human time. This team released a shared test set from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly brains and showed that one vision model can match people on many of those fixes.

t: Connectomic Analysis of Mitochondria in the Central Brain of Drosophila
sum: Connectome pictures of the fly brain also show mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories. This team catalogued millions of them, found that different neuron types place and size them differently, and put the catalog online so others can search it.

t: Convergence-divergence circuits for multimodal integration of innate and learned opponent valences
sum: Fruit flies must decide what is good or bad in a messy world, not just in a simple lab smell. This study uses a whole-brain wiring map to argue that a region called the superior protocerebrum mixes inborn and learned likes and dislikes before sending a compact signal onward.

t: DRIFT-EM enables direct wafer retrieval of ultrathin serial sections for large-volume electron microscopy
sum: Making a big electron-microscope map of a brain requires collecting thousands of extremely thin slices, which usually needs expensive special gear. This team shows a cheaper way to float those slices onto silicon wafers using ordinary static ionizers, 3D-printed parts, and open software.

t: Organization of circuits linking descending input to motor output in the Drosophila Male Adult Nerve Cord connectome
sum: To move, a fly’s brain must talk to motor neurons in the nerve cord, but those paths are hard to see. Using a complete male nerve-cord wiring map, this team shows that brain cells rarely plug straight into muscles and instead work through communities that look like walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control.

t: Organizational principles governing synapse types in a whole-brain connectome
sum: Textbooks say dendrites take messages in and axons send them out, but many neurons mix both on the same branches. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this team shows that mixed wiring is common, follows simple complexity rules, and often makes two-way connections.

t: Comparative connectomics of Drosophila descending and ascending neurons
sum: A fly’s brain and body are linked by a thin neck cable of neurons that send commands down and senses back up. This Nature paper stitches three electron-microscope maps to finish that cable in the female, compare it with the male, and tie many cell types to genetic tools used in experiments.

t: Connectome-driven neural inventory of a complete visual system
sum: Half of a fly’s brain is for seeing, with an enormous variety of cell types. This team mapped the right visual lobe of a male fruit fly in an electron microscope, named hundreds of types—many for the first time—and matched them to genetic tools so labs can turn those cells on and off.

t: Light-microscopy-based connectomic reconstruction of mammalian brain tissue
sum: Electron microscopes can map every connection, but they do not easily show which molecules sit at those connections. This team expands brain tissue in a gel, images it with light, and uses machine learning to trace cells and synapses while keeping molecular labels.

t: Building and Integrating Brain-Wide Maps of Nervous System Function in Invertebrates
sum: For tiny animals like worms and fruit flies, scientists can now record almost the whole brain while the animal moves, and they also have wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together so we can explain real behavior, not just one circuit at a time.

t: EM and XRM Connectomics Imaging and Experimental Metadata Standards
sum: Giant microscope maps of brains are hard to compare if every lab describes the experiment differently. This working-group paper proposes shared labels for how electron-microscope and X-ray volumes were made, so the files can be found, combined, and reused.

t: NeuroSC: Exploring Neurodevelopment via Spatiotemporal Collation of Anatomical Networks
sum: Worm brains have been mapped at several ages, but the tables of who touches whom are hard to browse. This team built a website that lets you jump from a simplified graph of neuron relationships down to the actual cell contacts that change as the worm grows.

t: Serotonergic modulation of swallowing in a complete fly vagus nerve connectome
sum: Swallowing is the moment food is truly taken in, but how the gut tells the brain ‘that worked’ is usually guessed, not wired out. Using a whole-larva fly electron-microscope map, this team finds stretch sensors in the esophagus that talk to six serotonin cells, which then boost the motor neurons that swallow.

t: WASPSYN: A Challenge for Domain Adaptive Synapse Detection in Microwasp Brain Connectomes
sum: Computers that find synapses in brain pictures often fail when the next sample was prepared a little differently. This team labeled synapses in tiny wasp brains from three different datasets and ran a public contest so methods can be compared fairly when the pictures change.

t: A complete reconstruction of the early visual system of an adult insect.
sum: Some tiny wasps have very small eyes but can still fly, which makes them a good place to look for the simplest flying visual circuit. This paper maps one such wasp’s eye and the first brain station behind it, finding only 29 facets per eye and six cell types in that first station.

t: A Novel Semi-automated Proofreading and Mesh Error Detection Pipeline for Neuron Extension
sum: When a computer map of a neuron is cut off too early, many of that cell’s connections are missing. This team looks at the shape of those dead ends, points proofreaders at the likely breaks, and shows that people fix mistakes faster when they are pointed in the right direction.

t: Cyclic structure with cellular precision in a vertebrate sensorimotor neural circuit
sum: Worm wiring is often described as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish eye-movement circuit, this team instead finds many three-cell loops, including loops that return to the same cell, which may help the brain hold a signal over time.

t: Data-driven motif discovery in biological neural networks
sum: Scientists want to know which small wiring patterns repeat in a brain map, but each map is usually one of a kind and too big to search blindly. This team offers a method and open software to find those patterns in a single connectome and to test whether they are really unusual.

t: Learning to Correct Sloppy Annotations in Electron Microscopy Volumes
sum: Drawing every neuron perfectly in electron-microscope pictures is slow, so people often sketch roughly. This team trains a network to tidy those sloppy sketches into accurate shapes, cutting tracing time on several examples and even working from blurrier, lower-resolution pictures.

t: Virtual Fly Brain—An interactive atlas of the Drosophila nervous system
sum: Fly neuroscience now has wiring maps, gene-expression maps, and thousands of pictures of labeled neurons, but they live in different websites. Virtual Fly Brain puts those layers on shared 3D templates so you can click a cell, see what it connects to, and find genetic tools that target it.

t: Edge-colored directed subgraph enumeration on the connectome
sum: Once a brain map is a network of cells and connections, you can count every small repeating pattern, including whether a connection is a ‘go’ or ‘stop’ type. This team did that counting at huge scale on eleven wiring diagrams and posted the catalogs so others can look for unexpected motifs.

t: Hierarchical Modular Structure of the Drosophila Connectome
sum: A fly hemibrain wiring map is so big that it is hard to see the natural groups of cells. This team uses a clustering method that looks at many zoom levels and finds nested communities, including known sensory paths and a layered navigation center, plus some new groupings.

t: Igneous: Distributed dense 3D segmentation meshing, neuron skeletonization, and hierarchical downsampling
sum: Once a computer has colored in every cell in a giant brain picture, you still need 3D surfaces and stick-figure skeletons to look at and analyze those cells. Igneous is open software that builds those objects in bulk on a computing cluster or in the cloud.

t: Imaging whole-brain activity to understand behavior
sum: To understand real behavior, it helps to watch almost every brain cell while an animal moves, not just a few cells in a dish. This review explains how that is now possible in worms, flies, and young fish, and why theories must include both the wiring diagram and the animal’s changing actions.

t: Joint reconstruction of neuron and ultrastructure via connectivity consensus in electron microscope volumes
sum: Computers usually color neurons and their inner parts as separate jobs, even though a mitochondrion should not jump between two cells. This paper ties those jobs together so membrane and organelle clues vote in one step, which they say makes the neuron maps more accurate.

t: NeuronBridge: an intuitive web application for neuronal morphology search across large data sets
sum: If you find an interesting cell in a fly electron-microscope map, you still need a genetic tool that lights up that cell. NeuronBridge is a website that searches light-microscope pictures of fly driver lines to find shapes that look like your cell.

t: Scalable graph analysis tools for the connectomics community
sum: Modern wiring diagrams are too big to hold in a normal computer’s memory, and they live in different databases. This team shares a set of open tools so scientists can search for repeated connection patterns across those huge graphs without building a new system each time.

t: SyConn2: dense synaptic connectivity inference for volume electron microscopy
sum: After cells in an electron-microscope volume are colored in, someone still has to find the synapses and ask which cell types they belong to. SyConn2 is open software that does that bookkeeping at large scale, including on songbird brain data with more than ten million synapses.

t: Towards a Comprehensive Optical Connectome at Single Synapse Resolution via Expansion Microscopy
sum: Electron microscopes can see every synapse but not easily the molecules in them, and they are slow. This review surveys dyes and genetic tags that still work after brain tissue is swollen in a gel, so ordinary light microscopes might map connections with molecular color.

t: A scalable and modular automated pipeline for stitching of large electron microscopy datasets
sum: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged at synapse scale is more than a million gigabytes of overlapping snapshots that must be sewn into one volume. This team’s ASAP software stitches and aligns those pictures as fast as the microscope can take them, using a database of positions instead of rewriting every image at each st

t: Circuits for integrating learned and innate valences in the insect brain
sum: Fruit-fly larvae have one brain area for inborn likes and dislikes and another for learned ones. This study maps how those two systems meet, and shows that some meeting-point cells control turning when an odor is attractive.

t: CONFIRMS: A Toolkit for Scalable, Black Box Connectome Assessment and Investigation
sum: Huge automated brain maps can hide tracing mistakes that ruin the wiring list. This paper offers free software to spot-check a finished map with people and with graph tests, instead of rechecking every cell.

t: Neural architectures in the light of comparative connectomics
sum: Most detailed wiring maps come from a handful of animals. This essay argues we should map more species so we can tell which circuit designs are ancient body-plan features and which evolved more than once.

t: Three-Dimensional Structure of Dendritic Spines Revealed by Volume Electron Microscopy Techniques
sum: Tiny bumps on brain-cell branches are where many connections sit, but their true 3D shape is only clear in electron-microscope stacks. This review gathers what those 3D pictures have shown about how the bumps are built and how they change with activity.

t: VICE: Visual Identification and Correction of Neural Circuit Errors
sum: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope stacks still glue or split big cells. This tool points people at likely wiring mistakes around one cell at a time, with 3D views, so they do not have to hunt through the whole volume pixel by pixel.

t: Accelerated EM Connectome Reconstruction using 3D Visualization and Segmentation Graphs
sum: After a computer paints neurons in a giant 3D brain picture, people still must glue pieces and cut wrongly joined blobs. This preprint describes a 3D editor that uses the computer's own confidence scores to speed those cuts and joins.

t: DotMotif: an open-source tool for connectome subgraph isomorphism search and graph queries
sum: A finished wiring diagram is a huge list of who talks to whom. This software lets scientists ask, in almost plain language, 'find me this little wiring pattern' across those giant lists.

t: Light microscopy based approach for mapping connectivity with molecular specificity
sum: Electron microscopes see connections but often lose the name tags that say which cell type is which. These authors expand tissue and paint cells many colors so a light microscope can both name cells and guess where they touch.

t: Toward a scalable framework for reproducible processing of volumetric, nanoscale neuroimaging datasets
sum: Brain pictures at synapse scale are so large that many labs cannot even run the analysis software. This paper packages those programs so they can be rerun the same way on big computers, with recipes for electron-microscope wiring maps and X-ray cell counts.

t: Biologically-Constrained Graphs for Global Connectomics Reconstruction
sum: Computers tracing brain cells often cut one cell into many pieces to avoid gluing two cells together. This method looks at cell shape across the whole volume and decides which pieces to join, using rules inspired by how neurons actually look.

t: Enabling FIB-SEM Systems for Large Volume Connectomics and Cell Biology
sum: A microscope that shaves tissue a few nanometers at a time makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to break down after days. This work keeps it running for months to years so much larger fly-brain pieces can be photographed at even detail in every direction.

t: A resource for the Drosophila antennal lobe provided by the connectome of glomerulus VA1v
sum: One smell-processing bead in a fruit-fly antenna brain was mapped so every connection inside it is listed, including hard-to-trace local cells. The map is meant as a recipe for the rest of the smell center.

t: Analyzing Image Segmentation for Connectomics
sum: Scoreboards that grade computer tracings of brain pictures often ignore whether the wiring list is still right. This paper adds tests that ask whether connections survive, and software to run those tests on bigger volumes.

t: Convergence of monosynaptic and polysynaptic sensory paths onto common motor outputs in a Drosophila feeding connectome
sum: A young fruit fly must eat using sensors in the gut, mouth, and skin that all talk to pumping muscles and hormone cells. This map shows some sensors plug straight into those outputs while other routes wander through extra cells, including a learning center.

t: A Multicore Path to Connectomics-on-Demand
sum: Many people assume mapping a brain from electron-microscope movies needs a warehouse of computers. These authors show that careful programming on one ordinary many-core machine can keep up with the microscope's flood of pictures.

t: Guided Proofreading of Automatic Segmentations for Connectomics
sum: People who fix computer tracings of brain cells spend most of their time just finding the mistakes. This method has a network suggest likely cuts and joins so a person mostly answers yes or no.

t: Micro-connectomics: probing the organization of neuronal networks at the cellular scale
sum: Scientists can now list which tiny brain cells connect in small animals and in bits of larger brains. This review asks whether those wiring patterns look like a compromise between saving biological resources and doing useful computations.

t: Scalable Interactive Visualization for Connectomics
sum: Petabyte electron-microscope stacks are hard even to open, let alone to edit and graph. This paper describes shared plumbing and web tools so people can browse, fix, and analyze those stacks without rewriting the storage layer each time.

t: Synaptic and peptidergic connectome of a neurosecretory center in the annelid brain
sum: Some brain centers talk more with secreted chemical messages than with classic synapses. In a marine worm larva, researchers listed those cells, their few synapses, and which peptide signals they could send and receive.

t: The comprehensive connectome of a neural substrate for ‘ON’ motion detection in Drosophila
sum: How a fly's eye tells which way something moves has been modeled for decades without a full parts list. This paper traces every input onto the key motion-sensing cells and finds wiring that could support more than one classic model.

t: Toward Streaming Synapse Detection with Compositional ConvNets
sum: Finding the contact points between brain cells is slower than tracing the cells themselves. This method teaches small networks to see membranes, gaps, and little packets separately, then combines those clues with simple biological rules so a regular computer can finish a large mouse-cortex volume in hours.

t: A Multi-Pass Approach to Large-Scale Connectomics
sum: Electron microscopes can now photograph brain tissue faster than ordinary analysis software can keep up. This preprint describes a two-speed computer pipeline: a quick first look, then a slower cleanup, so a single lab machine can finish a large published volume in hours.

t: Connectome studies on Drosophila: a short perspective on a tiny brain
sum: Fruit-fly brains are small enough that a full wiring list is becoming thinkable. This short essay explains why electron-microscope synapses, not just which cells sit near each other, are what you need to guess how the fly computes.

t: Flood-Filling Networks
sum: Usual computer programs first find cell edges and then flood-fill the insides as a separate step. This network grows each cell from the raw 3D picture in one learned loop, aiming to trace tangled brain wires more accurately.

t: From Cajal to Connectome and Beyond.
sum: A wiring list of the brain can mean very different things: regions, cell types, single cells, or actual synapses. This review walks through that ladder of detail from classical anatomy to electron microscopy and asks how to turn the flood of maps into understanding.

t: FusionNet: A Deep Fully Residual Convolutional Neural Network for Image Segmentation in Connectomics
sum: Computers must outline every cell in electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue. This network uses extra residual shortcuts so a very deep model can still learn, and the authors test it on drawing cell membranes and nuclei.

t: Registering large volume serial-section electron microscopy image sets for neural circuit reconstruction using FFT signal whitening
sum: Thousands of ultra-thin electron-microscope slices must be stacked so the same wires line up. This method tunes the matching process to be less fooled by changing tissue patterns, then looks through several slices at once so the stack stays smooth.

t: RhoanaNet Pipeline: Dense Automatic Neural Annotation
sum: Tracing every wire in a cubic millimeter of mouse brain by hand would be impractical. This updated software pipeline paints membranes with a modern network, glues slices into 3D cells, and publishes the test pictures so other labs can compare.

t: The Multilayer Connectome of Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: The worm's famous wiring diagram lists synapses, but cells also broadcast chemical messages that never use those contacts. This paper sketches those wireless monoamine and peptide networks and where they plug into the wired circuit.

t: A cellular and regulatory map of the cholinergic nervous system of C. elegans
sum: The worm wiring diagram says who touches whom, but not what chemical each cell uses. This study finds that acetylcholine is the most common messenger, maps every cell that uses it in both sexes, and names genes that turn that identity on.

t: A serial multiplex immunogold labeling method for identifying peptidergic neurons in connectomes
sum: Connectome maps show which neurons touch, but they usually do not say what chemical messengers those cells use. This paper tags neuropeptides with gold particles on just a few electron-microscope slices so the same cells can be followed through a whole larval worm.

t: Crowdsourcing the creation of image segmentation algorithms for connectomics
sum: Computers still struggle to outline every nerve fiber in electron-microscope pictures of brain. This group ran the first public contest for that 2D outlining task, and a deep-learning team with no prior electron-microscopy experience won.

t: Inter-individual stereotypy of the Platynereis larval visual connectome
sum: Scientists had mapped the visual wiring of one marine-worm larva and wondered whether the next animal would match. A second whole-body electron-microscope volume shows the same cell types, paths, and even some left–right wiring quirks.

t: A Context-Aware Delayed Agglomeration Framework for Electron Microscopy Segmentation
sum: Automatic neuron tracing often glues the wrong bits together, especially when mitochondria and nerve fibers look similar. This method sorts those bits into biological categories first and waits on shaky merge decisions, which the authors say cuts later human cleanup.

t: An automated images-to-graphs framework for high resolution connectomics
sum: Electron-microscope stacks of brain can in principle become wiring diagrams, but most software only solves one step, such as coloring cells or finding synapses. This paper strings those steps into a fully automatic pipeline that outputs a graph and scores how good that graph is.

t: Annotating Synapses in Large EM Datasets
sum: Finding every synapse in a large electron-microscope volume can take years if people scan every slice. This team has a computer guess the presynaptic T-bars in fly medulla and then asks humans to check them and mark partners, finishing a seven-column volume in months rather than years.

t: Design and Evaluation of Interactive Proofreading Tools for Connectomics
sum: Computers outline cells in electron-microscope stacks, but people still have to fix many mistakes. This paper builds two correction tools—one on the desktop, one in a web browser—and finds that non-experts fix more errors with the web tool in the same amount of time.

t: Graph-based active learning of agglomeration (GALA): a Python library to segment 2D and 3D neuroimages
sum: Automatic coloring of neurons in electron-microscope volumes still makes many mistakes, and people usually have to look at every pixel to find them. This Python library both improves the automatic coloring and highlights the spots most likely to be wrong.

t: The big data challenges of connectomics
sum: Brain wiring maps are starting to produce enormous computer files, more like genome projects than like classic microscope papers. This commentary argues that storing and turning those pictures into searchable maps is now harder than taking the pictures.

t: Toward large-scale connectome reconstructions.
sum: A few tiny circuits have been wired out by hand, but that pace cannot reach a whole brain. This review lists the imaging, synapse-finding, uncertainty-tracking, and analysis changes needed before large connectomes become routine.

t: ConnectomeExplorer: Query-Guided Visual Analysis of Large Volumetric Neuroscience Data
sum: A terabyte of brain electron-microscope data is too big to explore by scrolling around. This software lets neuroscientists build questions step by step and see the answers on the real volume, the colored cells, and the wiring at once.

t: Large-Scale Automatic Reconstruction of Neuronal Processes from Electron Microscopy Images
sum: Huge electron-microscope stacks of brain are now easy to take but hard to turn into 3D cell shapes. This pipeline learns from a few human scribbles, proposes outlines on each slice, glues them into 3D objects, and offers a tool to fix leftover merges.

t: Why not connectomics?
sum: Some scientists think mapping every synapse is a bad investment. This essay says those maps will show wiring patterns that no handful of recordings can see, and that without them the gap between single cells and whole-brain function stays a black box.

t: Ome sweet ome: what can the genome tell us about the connectome?
sum: When genome sequencing was proposed, many people said it was too hard and not useful—until it became central to biology. This 2008 essay asks whether mapping brain wiring deserves the same kind of big, shared effort, while admitting brains may be more variable than genomes.

t: Hierarchical Community Structure of the Adult Drosophila Connectome Reveals Conserved Circuit Archetypes
sum: The fruit-fly whole-brain wiring map can be carved into neighborhoods of neurons that talk among themselves. This study finds about 1,500 small neighborhoods and then groups them into 45 repeating circuit styles, including some unusual mixing in the visual system.

t: Hippocampal CA3 connectomics reveals a gradient of mossy fiber inputs and selective feedforward inhibition onto pyramidal cells.
sum: A famous hippocampal pathway was thought to help the brain tell similar memories apart, but nobody had a large wiring diagram of those contacts. This team reconstructs a millimetre-scale slab of mouse CA3 and finds a gradient of mossy-fiber inputs plus a selective inhibitory loop onto one pyramid type.

t: Signed motif analysis of the Caenorhabditis elegans neuronal network reveals positive feedforward and negative feedback loops
sum: The worm’s complete wiring diagram can now be read with plus and minus signs on the connections, not just lines. This study finds that certain three-cell loops—especially positive feedforward and negative feedback—show up more often than chance, with typical sensory-to-motor layouts.

t: The Drosophila connectome reveals axo-axonic synapses on descending neurons
sum: Some synapses land on the outgoing cable of a neuron rather than on its branches, and can strongly change whether a spike leaves the brain. Using the fly’s ventral-cord wiring map, this team finds those contacts on descending neurons and shows that a small set of ascending cells can make the giant escape neurons easier

t: Synaptic architecture of a memory engram in the mouse hippocampus
sum: A memory is supposed to live in a set of brain cells that fired together, but it was unclear how their connections actually change. In mouse hippocampus, this electron-microscope study finds that those cells do not mainly link to each other; they grow multi-contact boutons and enlarge selected synapses instead.

t: Brain functions emerge as thermal equilibrium states of the connectome
sum: We have a nearly complete wiring diagram of the worm, but not a simple rule that turns that diagram into functions such as sensing or crawling. This theory paper treats the wiring as a kind of quantum-inspired network and reads ‘functions’ off its equilibrium states.

t: Connectome-constrained networks predict neural activity across the fly visual system
sum: We can now list every connection in a fly visual circuit, but we still do not know how strongly each cell responds or how fast each synapse is. This team freezes the real wiring, tunes the unknown knobs so the network detects motion, and finds that the predicted activity matches many published experiments.

t: Multiplexed volumetric CLEM enabled by scFvs provides insights into the cytology of cerebellar cortex
sum: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot show which molecular tags sit on which cells. This team makes small fluorescent antibody fragments that stain mouse cerebellum without punching holes in membranes, then takes both color pictures and an electron-microscope volume of the same piece of tissue.

t: Prediction of neural activity in connectome-constrained recurrent networks
sum: Having a full wiring diagram does not automatically tell you how the network will fire, because each cell still has unknown speeds and strengths. This theory paper shows that a little bit of recorded activity from well-chosen cells can pin down the rest, while wiring alone often cannot.

t: A Scalable Staining Strategy for Whole-Brain Connectomics
sum: To map every synapse in a mouse brain, the whole organ must be stained so membranes show up in the electron microscope—without splitting the tissue. This protocol uses X-ray movies of stain moving through the brain to time a twelve-step osmium recipe that the authors say soaks the entire brain without cracks.

t: Heterogeneity of synaptic connectivity in the fly visual system
