sum: The fly eye is usually described as 800 repeating columns with the same cell types doing the same jobs. One cell type, Tm9, breaks that rule: its wiring partners differ from column to column, which may explain why its electrical responses also vary.

t: All-optical visualization of specific molecules in the ultrastructural context of brain tissue
sum: Electron microscopes show the fine shape of brain tissue but not named proteins; ordinary microscopes show named proteins but not that fine shape. This method swells the tissue many times, stains all proteins and lipids so the scene looks EM-like, and still tags specific molecules—on a confocal microscope.

t: Petascale pipeline for precise alignment of images from serial section electron microscopy
sum: Before computers can color neurons in a stack of electron-microscope slices, those slices must be lined up. This paper’s software learns to align neighboring pictures, votes to ignore damaged patches, and stitches blocks of a whole fly brain—and a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex—without a slow whole-volume optimizatio

t: Synaptic wiring motifs in posterior parietal cortex support decision-making
sum: When a mouse chooses left or right, some parietal neurons fire for one choice. This study lines up those recordings with an electron-microscope wiring map and finds a push–pull motif: cells that like the same choice excite local inhibitors, which then suppress the opposite-choice cells.

t: Bridging the Gap: Point Clouds for Merging Neurons in Connectomics
sum: When several electron-microscope slices in a row are unusable, automatic neuron coloring breaks into pieces above and below the hole. This paper turns those pieces into sparse 3D point clouds and trains a geometric network to guess which pieces belong to the same cell.

t: Desmosomal connectomics of all somatic muscles in an annelid larva
sum: Muscles do not float; they glue to skin, bristles, and skeleton-like rods through tiny adhesive junctions. This team maps every such glue point in a whole marine-worm larva and shows that the internal bristle rods are the busiest attachment hubs, matching how freely those rods move on video.

t: Methods for analyzing neuronal structure and activity in Caenorhabditis elegans.
sum: The tiny worm C. elegans is see-through and has a simple, stereotyped set of nerve cells. This methods chapter explains how to name those cells with fluorescent tags, map their connections, and watch them fire with calcium sensors.

t: An anatomical substrate of credit assignment in reinforcement learning
sum: When a bird practices song, the brain must decide which tiny contacts to strengthen after a better or worse attempt. This study maps those contacts in a song-learning region and finds two kinds of incoming wires land on different parts of the same cells, which a model says could let learning happen locally.

t: Molecular topography of an entire nervous system
sum: To understand how each worm nerve cell gets its identity, this team measured which genes are on in every one of the 302 neurons. The catalog shows each cell type has its own mix of chemical-messenger genes and points to DNA switches and sticky proteins that may help cells wire up.

t: Neuronal Subcompartment Classification and Merge Error Correction
sum: Computers that glue bits of nerve cells together sometimes fuse an axon onto a dendrite by mistake. This method looks at the 3D shape of each bit, labels it as axon, dendrite, or cell body, and uses those labels to find and cut many of those bad fusions.

t: Joint Deformable Registration of Large EM Image Volumes: A Matrix Solver Approach
sum: A whole fly brain is photographed as millions of slightly overlapping snapshots that must be stitched and stacked without tearing the tissue digitally. This paper turns that puzzle into a large math problem a standard linear solver can handle, and uses it on the first complete adult fruit-fly brain volume.

t: Plasticity of the electrical connectome of C. elegans
sum: Worms can change how their nerve cells are electrically coupled when they enter a hardy “dauer” state. This study maps which gap-junction proteins each neuron makes, shows those recipes change in most cell types in dauer, and links some of those changes to crawling and smell.

t: Robust neural circuit reconstruction from serial electron microscopy with convolutional recurrent networks
sum: Computer programs that outline nerve cells in electron-microscope pictures often work well only on the pictures they were trained on. This paper sets a harder test that mixes sources and tissues, shows leading methods stumble, and offers a new network that does better on that test.

t: Morphological Error Detection in 3D Segmentations
sum: When a computer accidentally glues two nerve cells into one, people can often see that the shape looks wrong. This network learns that kind of shape sense without extra hand labels and can flag glued cells in new datasets, though it cannot always cut them apart by itself.

t: NeuroBlocks – Visual Tracking of Segmentation and Proofreading for Large Connectomics Projects
sum: When many people edit a giant brain-map project with different computer programs, it is easy to lose track of what is done and who changed what. This paper describes a shared website that follows segmentation and proofreading progress across those tools.

t: A resource from 3D electron microscopy of hippocampal neuropil for user training and tool development
sum: This paper shares three tiny but complete 3D electron-microscope maps of rat hippocampus, with every axon, dendrite, glial bit, and synapse traced. Students and computer programs can use them as a practice set for reading brain ultrastructure.

t: The Open Connectome Project Data Cluster: Scalable Analysis and Vision for High-Throughput Neuroscience
sum: Brain microscopes now generate more pictures than a single lab computer can hold. This paper describes a shared computer cluster and web services that store those pictures, run analysis jobs, and let scientists work through the internet.

t: Highly Nonrandom Features of Synaptic Connectivity in Local Cortical Circuits
sum: Are local brain circuits just random spaghetti, or do they have a hidden pattern? Recordings from groups of rat visual-cortex cells show extra two-way links, extra triangles, and a few very strong contacts that tend to hang together—more like a sturdy skeleton than a uniform mesh.

t: Connectome-scale self-supervised representation learning reveals neuronal organization beyond canonical labels
sum: A whole-fly wiring map is so big that people cannot sort every cell by hand. This study trains a computer to learn each cell’s shape and who it talks to from the FlyWire map, then uses those learned fingerprints to find groups that standard name tags miss.

t: Developmental Continuity of Brain Network Core Organization in C. elegans
sum: Even a tiny worm brain keeps growing new connections after hatching. This study watches that wiring over larval life and finds a stable inner club of cells plus some members that come and go, while the club’s links get denser.

t: FEABAS: A Stitching and Alignment Tool for Serial EM Data
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of brain slices often wrinkle, tear, or fold, which makes stacking them into a 3D volume hard. This free software treats the stack like a physical mesh and stretches it smoothly around those defects instead of forcing a simple warp.

t: Isotropic Reconstruction of Anisotropic vEM Volumes with ViT-Guided Diffusion
sum: Many 3D electron-microscope stacks are sharp from above but blurry when viewed from the side because slices are thick. This method teaches a generative model what real thin slices look like, then invents the missing in-between slices more cleanly than simple stretching.

t: Long-range axon branching: contributions to brain network plasticity and repair
sum: Big-picture brain scans show networks rewiring after injury, but it is unlikely that brand-new long cables grow in adults. This review asks whether existing, highly branched axons—some barely making synapses—could be used to recruit extra brain areas instead.

t: Proprioceptive limit detectors contribute to sensorimotor control of the Drosophila leg
sum: Flies have tiny hair sensors that fire when a leg is about to go too far. This study shows one hip-joint sensor both feels a forward stretch and is wired to pull the leg back, and it uses the fly nerve-cord wiring map to guess what the other hair sensors do.

t: The Connectome and the Quest for the Functional Logic of the Drosophila Early Olfactory System
sum: Having a complete wiring diagram of the fly’s early smell circuit is not the same as knowing how smell works. This essay argues that local feedback loops and a model of real-world odors are what turn the map into a theory of computation.

t: Thermodynamic connectivity reveals functional specialization and multiplex organization of extrasynaptic signaling
sum: Worms talk both through wired synapses and through slower chemical broadcasts. This study puts both maps in one framework and argues each mode is tuned for a different job: fast reflexes, motor stability, whole-body states, or staying alive.

t: Accelerating Neuron Reconstruction with PATHFINDER
sum: Tracing every axon in a mouse brain by hand would take forever and cost a fortune. This AI system glues axon pieces together by judging which shapes look like real neurons, and the authors say it makes far fewer mistakes than earlier automatic tracers.

t: Functional connectomics reveals general wiring rule in mouse visual cortex
sum: Brain cells that like the same pictures tend to wire to each other, not just next door but across visual areas. This mouse study finds that pattern in a cubic-millimeter wiring-and-activity map, and a simple artificial network grows the same habit when trained to classify.

t: Perisomatic ultrastructure efficiently classifies cells in mouse cortex
sum: In a huge electron-microscope block of mouse cortex, most cells are only partly traced, so naming them from their full shape is impossible. This paper shows that measurements around the cell body are enough to assign types and to find rare wiring patterns.

t: Synapse Detection Efficiency in EM Drosophila Connectomics
sum: Fruit-fly wiring maps from different microscopes do not agree on how many synapses they see. This comparison finds that 3D ion-beam microscopes usually show over 40% more human-visible synapses than sliced transmission-EM volumes of matching regions.

t: A split-GAL4 driver line resource for Drosophila neuron types
sum: Fruit-fly neuroscientists need genetic switches that turn on in just one kind of nerve cell. This huge collection of split-GAL4 fly stocks, with pictures matched to electron-microscope maps, makes it much easier to grab the cell type you want.

t: Cell nuclei segmentation in mm-scale x-ray holographic nanotomography images of mouse brain tissue
sum: A new X-ray microscope can photograph a cubic millimetre of mouse brain in enough detail to see cell nuclei, but there are tens of thousands of them. This paper trains a computer to find those nuclei and puts the results in a browser so people can check the work.

t: Comprehensive analysis of the C. elegans connectome reveals novel circuits and functions of previously unstudied neurons
sum: The worm’s complete wiring list has been updated to include muscles and both sexes, but many cells still had no known job. This analysis splits the network into ten behavior-related groups and points to overlooked cells—including two that collect touch from the whole body.

t: Mapping of Multiple Neurotransmitter Receptor Subtypes and Distinct Protein Complexes to the Connectome
sum: A wiring diagram says who talks to whom, but not which molecular “mailbox” sits at each contact. This fly study tags native transmitter receptors, looks at them in super-resolution, and shows that different mailboxes sit in different neighborhoods on motion-detecting cells.

t: Neuropeptide signaling network of Caenorhabditis elegans: from structure to behavior
sum: Besides wired synapses, worm neurons broadcast many small peptides that change behavior over seconds to hours. This review maps that chemical network and explains the repeating circuit tricks—push, pull, loops—that peptides use.

t: Systematic annotation of a complete adult male Drosophila nerve cord connectome reveals principles of functional organisation
sum: A complete wiring diagram of a male fruit-fly nerve cord is only useful if every cell has a name and a job description. This companion paper labels tens of thousands of neurons, matches many of them across body segments, and posts the phone book next to the map.

t: Brain wiring determinants uncovered by integrating connectomes and transcriptomes.
sum: Fruit-fly visual neurons pick specific partners among many nearby cells. This paper matches wiring maps with gene and protein-binding data and finds adhesive receptor–ligand pairs that keep related motion-sensing cells in the correct layers.

t: Chemical cognition: chemoconnectomics and convergent evolution of integrative systems in animals
sum: Animal thinking is often treated as a product of wired nerve cells, but much signaling is chemical and may have evolved more than once. This review argues we should map those chemical conversations, especially in comb jellies, placozoans, and sponges.

t: msemalign: a pipeline for serial section multibeam scanning electron microscopy volume alignment
sum: Giant electron-microscope brain volumes are photographed as millions of tiny overlapping tiles that must be stitched into a smooth 3D picture. This paper describes software built to do that stitching at huge scale without warping the original photos more than necessary.

t: Identifying Inputs to Visual Projection Neurons in Drosophila Lobula by Analyzing Connectomic Data
sum: A part of the fruit-fly visual brain is thought to spot objects such as other flies, but many of its incoming wires were unnamed fragments. This study groups those fragments by shape and connections and proposes which known cell types they are.

t: A connectome is not enough - what is still needed to understand the brain of Drosophila?
sum: A complete wiring diagram of a fruit-fly brain is nearly in hand, but wires alone do not explain behavior. This essay asks what else—activity, chemistry, and experiments—still has to be measured to understand that brain.

t: Circuit motifs and graph properties of connectome development in C. elegans
sum: As a worm grows, its wiring diagram changes in patterned ways. This preprint counts small repeating circuit shapes across ages and shows that some shapes explode in number while others barely keep pace.

t: Postnatal connectomic development of inhibition in mouse barrel cortex
sum: Inhibitory brain cells must learn which parts of other cells to contact as a mouse grows. Electron-microscope maps at many ages show that some targeting is present from the start, while other targeting is sculpted by removing misplaced contacts.

t: A Student’s Guide to Neural Circuit Tracing
sum: There are now many ways to label who talks to whom in the mammalian brain, from old dyes to engineered viruses. This student-oriented review explains those tools and warns that a wiring list is only one of several ways to classify neurons.

t: Comparisons between the ON- and OFF-edge motion pathways in the Drosophila brain
sum: Fruit flies sense moving light and dark edges with two related circuits. This paper maps both in one electron-microscope volume and shows they share a three-input layout but are not wired identically.

t: Learning and Segmenting Dense Voxel Embeddings for 3D Neuron Reconstruction
sum: Computers must color in every nerve cell in a 3D brain picture without breaking thin branches. This method teaches a network to give nearby bits of the same cell similar codes, then groups them, and is especially helpful for very skinny processes.

t: Segmentation-Enhanced CycleGAN
sum: Each new electron-microscope brain volume usually needs a custom training set painted by people. This preprint translates pictures from one volume into the style of another so an existing tracing program can be reused without new labels.

t: A genetic, genomic, and computational resource for exploring neural circuit function
sum: A wiring diagram does not say which chemical each cell uses. This resource measures gene activity in dozens of genetically labeled fruit-fly visual cells and posts the catalog for use with existing connection maps.

t: Effective automated pipeline for 3D reconstruction of synapses based on deep learning
sum: Finding every tiny contact in electron-microscope pictures is slow by hand. This software spots synapses, throws out likely false alarms using neighboring slices, and outlines the gap between cells, with high reported precision.

t: Hub connectivity, neuronal diversity, and gene expression in the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome
sum: Some worm neurons are unusually well connected, like busy hubs. Those hubs also tend to turn on similar genes, not because they sit near each other, but because many of them are the command cells that help the animal crawl.

t: Synaptic transmission parallels neuromodulation in a central food-intake circuit
sum: A small set of fly neurons uses a peptide related to a mammalian hunger signal. Mapping every contact of those cells shows they also use a fast chemical transmitter and sit between taste sensors and hormone cells.

t: Image-based correction of continuous and discontinuous non-planar axial distortion in serial section microscopy
sum: When brain tissue is sliced for the electron microscope, slices are not perfectly even or always in order, which warps the 3D picture. This paper infers the true spacing and order from the images themselves and offers free software to correct it.

t: Automated Detection of Synapses in Serial Section Transmission Electron Microscopy Image Stacks
sum: In stacked electron-microscope photos, connections look like tiny dark patches that are easy to miss. This program learns from a few human clicks to find those patches automatically in mouse visual cortex.

t: NEUROMODULATION OF NEURONAL CIRCUITS: BACK TO THE FUTURE
sum: A static wiring diagram is only a starting point: chemical modulators can retune cells and connections so the same map produces different rhythms. This review explains that idea with lessons from small circuits.

t: Exploring the retinal connectome
sum: Researchers photographed a column of rabbit retina in enormous detail and labeled which cells use which chemicals. The map confirms textbook connections but shows the famous AII pathway is far more mixed than a simple night-vision circuit.

t: As-rigid-as-possible mosaicking and serial section registration of large ssTEM datasets
sum: Huge electron-microscope montages of a young fruit-fly brain are warped and shuffled by cutting and staining. This method finds matching landmarks and gently aligns thousands of tiles so cells stay continuous through depth.

t: Machines that learn to segment images: a crucial technology for connectomics.
sum: Listing every connection in a brain means coloring in every cell in a huge picture, which people do slowly. This review explains how computers that learn from corrected examples were starting to make that coloring accurate enough to edit rather than draw from scratch.

t: The Human Connectome: A Structural Description of the Human Brain
sum: To understand the human brain as a network, scientists needed a name and a plan for its full connection list. This article coined “connectome” and argued such a map should be built, even though none existed yet.

t: A comprehensive mechanosensory connectome reveals a somatotopically organized neural circuit architecture controlling stimulus-aimed grooming of the Drosophila head
sum: Flies scratch the part of the head that was touched, so the brain must keep a map of where each bristle sits. This study lists almost all the central partners of those touch cells and finds a developmentally related group that preserves location.

t: A quantitative census of millions of postsynaptic structures in a large electron microscopy volume of mouse visual cortex
sum: Whether a contact lands on a spine or a smooth branch changes what it might do, but counting millions of those landings by hand is impossible. This preprint reads the 3D surface of each cell cheaply and labels those targets across a mouse cortical volume, then checks a human volume.

t: Advances in brain connectomics: integrating light and electron microscopy for multiscale neural mapping
sum: Brain maps now mix ultra-detailed electron-microscope wiring with larger-scale light-microscope pictures of cells and activity. This review walks through how those pictures are made, combined, and sometimes aimed at disease.

t: Approaching a connectome of the human foveal retina
sum: When we look straight at something, a tiny patch of retina called the fovea does the work with tightly packed cell types. This team used computer vision to draft a wiring diagram of a piece of human fovea and found fewer output cell types than in mouse retina, dominated by high-precision pathways.

t: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator circuit for fly walking
sum: Animals can walk with rhythmic muscle patterns even without timed sensory input, but the exact cells that make that rhythm were unknown. Fly nerve-cord simulations pick out a tiny three-cell circuit, and experiments confirm a second command path that also makes the legs tick.

t: Eyewire II – A connectomic resource for resolving cell types and circuits of the mouse retina
sum: A mouse retina was photographed over a much larger patch than before, after some cells’ visual responses were recorded. Volunteers and labs are correcting the computer’s cell tracings so rare types and big dendritic trees can be named.

t: Uncovering Sex Differences in the Drosophila Ventral Nerve Cord Through Connectome Alignment
sum: Male and female flies control different body actions through the nerve cord, but naming matching cells by hand is slow. This preprint lines up whole wiring diagrams using only who-connects-to-whom and then lists which cell types differ by sex.

t: Spatial and morphological organization of mitochondria in neurons across a connectome
sum: Energy-producing mitochondria are not sprinkled at random inside brain cells. Across a fly wiring diagram they have characteristic shapes per cell type and sit a few microns from particular synapses, with some of the same ideas holding in mouse cortex.

t: A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing
sum: A complete map of the fruit-fly brain still leaves open how those wires produce behavior. The authors built a computer model of every neuron firing and showed it can predict which cells drive feeding and grooming, then checked many of those predictions in real flies.

t: Deciphering the genetic code of neuronal type connectivity through bilinear modeling
sum: Different kinds of brain cells wire to specific partners, but it is unclear which genes write those pairing rules. This paper trains a model that reads gene lists from both sides of a connection and tries to reconstruct who talks to whom.

t: Sparse Annotation is Sufficient for Bootstrapping Dense Segmentation
sum: Teaching a computer to color in every cell in a 3D microscope stack usually takes huge amounts of hand drawing. The authors show that a few 2D sketches plus a second network that links slices can stand in for that labor.

t: BIFROST: a method for registering diverse imaging datasets
sum: Pictures of fly brains taken in different labs do not sit in the same coordinate system, so activity maps are hard to overlay on wiring diagrams. This paper builds a shared living-brain atlas and a registration pipeline that lines those pictures up to within a small fraction of a millimeter.

t: Heterogeneous receptor expression underlies non-uniform peptidergic modulation of olfaction in Drosophila
sum: A chemical messenger is spread evenly through the fly’s smell center, yet it turns some smell channels down and others up. The authors show that the difference comes from which cells carry the receptor, not from where the messenger is released.

t: Mapping Alzheimer’s Molecular Pathologies in Large-Scale Connectomics Data: A Publicly Accessible Correlative Microscopy Resource
sum: Alzheimer’s proteins are usually seen in glowing light-microscope stains, while wiring is seen in electron-microscope pictures, and the two rarely overlap. This study stains those proteins in a mouse hippocampus and then images the same piece of tissue in 3D electron microscopy so both can be studied together.

t: Nested neural circuits generate distinct acoustic signals during Drosophila courtship
sum: Male fruit flies sing two different songs with the same wings. This paper maps the nerve-cord cells that make those songs and finds that the simpler song is made by a subset of the circuit that makes the more complex one.

t: Bisected graph matching improves automated pairing of bilaterally homologous neurons from connectomes
sum: The two sides of a brain often contain matching cell types, and computers can guess those pairs from who connects to whom. This paper shows that connections that cross the midline, usually ignored, can make those guesses better.

t: Neural signal propagation atlas of C. elegans
sum: A wiring diagram of the worm brain does not by itself say how signals actually travel. The authors turned cells on one at a time and watched the rest of the head, building a map of who can make whom respond.

t: RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Cell-level Microscopy Image Segmentation
sum: Computers that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures still glue cells together or break them apart by mistake, and people usually fix that by hand. This paper trains a set of learning agents to find and repair those mistakes automatically.

t: Unveiling the sensory and interneuronal pathways of the neuroendocrine connectome in Drosophila
sum: Hormone-releasing brain cells keep the body stable, but it is often unclear which sensory paths tell them when to fire. Using a complete larval fruit-fly wiring map, the authors trace those incoming paths and find a carbon-dioxide-related route onto particular peptide cells.

t: ZeVis: A Visual Analytics System for Exploration of a Larval Zebrafish Brain in Serial-Section Electron Microscopy Images
sum: A whole baby-zebrafish brain imaged in electron microscopy is enormous and hard to look through. The authors built a viewing system that shows slices and 3D shapes together so scientists can count and compare cell nuclei in different brain regions.

t: Raising the Connectome: The Emergence of Neuronal Activity and Behavior in Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: The adult worm’s wiring diagram grows from a developing embryo, not all at once. This article argues that the order in which cells mature, and simple competitive rules for who synapses first, help explain that adult pattern.

t: Synaptic polarity and sign-balance prediction using gene expression data in the Caenorhabditis elegans chemical synapse neuronal connectome network
sum: Whether a worm synapse turns the next cell on or off is often unknown. This paper guesses those plus and minus signs from which transmitters and receptors each cell makes, and finds about four excitatory connections for every inhibitory one.

t: Neuronal cell types in the fly: single-cell anatomy meets single-cell genomics.
sum: Fruit-fly brains have about 150,000 cells, too many to think about one by one unless similar cells are grouped into types. This review explains how cell shape and gene activity are being used together to make those groups.

t: Revealing the Synaptic Hodology of Mammalian Neural Circuits With Multiscale Neurocartography
sum: Mapping every mammal synapse will take a very long time, but other microscopes can already chart which cell types project where and where synapses sit on dendrites. This review surveys those complementary mapping methods.

t: Toward A Reproducible, Scalable Framework for Processing Large Neuroimaging Datasets
sum: Huge brain pictures are useless if only one lab’s custom computer setup can run the analysis. This paper describes a shared, containerized workflow system so different labs can process large electron-microscope and X-ray brain datasets in a repeatable way.

t: Detecting Synapse Location and Connectivity by Signed Proximity Estimation and Pruning with Deep Nets
sum: To turn an electron-microscope volume into a wiring diagram, a computer must find each contact and which cell is sending versus receiving. This paper trains two networks to mark those contacts in both mouse and fruit-fly tissue.

t: FluoEM, virtual labeling of axons in three-dimensional electron microscopy data for long-range connectomics
sum: Most of the wires entering a small piece of mouse cortex come from far away, but electron-microscope pictures are black-and-white. This method matches glowing axons from a light microscope to the same axons in the electron-microscope volume by the unique paths they take.

t: A Deep Structured Learning Approach Towards Automating Connectome Reconstruction from 3D Electron Micrographs
sum: Computers must trace every neuron through a 3D electron-microscope stack without breaking or gluing cells. This paper trains a network to judge which tiny voxels belong together, then groups them, and reports large accuracy gains on three test sets.

t: Correlated Light-Serial Scanning Electron Microscopy (CoLSSEM) for ultrastructural visualization of single neurons in vivo
sum: A light microscope can follow one glowing neuron a long way, but only an electron microscope can see its synapses, and the two pictures are hard to match. The authors genetically stain a single mouse neuron so it is visible in both, then zoom the electron microscope onto that cell.

t: Large-Scale Electron Microscopy Image Segmentation in Spark
sum: A fruit-fly brain imaged at synapse resolution is too big for one computer to color in every neuron. This paper describes a cluster computing system that splits the work across many machines without one local mistake wrecking the whole map.

t: Reconstruction of genetically identified neurons imaged by serial-section electron microscopy
sum: Reconstructing every wire in an electron-microscope stack is extremely slow. The authors genetically darken chosen neurons so the microscope can zoom only on those cells and a computer can trace them much faster.

t: Vulnerability-Based Critical Neurons, Synapses, and Pathways in the Caenorhabditis elegans Connectome
sum: If you knock out one worm neuron or synapse in a computer model, some removals barely matter and a few scramble the whole network. This study finds a small set of those high-impact cells and links, including ones used for backing up.

t: Image Segmentation by Size-Dependent Single Linkage Clustering of a Watershed Basin Graph
sum: A common computer method floods an image like a landscape and cuts it into too many tiny pieces. This paper merges those pieces using rules about how big real objects should be, so brain scans can be segmented quickly without wrongly gluing neurons together.

t: Nanoconnectomic upper bound on the variability of synaptic plasticity
sum: Some synapses on a neuron are big and some are small, which may be how memories are stored. By finding pairs of contacts that have always been used together, the authors show those pairs are almost the same size, meaning the brain can set synapse strength very precisely.

t: A genetically specified connectomics approach applied to long-range feeding regulatory circuits
sum: Scientists can genetically mark hunger-related brain cells, but seeing their tiny synapses in an electron microscope usually destroys the tissue or loses the genetic label. This paper puts an enzyme inside the cells’ release packets so those synapses show up as dark spots without ruining the structure.

t: Dissecting a neuron network: FIB-SEM-based 3D-reconstruction of the visual neuropils in the sea spider Achelia langi (Dohrn, 1881) (Pycnogonida)
sum: Sea spiders have simple eyes whose inner wiring had not been mapped at synapse scale. Using a focused-ion-beam electron microscope, the authors reconstruct those visual centers and find circuit parts that look like both spider-style and insect-style eyes.

t: Mojo 2.0: Connectome Annotation Tool
sum: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope pictures still make mistakes, and fixing a trillion-pixel stack by painting every pixel is hopeless. This tool lets a person scribble a few strokes to join or split those computer labels.

t: 'The genetic analysis of functional connectomics in Drosophila'
sum: Fruit flies now have increasingly complete wiring maps, and genetic tricks can turn identified cells off or on. This review explains how combining those maps with those tricks can show which cells actually cause a behavior, not merely which cells are active when it happens.

t: Automated Detection and Segmentation of Synaptic Contacts in Nearly Isotropic Serial Electron Microscopy Images
sum: Finding every synapse in a stack of electron-microscope pictures is slow and people miss some. This team trains a computer on a few examples in 3D and reports accuracy similar to expert humans on rat cortex.

t: Topological Cluster Analysis Reveals the Systemic Organization of the Caenorhabditis elegans Connectome
sum: The tiny worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram of its neurons. This paper groups those neurons into a handful of clusters that line up with known sensing and movement circuits, and it uses that map to guess what some poorly studied cells might do.

t: A frozen rate operator from the complete larval connectome: degree and weight govern the gross response, exact wiring governs input routing and mushroom-body modes
sum: A wiring diagram lists who talks to whom, but some brain-like behavior might come just from how many connections each cell has. This study freezes the larval fruit-fly connectome into a simple mathematical operator and shows that the overall response looks like a randomly rewired network, while where activity is routed

t: Comparative connectomics of parasite esophagus suggests evolutionary simplification of a nervous system
sum: Some parasites seem to have simpler nervous systems than free-living relatives. This team maps the feeding-organ wiring of a soybean pest worm and finds the same number of nerve cells as in laboratory worms, but far fewer connections onto muscle and new links to gland cells that help it infect plants.

t: Connectome analysis reveals brainwide visual processing in Drosophila
sum: A fruit fly’s eyes do not work as isolated cameras: they send messages into the rest of the brain and to the other eye, and they get messages back. This study sorts those long-range cells in a whole-brain wiring diagram into outgoing, incoming, and left–right groups and describes how visual features are bottled, return

t: NTAC: Neuronal type assignment from connectivity
sum: Once a brain’s wiring is mapped, someone still has to name the cell types. This method sorts neurons using only who they connect to, either starting from a few labeled examples or from scratch, and the authors say it runs on a laptop in minutes for fly brains.

t: Peripheral anatomy and central connectivity of proprioceptive sensory neurons in the Drosophila wing
sum: Fruit-fly connectome maps usually start after the sensory cells in the wing have been cut off. This study traces those wing sensors back from a nerve-cord electron-microscope volume, matches them to organs on the wing, and finds specialized cells that talk directly to steering muscles.

t: Comparative connectomics of two distantly related nematode species reveals patterns of nervous system evolution
sum: Two kinds of roundworm split more than 100 million years ago. Mapping both brains with electron microscopy shows a shared core wiring plan, but also many local changes—even in cells that still look the same—and some rewiring that does not obviously change behavior.

t: Divergence in neuronal signaling pathways despite conserved neuronal identity among Caenorhabditis species
sum: Three related roundworm species still use the same menu of neuron types after tens of millions of years. What changes is the chemical listening gear: many cells keep making the same transmitters but gain or lose the receptors that would let them hear them, and peptide signals drift while the overall peptide-network sha

t: Divergent neural circuits for proprioceptive and exteroceptive sensing of the Drosophila leg
sum: A sense organ in the fly’s leg feels both the joint’s own motion and vibrations from the ground. By following the wiring, this team shows those two jobs use different cells and different central pathways—one staying local for motor control, the other going up to the brain after combining legs.

t: From Synapses to Dynamics: Obtaining Function from Structure in a Connectome Constrained Model of the Head Direction Circuit
sum: A compass circuit in the fly brain keeps track of heading, but the wiring map does not list how strong each synapse is. This study learns a few numbers per cell type, not per cell, and still gets a working compass that can integrate turns—then it virtually removes cell types to see what each one is for.

t: Connectomic reconstruction predicts visual features used for navigation
sum: Flies steer using a visual pathway that feeds a compass in the center of the brain. This team reconstructs every cell in that pathway from electron microscopy, guesses what each channel sees, and checks some of those guesses with recordings.

t: Learning dynamic representations of the functional connectome in neurobiological networks
sum: A wiring diagram is a still photo, but brain cells team up in different groups depending on the moment. This method finds those changing teams in calcium recordings of living animals and, in a worm test, correctly predicted that turning off one cell type would change salt avoidance.

t: Predicting visual function by interpreting a neuronal wiring diagram
sum: Most cell types in the fly’s visual system have been named from shape, not from what they see. This paper reads the wiring of a few of those types and predicts they detect the tilt of local edges, a claim that can be checked with recordings.

t: Retinal Connectomics: A Review.
sum: The back of the eye is a small computer that preprocesses vision. This review explains how electron-microscope maps of retinal wiring have shown those circuits to be more tangled than textbooks suggested, and why complete maps matter for disease and for models of seeing.

t: Synaptic architecture of leg and wing premotor control networks in Drosophila
sum: Flies walk and fly with different muscles, but both are driven by networks that sit just upstream of motor neurons. This connectome study finds those networks come in modules, with a size-based recruitment ladder in the leg that the wing steering system does not copy.

t: Synaptic promiscuity in brain development
sum: Brain cells can plug into the wrong partners if you take them out of context, yet adult brains are wired precisely. This review says messy, overlapping synapse formation during growth is often a feature: later steps and earlier positioning keep the wrong connections from lasting.

t: A leaky integrate-and-fire computational model based on the connectome of the entire adult Drosophila brain reveals insights into sensorimotor processing
sum: If you know who is connected to whom in a fly brain, can you guess how tasting sugar leads to eating? This team builds a simple whole-brain spiking model from the wiring diagram, then checks many of its guesses with real fly experiments and reports that most of them hold.

t: Diversity of visual inputs to Kenyon cells of the Drosophila mushroom body
sum: Most of the fly’s learning center cells smell the world; a minority mostly see it. Mapping who talks to those visual cells shows they mix a small set of visual channels at random, more like a constrained code than the huge combinatorial smell code.

t: Efficient Search for Circuit Structure by ‘Smooth-Index’ Matrix-Reordering
sum: A huge table of who connects to whom is hard to read until the cells are lined up in a sensible order. This paper treats each cell’s place in line as a sliding number, slides those numbers to reduce messy loops, then snaps them back to a ranking that reveals feedforward versus feedback.

t: From connectome to effectome: learning the causal interaction map of the fly brain
sum: A wiring diagram shows possible routes, not which routes actually change activity. This paper proposes combining random optogenetic pokes with the fly connectome as a statistical prior so that a causal “effect map” of the brain might be learned from many small circuits rather than one impossible whole-brain recording.

t: Deep residual contextual and subpixel convolution network for automated neuronal structure segmentation in micro-connectomics
sum: Tracing every neuron in electron-microscope pictures is exhausting. This paper trains a deep network, then tidies its predictions with a grouping algorithm, and reports high scores on a public EM challenge and on mouse cortex stacks.

t: Neuronal contact predicts connectivity in the C. elegans brain
sum: Do worm neurons pick partners with a molecular lock, or do they mostly synapse on whoever they physically touch? Using many wiring and contact maps, this paper argues that how much two cells touch—and which bundle they travel in—goes a long way toward predicting connections.

t: Rewarding Capacity of Optogenetically Activating a Giant GABAergic Central-Brain Interneuron in Larval Drosophila
sum: A huge inhibitory cell in the larval fly brain is known for quieting the learning center so smells stay sparse. Turning that cell on together with an odor can nonetheless teach the larva to like the odor, and that teaching seems to need dopamine neurons.

t: Bayesian reconstruction of memories stored in neural networks from their connectivity
sum: If a network stores memories in its connection strengths, can you read those memories from a wiring diagram? This theory paper gives conditions and an algorithm for attractor networks, and explains when ordinary tricks like PCA are not enough.

t: Dopamine modulation of sensory processing and adaptive behavior in flies
sum: Dopamine is famous as a reward chemical, but in flies it also helps the brain mix what is happening now with hunger, memory, and context. This review explains how dopamine cells feeding the mushroom body give the fly a flexible decision switch, and why fly wiring diagrams make that switch studyable.

t: Large-scale image segmentation based on distributed clustering algorithms
sum: Stitching tiny pieces of a brain image into neurons usually requires looking at the whole volume at once, which will not fit in memory. This paper splits the job across computers but postpones glue decisions at the edges until the pieces are large enough, so the answer matches doing it all in one step.

t: Neuronal circuits integrating visual motion information in Drosophila
sum: Flies see motion with cells that prefer bright or dark edges moving in four main directions. This reconstruction maps who those cells talk to next, showing how bright and dark paths join, how opposite directions cancel, and how new directions and messages into another visual area may be built.

t: Capillary-Based and Stokes-Based Trapping of Serial Sections for Scalable 3D-EM Connectomics
sum: Cutting thousands of ultras-thin brain slices is one thing; picking them up without wrecking them is another. This paper describes a water-boat trap that parks each slice in the same spot so a robot can lift it, with only a small fraction lost in tests of a hundred-plus sections.

t: Cell-type specific innervation of cortical pyramidal cells at their apical dendrites
sum: The treetops of cortical neurons meet in the upper layers, where they receive a mix of go and stop synapses. Mapping those contacts in mouse cortex shows layer-2, layer-3, and layer-5 cells are not wired the same: inhibition is aimed differently depending on cell type and on whether you look at the main fork or the fin

t: Computing Temporal Sequences Associated With Dynamic Patterns on the C. elegans Connectome
sum: A wiring diagram can be run as a simple simulation to see what activity patterns it can produce. This team finds that a feeding-circuit simulation in the worm looks locomotion-like, but almost all of the signaling paths change once that circuit is placed back inside the full nervous system.

t: Graph Properties of the Adult Drosophila Central Brain
sum: A nearly complete wiring diagram of part of a fruit-fly’s central brain can be treated like a directed map of who talks to whom. This preprint reports that fly neurons have many inputs and outputs, paths are short, compartments differ, and the wiring is not random.

t: The growing topology of the C. elegans connectome
sum: As a worm’s neurons are born, the wiring diagram grows a shape that ordinary network scores can miss. This study tracks holes in that growing graph and finds the shape is fairly robust to noisy birth times and is not explained by simple growth models.

t: The hourglass organization of the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome
sum: Information entering a worm’s sensors has to reach muscles through a tangle of interneurons. This paper finds that the useful forward paths squeeze through a small set of about a dozen cells that were already known as a densely linked “rich club.”

t: The Wiring Logic of an Identified Serotonergic Neuron That Spans Sensory Networks
sum: A serotonin cell can wander through many smell-processing areas, so it is hard to know whom it actually talks to. This EM reconstruction of one identified fly neuron shows different wiring rules in different regions and strong input from outside olfaction.

t: Two Stream Active Query Suggestion for Active Learning in Connectomics
sum: Experts cannot label every synapse and mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope volume. This paper picks which examples to label next by combining a network trained on labels with another trained on all the raw pictures, and it reports better proposals than earlier active-learning methods.

t: Useful road maps: studying Drosophila larva’s central nervous system with the help of connectomics
sum: The fruit-fly maggot has a small nervous system, so wiring, activity, and behavior can be studied together. This review gathers recent maps of how the larva combines senses, learns, and chooses actions.

t: What would a synthetic connectome look like?
sum: Most brain-wiring research takes animals apart; a complementary idea is to design and build wiring on purpose. This review asks what a synthetic connectome would be for and how one might start making one.

t: A multilayer circuit architecture for the generation of distinct locomotor behaviors in Drosophila
sum: The same larval muscles have to crawl both forward and backward. This study maps every motor neuron and its premotor partners in one body segment, then shows that timing—not a separate muscle set—distinguishes the two gaits.

t: Leveraging Domain Knowledge to Improve Microscopy Image Segmentation With Lifted Multicuts
sum: Automatic cell cutting in microscope images still glues the wrong objects together because the computer only looks at a small neighborhood. This paper turns extra biological knowledge into long-distance “don’t merge these” links and shows cleaner cells in several hard datasets.

t: Modular integration of neural connectomics, dynamics and biomechanics for identification of behavioral sensorimotor pathways in Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: A worm’s wiring diagram does not by itself crawl. This modeling kit chains neurons, muscles, and body physics so simulated pokes and ablations can be compared with real locomotion.

t: The connectome of the Caenorhabditis elegans pharynx
sum: The worm’s throat has its own tiny nervous system of twenty cells. A new electron-microscope map finds that most of those cells both sense and drive muscle, in shallow modules matched to parts of the pharynx.

t: The neuroanatomical ultrastructure and function of a biological ring attractor
sum: Flies keep an internal compass of which way their head points, and theories say that takes a ring of cells that excite neighbors and inhibit opposites. This team checks the actual synapses and finds the predicted parts plus extra loops the models did not include.

t: Neural circuit basis of aversive odour processing in Drosophila from sensory input to descending output
sum: Female fruit flies refuse to lay eggs where they smell a mold chemical. This study follows that smell from the antenna through many brain cells to the neurons that send the “don’t lay here” command, and it finds both a private line and a lot of mixing with other bad smells.

t: Synaptic partner prediction from point annotations in insect brains
sum: In a fly brain, one sending site often talks to several receiving sites, so finding “who synapses with whom” is harder than circling a dark blob. This method learns those pairs from simple point clicks and led a public challenge at the time.

t: Optimal synaptic signaling connectome for locomotory behavior in Caenorhabditis elegans: Design minimizing energy cost
sum: Knowing who is wired to whom in a worm does not say whether each wire pushes or brakes. A computer search over a seven-cell locomotion circuit finds that the best match to crawling data is inhibition on essentially every connection.

t: Recursive Training of 2D-3D Convolutional Networks for Neuronal Boundary Detection
sum: Serial-section electron-microscope stacks are sharp in the plane of the slice and fuzzy between slices, which makes cell outlines hard for computers. This paper uses a deeper 3D-aware network twice—once for a draft outline, then again to clean it—and reports a clear accuracy jump.

t: Wiring cost and topological participation of the mouse brain connectome
sum: Brains might save wire by keeping connections short, but some regions still make costly long-distance links. In the mouse, those expensive hubs sit where modules meet and line up with genes used in learning and memory.

t: Deep and Wide Multiscale Recursive Networks for Robust Image Labeling
sum: Computers that paint every pixel as “cell edge or not” still make enough mistakes to wreck a wiring diagram. This 2013 network looks at a large 3D neighborhood, uses thousands of features, and refines its own labels in extra passes.

t: Building Retinal Connectomes
sum: You cannot guess a retina’s full wiring from recordings alone—there are too many possible graphs. This review says complete maps need very high-resolution electron microscopy plus molecular tags, and that even “known” cells are turning out more connected than textbooks suggested.

t: Detection of Neuron Membranes in Electron Microscopy Images using a Serial Neural Network Architecture
sum: Cell outlines in electron-microscope pictures are easy for people and hard for computers because of noise and look-alike dark blobs. This 2010 method stacks several small neural nets so each one can use the last one’s guess as extra context.

t: A First Step for Expansion X-Ray Microscopy: Achieving Contrast in Expanded Tissues Sufficient to Reveal Cell Bodies
sum: Expanding tissue makes tiny neural details larger, but then there is much more volume to photograph. This early report shows cell bodies in expanded tissue under an X-ray microscope, while still missing the thin wires needed for a wiring diagram.

t: Bilateral Neuron Pairs Share Redundant Network Roles Despite Incomplete Connection Symmetry in Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: Worm neurons often come in left and right twins that are not wired identically. This paper shows those twins still play similar network roles, and that the unmatched wires are part of how they stay similar.

t: Centralized brain networks controlling antennal grooming coordination
sum: When a fly grooms an antenna, its head, feelers, and front legs move together. This study argues that a central brain circuit, not feedback from each limb, keeps those parts in sync, and that turning off a class of widely broadcasting inhibitory cells disrupts the coordination.

t: Connectome quality converges predictably to reveal optimal stopping points during proofreading
sum: Fixing computer mistakes in a huge brain map can consume years, and it is hard to know when the map is “good enough.” This preprint watches a few whole-network statistics as edits roll in and argues they level off at a sensible stopping point.

t: Flexible circuits for visually guided flight control in Drosophila.
sum: Fruit flies steer in midair with a relatively small brain. This review says they do it by stacking fast stabilizing reflexes under more flexible, goal-seeking circuits, and by changing how vision is processed depending on whether they are flying.

t: Geometric developmental principles for the emergence of brain-like weighted and directed neuronal networks
sum: Brains from worms to mice look alike in some wiring statistics, as if development followed simple geometric rules. This study shows that how far cells are apart, plus two “rich-get-richer” rules for synapses and branches, can recreate those statistics—unless you zoom out to whole brain areas.

t: Harnessing cortical geometry, wiring, and function as inductive biases for recurrent neural networks
sum: A mouse visual-cortex dataset that includes both wiring and activity can be used as a recipe for artificial recurrent networks. This study finds that starting from real functional relationships, then respecting where cells sit in space, helps those networks learn faster and look more brain-like.

t: iBrAVE: a unified framework for 3D interactive and integrative analysis of brain atlas data across modalities and scales
sum: Brain atlases now mix genes, cell shapes, activity, and electron-microscope wiring, but they live in different files. This software puts them in one 3D space so researchers can click from a neuron’s shape to nearby genes or to a matching EM cell.

t: Neuron Segment Connectivity Prediction With Multimodal Features for Connectomics
sum: Computers often chop one neuron into many pieces in electron-microscope stacks. This paper looks at both the big 3D shape of those pieces and the close-up pictures at the join, then decides which pieces belong together, the way a human proofreader would.

t: NuGraph: Graph-Based Reasoning over 3D Primitives for Nucleus Segmentation Correction
sum: Nucleus outlines in huge electron-microscope brain maps still get stuck together or split apart. This team treats the broken pieces as a graph, groups them back into whole nuclei, and reports that the cleanup is far faster than doing it by hand.

t: From Sensory Detection to Motor Action: The Comprehensive Drosophila Taste-Feeding Connectome
sum: Taste cells in the fruit fly sit on several body parts and steer feeding and courtship, but their full wiring was missing. This team reconstructs those sensors through brain and nerve cord and sketches how taste reaches muscles, hormones, and social circuits.

t: Graph embeddings for identifying symmetries in Connectomes
sum: Some brain circuits are wired as if neurons sit on a ring or a map of space. This paper learns a layout of the fly’s wiring that reveals those hidden shapes, helping guess what variables a circuit is computing.

t: A Differentiable Model for Optimizing the Genetic Drivers of Synaptogenesis
sum: The idea is to set a neuron’s genes so that the synapses it grows already implement a useful circuit. This paper offers a math model of that process and tests it only in simulations of learning tasks.

t: Ensemble learning and ground-truth validation of synaptic connectivity inferred from spike trains
sum: Watching spikes is easier than seeing synapses, but turning spike trains into a wiring diagram is error-prone. This team tests several inference recipes against known connections in dishes and simulations, then combines them with a neural net that does better, especially on inhibitory links.

t: Fibration symmetries and cluster synchronization in the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome
sum: If two neurons are wired as copies of each other, they may fire in lockstep. This paper looks for those copy-paste patterns in the worm’s walking circuits and checks the idea in simulations.

t: Synaptic connectome of the Drosophila circadian clock
sum: The fly’s daily clock was thought to be about 150 neurons. Using a whole-brain wiring map, this team finds more clock cells, left–right connections, extra light routes, and a likely big role for peptide signals rather than only direct synapses.

t: Temperature cues are integrated in a flexible circadian neuropeptidergic feedback circuit to remodel sleep-wake patterns in flies
sum: Flies sleep and move differently when it is hot or cold. This study finds a small circadian cell group that hears both the clock and temperature sensors and uses peptide signals to keep evening activity in a safe range.

t: An Out-of-Domain Synapse Detection Challenge for Microwasp Brain Connectomes
sum: Computers that find synapses are usually trained on a tiny labeled patch and then asked to work on a huge, differently looking brain. This paper sets up a contest on microwasp volumes so methods can be tested when the training and test images do not match.

t: Exploiting large neuroimaging datasets to create connectome-constrained approaches for more robust, efficient, and adaptable artificial intelligence
sum: Brain wiring diagrams might teach computers to learn with less data and power. This group tries several fly- and cortex-inspired tricks—repeated motifs, a heading circuit on a robot, memory replay, and trimmed attention—and reports gains on a few test tasks.

t: Imaging brain tissue architecture across millimeter to nanometer scales
sum: Electron microscopes see every cell but not easily every molecule; ordinary light microscopes see molecules but not the dense packing of tissue. This method stains the spaces between cells so light microscopy can map tissue and likely synapses from mouse hippocampus to human pathology samples.

t: Lineages to circuits: the developmental and evolutionary architecture of information channels into the central complex
sum: Insect brains grow from about a hundred stem cells per side, each producing a family of sister neurons with a shared path into the brain. This review argues those families are how different species plug new senses into a shared navigation center.

t: Neural circuit mechanisms for transforming learned olfactory valences into wind-oriented movement
sum: Flies that learned an odor predicts sugar will walk into the wind to find it. This paper finds a small group of neurons that read mushroom-body memory outputs and help turn that good-versus-bad signal into upwind walking.

t: Neural Networks for Navigation: From Connections to Computations.
sum: Animals can walk toward a place they cannot see because the brain keeps a map with a bump of activity that stands for direction or goal. This review says those maps are not a fixed wiring diagram: synapses are constantly chosen from a larger anatomical menu.

t: Stimulus-Specific Modulation is Enabled by Differential Serotonin Receptor Expression
sum: Serotonin is often treated as a volume knob for a whole cell class. In the fly nose’s output cells, different neurons carry different serotonin receptor mixes, so the same chemical can retune different odors differently.

t: Toolkits for detailed and high-throughput interrogation of synapses in C. elegans
sum: Seeing every synapse in the worm with electron microscopy is slow. This team shares fluorescent worm strains and software that count synapse-like dots in many animals, stages, and both sexes.

t: Computational Inference of Synaptic Polarities in Neuronal Networks
sum: Knowing who connects to whom is not enough: you also need plus versus minus. This paper guesses excitatory versus inhibitory synapses in the worm from genes, receptors, and network patterns, filling in hundreds of missing signs on the computer.

t: Connectomics Annotation Metadata Standardization for Increased Accessibility and Queryability
sum: Huge electron-microscope brains are hard to reuse because every lab stores cell and synapse labels differently. This perspective argues for shared metadata so anyone can query “what is this object?” without downloading raw annotation dumps.

t: Heavy-tailed neuronal connectivity arises from Hebbian self-organization
sum: In many animals a few neuron pairs are wired much more strongly than everyone else. This paper shows a simple grow-and-prune rule, mixing “fire together, wire together” with randomness, that can grow those heavy tails and also clumps of connections.

t: Multisensory Integration in Caenorhabditis elegans in Comparison to Mammals
sum: Animals mix sight, smell, touch, and more into one decision. This review collects how the tiny worm does that mixing and argues we can watch almost every neuron at once, something we cannot yet do in mammals.

t: Reprogramming the topology of the nociceptive circuit in C. elegans reshapes sexual behavior
sum: Male and female worms can sense a nasty cue with the same sensory cells but then act differently. This paper models the downstream wiring, tweaks a few connections, and reports that behavior—and even mating success—can flip with those tweaks.

t: An effective AI integrated system for neuron tracing on anisotropic electron microscopy volume
sum: Following one neuron through a stack of stretched electron-microscope slices is hard when the slices do not line up. This system uses a memory network plus a U-Net, starting from a seed, to keep tracing despite those jumps.

t: Drosophila gustatory projections are segregated by taste modality and connectivity
sum: Taste cells from the fly’s mouthparts send axons into the brain that talk not only to other cells but also to each other. This reconstruction shows those axons cluster by taste type and mostly synapse within their own group.

t: Establishment and Maintenance of Neural Circuit Architecture
sum: Brains must wire the right partners together and then keep those contacts for years without freezing all change. This review walks through the molecular and cellular rules that build and maintain circuits, using connectomes as maps.

t: Neuromuscular connectomes across development reveal synaptic ordering rules
sum: Baby muscles are wired in a messy many-to-many pattern that later becomes one axon per muscle fiber, recruited from small to large. This team maps that cleanup and finds axons stay partners longest with others that rank near them, probably because they fire similarly.

t: The Nereid on the rise: Platynereis as a model system
sum: Platynereis is a marine worm used for development and evolution, and now also for mapping every neuron in a tiny whole body. This review introduces the animal and why its young stages suit volume electron microscopy.

t: Leveraging Tools from Autonomous Navigation for Rapid, Robust Neuron Connectivity
sum: Instead of painting every pixel as a neuron, this method sends software “robots” through electron-microscope volumes to walk along cells and note synapses, aiming for a wiring graph at lower computer cost.

t: Multilayer network analysis of C. elegans: Looking into the locomotory circuitry
sum: The worm’s walking circuit can be drawn as stacked networks of different chemical signals. This modeling paper picks likely walking neurons, simulates their rhythms, and tests which cells, when silenced in the model, break coordinated muscle waves.

t: Uncovering the genetic blueprint of the C. elegans nervous system
sum: If each neuron’s gene list is its identity card, there should be rules for which cards are allowed to form a connection. This paper infers such rules for worm gap junctions from wiring plus innexin expression.

t: A developmental framework linking neurogenesis and circuit formation in the Drosophila CNS
sum: Fruit-fly nerve-cord cells remember which stem cell they came from, which sister they are, and when they were born. This paper finds those developmental labels still show up in where synapses sit and who talks to whom.

t: GCIB-SEM: A path to 10 nm isotropic imaging of cubic millimeter volumes
sum: Brain maps at synapse resolution usually force a choice between a tiny, very sharp 3D stack and a large stack that is too coarse in depth. This method mills thick slices in tiny steps so both large area and fine depth become possible.

t: Refined parcellation of the nervous system by algorithmic detection of hidden features within communities.
sum: Brain maps are often grouped into neighborhoods of tightly linked cells, but those neighborhoods can hide smaller closed loops. This paper looks for those inner units in the worm wiring diagram.

t: A Single-Cell Level and Connectome-Derived Computational Model of the Drosophila Brain
sum: Computer models of whole brains are usually too big to build cell by cell. This team turns fruit-fly neuron pictures into a spiking network and finds that the real wiring is easier to keep calm than shuffled wiring.

t: Ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptor-cell circuits form a spectral depth gauge in marine zooplankton
sum: Some animals have two kinds of light sensors that evolved separately. In a marine worm larva, the UV sensor tells the animal to swim down and can overrule the eyes that swim toward light, which may help it pick a depth.

t: Estimating the impact of structural directionality: How reliable are undirected connectomes?
sum: Human brain scans cannot tell which way a fiber points, so maps treat every link as two-way. This paper asks how much that guess scrambles who the hubs are, using animal maps where direction is known.

t: Multilayer adaptive networks in neuronal processing
sum: A wiring diagram of synapses is not the whole conversation among neurons. Chemicals that retune cells can change what the same wires do, and this paper sketches a layered network picture of that extra talk.

t: OpenWorm: overview and recent advances in integrative biological simulation of Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: The tiny worm C. elegans is simple enough that people hope to simulate the whole animal in a computer. This perspective explains an open project that tries to stitch many small models into one worm.

t: Optimal degrees of synaptic connectivity
sum: Some neurons listen to only a few partners; others listen to thousands. This theory says a few well-chosen inputs can make a cleaner, more useful activity pattern than a thicket of wires—unless those input wires are trained.

t: Comparative Connectomics.
sum: Looking at wiring diagrams from simple animals up to more complex brains may show which network tricks everyone shares. This review names that comparison and highlights communities, hubs, and rich clubs as recurring themes.

t: Deep Contextual Networks for Neuronal Structure Segmentation
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are huge and messy, so people cannot outline every cell by hand. This paper trains a deep network that looks at both fine edges and wider context to draw those outlines.

t: Genetically targeted 3D visualisation of Drosophila neurons under Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microscopy using miniSOG
sum: Light microscopy can color specific neurons, but electron microscopy sees every membrane. This paper makes a genetic stain that shows up in electron images so chosen fly neurons can be found in 3D ultrastructure.

t: Graph Theoretic and Motif Analyses of the Hippocampal Neuron Type Potential Connectome
sum: The hippocampus has many named cell types, but we rarely know which types actually synapse. This paper guesses the full menu of possible connections from where axons and dendrites overlap, then studies that map as a network.

t: Efficient Semi-Automatic 3D Segmentation for Neuron Tracing in Electron Microscopy Images
sum: Computers can sketch neurons in electron-microscope stacks but still make mistakes. This method asks a person only to check suggested merges, which is much faster than tracing everything.

t: Large-scale EM Analysis of the Drosophila Antennal Lobe with Automatically Computed Synapse Point Clouds
sum: Finding every wire in a fly’s smell center would take forever if people had to mark each synapse. This team lets a computer drop a cloud of synapse dots on a huge electron-microscope volume to show where the action is.

t: Object-based representation and analysis of light and electron microscopic volume data using Blender
sum: Staring at raw microscope pixels makes it hard to compare many genes or many reconstructed neurons at once. This team turns those pictures into 3D objects inside Blender so they can be labeled and analyzed together.

t: Principles of connectivity among morphologically defined cell types in adult neocortex
sum: The cortex is built from many kinds of inhibitory cells whose wiring was known only in bits. This team records from many cells at once in adult mouse visual cortex and finds a few connection recipes reused across layers.

t: Focused Proofreading: Efficiently Extracting Connectomes from Segmented EM Images
sum: Fixing computer-drawn neurons in electron-microscope pictures takes too long if people wander the whole volume. This method sends proofreaders only to the mistakes that would most change the wiring diagram.

t: Generation of dense statistical connectomes from sparse morphological data
sum: Nobody can photograph every synapse in a whole cortical area. This software fills a realistic 3D model of rat whisker cortex with many reconstructed cells and estimates how often they should touch.

t: The Viking viewer for connectomics: scalable multi-user annotation and summarization of large volume data sets
sum: A retina connectome can be tens of terabytes, too big for one person’s computer. Viking is a website that lets many researchers mark cells and synapses on that volume together.

t: Connectome-seq: high-throughput mapping of neuronal connectivity at single-synapse resolution via barcode sequencing.
sum: Electron microscopes can see synapses up close but not easily follow long-distance paths with each cell’s molecular name. Connectome-seq uses viral barcodes and sequencing to list which mouse neurons touch, together with their gene signatures.

t: Developmental patterns of the C. elegans neural circuits using community detection.
sum: As a worm grows, its nerve cells form bigger and more specialized teams. This paper uses a computer method that finds overlapping groups in the wiring diagram at each larval stage.

t: From the fly connectome to exact ring attractor dynamics
sum: Fruit flies keep a sense of which way their head points using a ring of neurons. This theory shows more than one wiring recipe in real fly connectomes can still make that compass work.

t: vEMINR: Ultra‐Fast Isotropic Reconstruction for Volume Electron Microscopy With Implicit Neural Representation
sum: Electron-microscope stacks are usually much blurrier in depth than sideways because slices are thick. This method teaches a neural network to fill in that missing sharpness much faster than earlier software.

t: Volumetric denoising enables high-throughput volume electron microscopy and efficient downstream analysis.
sum: Taking electron-microscope pictures slowly makes them look cleaner but limits how much brain you can image. This team shows that keeping thin slices and then denoising the 3D stack can be better than shooting slowly.

t: Biological Processing Units: Leveraging an Insect Connectome to Pioneer Biofidelic Neural Architectures
sum: A baby fruit fly’s complete wiring diagram is small but evolved. This team freezes that wiring as a computer network and finds it can classify pictures and help solve chess puzzles surprisingly well.

t: Connectomics of predicted Sst transcriptomic types in mouse visual cortex
sum: Gene labels and electron-microscope wiring usually live in different experiments. This study matches cell shapes so somatostatin inhibitory types from Patch-seq can be found in a huge EM volume, revealing that they do not all inhibit the same way.

t: Reconstruction of a connectome of single neurons in mouse brains by cross-validating multi-scale multi-modality data
sum: Most “whole-brain” mouse maps average many cells in a region. This resource estimates which individual reconstructed neurons could connect across the brain by pairing axons with dendrites and with axonal boutons.

t: A generative model of the connectome with dynamic axon growth
sum: Most computer models of brain networks add links by abstract rules, not by growing axons. This model lets simulated growth cones follow chemical attraction and still ends up with brain-like bundles and network statistics.

t: Asymmetry in synaptic connectivity balances redundancy and reachability in the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome
sum: Worms look left–right symmetric, but their synaptic partners often are not the same cells on each side. This paper shows that leftover asymmetry can be tuned so backup paths win out over reaching as many different partners as possible.

t: Comparative connectomics of dauer reveals developmental plasticity
sum: When food is scarce, a worm can pause as a hardy dauer larva with special behaviors. This team mapped that stage’s synapses and found the same overall nerve plan with important local rewiring.

t: Discovering motifs to fingerprint multi-layer networks: a case study on the connectome of C. Elegans
sum: The worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram that can be split by synapse type. This paper counts small repeating wiring patterns in each layer and shows that most of those patterns are not what you would get from a random network of the same size.

t: EM-Compressor: Electron Microscopy Image Compression in Connectomics with Variational Autoencoders
sum: Brain electron-microscope movies are so large that storing them is becoming a problem. This team trains a neural compressor that can shrink human cortex images to as little as one 128th of the original size while still allowing computers to find cell membranes.

t: Nanoscale Connectomics Annotation Standards Framework
sum: Huge electron-microscope and X-ray brain maps are expensive to make, and they are hard to reuse if every lab stores labels differently. This paper sketches a shared standards plan so those labels can be found, shared, and compared across tools and species.

t: Recurrent connections enable point attractor dynamics and dimensionality reduction in a connectome-constrained model of the insect learning center
sum: Fruit-fly learning cells talk to each other as well as to the next layer. This team builds a computer model from the real wiring map and finds that those extra loops can shrink the activity pattern and hold a few stable “memories.”

t: Social state alters vision using three circuit mechanisms in Drosophila
sum: When a fruit fly is aggressive or courting, it needs to pay extra attention to other flies. This Nature paper uses the wiring diagram to find three circuit tricks that retune vision, then shows they actually work in behaving flies.

t: Tango-seq: overlaying transcriptomics on connectomics to identify neurons downstream of Drosophila clock neurons
sum: Electron-microscope wiring maps cannot easily show how a fly’s connections change from day to night. This team tags cells downstream of clock neurons, sequences them, and finds preferred partners among other clock cells and learning-center cells.

t: Tracing nerve fibers with volume electron microscopy to quantitatively analyze brain connectivity
sum: This team traces every nerve fiber in small 3D electron-microscope blocks of mouse hippocampus and cortex. They find the wires are packed extremely tightly—up to about nine kilometers of fiber in a cubic millimeter—and they count how synapses sit on spines versus shafts.

t: Two- and three-dimensional electron microscopy techniques: powerful tools for studying the brain under physiological and pathological conditions
sum: Electron microscopes can show both the proteins sitting in a neuron’s membrane and the 3D wiring between cells. This review explains two modern toolkits for those jobs and why they matter for healthy and diseased brains.

t: 3D reconstruction of the cerebellar germinal layer reveals tunneling connections between developing granule cells
sum: In the developing cerebellum, young granule cells were found to be linked by tiny tunnels in 3D electron-microscope reconstructions. The cells on either end can be dividing, migrating, or switching between those jobs.

t: A Soma Segmentation Benchmark in Full Adult Fly Brain
sum: Finding every cell body in a fruit-fly electron-microscope brain has been hard because training labels for cell bodies were missing. This CVPR paper adds a labeled dataset, a two-step computer vision method, and a first full-brain soma map.

t: Comparative connectomics reveals noncanonical wiring for color vision in human foveal retina
sum: Humans, macaques, and marmosets all see color, but their foveal wiring is not the same. This paper maps the “blue” cone circuit at synapse resolution and finds contacts and cell shapes in humans that the monkey models lack.

t: Domain Adaptive Synapse Detection with Weak Point Annotations
sum: Computers trained to find synapses in one electron-microscope stack often fail on the next brain region. This method uses rough point clicks, adapts to the new images, and won an ISBI 2023 challenge on wasp-brain data.

t: Electrical synapses for a pooling layer of the convolutional neural network in retinas
sum: Night vision has to catch single photons and average them without fancy pattern matching. This perspective treats the retina’s electrical synapses as a pooling step like in a convolutional network, comparing mouse and monkey rod pathways.

t: Fast Compressed Segmentation Volumes for Scientific Visualization
sum: Coloring every voxel in a 3D scan with a cell or material label makes huge files. This paper compresses those label volumes tightly and still draws them in real time on a graphics card.

t: High-Speed Automated Reconstruction of Drosophila Larval Brain from Volumetric EM Data
sum: Tracing every neuron in a larval fruit-fly electron-microscope stack usually takes too long for a small lab. This conference paper speeds up a standard tracing network and says reconstruction finishes much faster on their larval-brain dataset.

t: Integrating EM and Patch-seq data: Synaptic connectivity and target specificity of predicted Sst transcriptomic types
sum: Inhibitory cells in mouse visual cortex have been typed by shape, electricity, and genes. This team guesses those types from electron-microscope shape alone and finds that different predicted types wire to different partners and wrap their axons in different amounts of myelin.

t: Mechanosensory and command contributions to the Drosophila grooming sequence
sum: Flies clean themselves from front to back, and the thorax is last. This paper finds a command cell that starts chest-sweeping with the hind legs, shows that actual touching is needed to start leg-rubbing, and finds an inhibitory cell that can cancel chest cleaning when other itches come first.
