t: New insights into retinal circuits through EM connectomics: what we have learnt and what remains to be learned
sum: The retina is a layered computer made of cells whose connections are now being mapped with 3D electron microscopy. This short review says what those maps have taught us and what still needs mapping, especially in primates.

t: Studying zebrafish nervous system structure and function in health and disease with electron microscopy
sum: Zebrafish are widely used to study brains in health and disease, and electron microscopy can show synapses and whole-circuit layout. This review is a guidebook to which EM methods fit which zebrafish questions.

t: A functionally ordered visual feature map in the Drosophila brain.
sum: In the fruit fly, some visual cells each dump their output into a little knot in a fixed place in the brain. This Neuron paper records those knots and finds they are arranged by what they see—looming versus drifting, and object size—so downstream cells can mix related features.

t: A graph network model for neural connection prediction and connection strength estimation
sum: Instead of only looking at electron-microscope pictures of worm synapses, this study uses calcium activity and a graph neural network to guess which cells connect and how strongly. It also tries to say whether a connection is excitatory or inhibitory.

t: Connectomic analysis of the Drosophila lateral neuron clock cells reveals the synaptic basis of functional pacemaker classes
sum: Fruit-fly clock cells keep daily time, but they need to be wired to each other—and maybe to cells that are not clocks themselves. This preprint maps those synapses and says known clock-cell groups are also distinct wiring types, with a few highly connected hubs.

t: Dynamic Functional Connectivity in the Static Connectome of C. elegans
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram looks almost the same from animal to animal, yet the worm behaves differently depending on hunger and other states. This review explains that chemical messengers can retune which wired-up cells actually work together.

t: Fear memory-associated synaptic and mitochondrial changes revealed by deep learning-based processing of electron microscopy data.
sum: After mice learn a fear, their auditory cortex synapses and mitochondria change shape and number. This paper uses a deep-learning helper on electron-microscope stacks to count those changes at huge scale.

t: Scalable Biologically-Aware Skeleton Generation for Connectomic Volumes
sum: Once a computer has colored in all the neurons, you still need stick-figure centerlines for measuring and checking them. This paper builds those skeletons in a way that respects cell bodies and synapses and runs fast on huge volumes.

t: The synaptic organization in the C. elegans neural network suggests significant local compartmentalized computations
sum: Worm neurons are simple cables, so it was easy to assume they mix all their inputs together. This study shows synapses sit in clumps, which could let different bits of the same cable do different mini-computations.

t: U-RISC: An Annotated Ultra-High-Resolution Electron Microscopy Dataset Challenging the Existing Deep Learning Algorithms
sum: This team published extremely zoomed-in electron-microscope pictures of cell membranes and ran a contest. Today’s best programs still lose to humans on this set, unlike an older easier contest.

t: A Programmable Ontology Encompassing the Functional Logic of the Drosophila Brain
sum: Having a fly wiring diagram is not the same as having a working model of what the circuits do. This preprint adds a programmable language, a search box for English questions, and demo models of smell circuits full of feedback loops.

t: A weighted network analysis framework for the hourglass effect—And its application in the C. elegans connectome
sum: In a worm, many sensors and muscles might talk through a small set of in-between cells, like sand in an hourglass. This paper counts those paths using synapse size and number, and finds different “waist” cells in males and hermaphrodites.

t: Multi-scale light microscopy/electron microscopy neuronal imaging from brain to synapse with a tissue clearing method, ScaleSF
sum: Seeing a whole brain and then the same cell’s synapses usually requires different preparations. This paper clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so researchers can zoom from brain-wide maps down to individual contacts.

t: Protocol for preparation of heterogeneous biological samples for 3D electron microscopy: a case study for insects
sum: Insect heads mix hard cuticle, brain, eye, and muscle, so they are hard to stain and cut for 3D electron microscopy. This team reports a lab-friendly preparation that lets them image a whole tiny wasp head at cellular and synaptic detail.

t: Synaptic inputs to broad thorny ganglion cells in macaque retina
sum: A motion-sensitive cell in the monkey retina gets almost none of its synapses from the usual excitatory bipolar cells. Most of its contacts come from many kinds of amacrine cells, which may help it notice small moving things.

t: The Prop1-like homeobox gene unc-42 specifies the identity of synaptically connected neurons
sum: A single gene in the worm is on in 15 neuron types that all connect to each other. When the gene is missing, those cells fail to take on their adult identities and their wiring goes wrong, so the gene looks like a circuit-building switch.

t: Ultrastructural readout of in vivo synaptic activity for functional connectomics
sum: Electron-microscope maps of brain wiring usually cannot say which synapses were firing. This team stains recently used vesicles in living mice, then images them in 3D EM, and finds that even boutons on the same axon can release very differently.

t: What connectomics can learn from genomics
sum: A huge project has been proposed to map every synapse in a mouse brain, like sequencing the human genome. This commentary says the map will help most if it is built with biologists who already have questions about circuits and behavior, not as a map for its own sake.

t: A Color Vision Circuit for Non-Image-Forming Vision in the Primate Retina
sum: Some ganglion cells that set our body clock also respond to blue light in a special OFF way in primates. This paper finds a new inhibitory cell in the monkey retina that is wired only to blue-sensitive cones and can create that blue-OFF signal.

t: Beyond the connectome: A map of a brain architecture derived from whole-brain volumetric reconstructions
sum: The worm’s brain was long treated as a tangle of axons with a fixed wiring diagram. By rebuilding two nerve rings in 3D, this team finds five bundles, a stable core plus variable extra connections, and a layered layout that looks a bit like a residual neural network.

t: Circuit reorganization shapes the developing human foveal midget connectome towards single-cone resolution
sum: The sharpest part of human vision uses a private line from one cone to one bipolar cell to one ganglion cell. Serial EM of fetal foveas shows that this wiring is carved by remodeling, not born perfect.

t: Learning the architectural features that predict functional similarity of neural networks
sum: Two brain-like networks can look different as graphs but fire the same way. This simulation study finds that matching each cell’s total incoming and outgoing synapse strength predicts similar activity better than usual network scores.

t: Network structure of the mouse brain connectome with voxel resolution
sum: Most mouse brain maps average connections into large named regions. This study looks voxel by voxel and finds source-versus-sink hubs, a special role for neuromodulatory nuclei, and cortical gradients like those described in primates.

t: Systematic errors in connectivity inferred from activity in strongly recurrent networks
sum: People often try to guess which neurons are wired together just from how they fire. This paper shows that in tightly looped circuits those guesses stay systematically wrong even with huge amounts of data, unless you perturb the network out of its usual rhythm.

t: Connectomics and function of a memory network: the mushroom body of larval Drosophila.
sum: The fruit-fly larva has a small learning center that is now mapped at the synapse. This review explains how that wiring, plus timed dopamine signals, can make an odor feel rewarding or punishing, and how different kinds of memory can be pulled apart with genetics.

t: Multiscale and Multimodal Imaging for Connectomics
sum: The brain has to be seen both up close (tiny synapses) and all at once (the whole organ), and both in a flash and over years. This chapter surveys optical microscopes meant to do that, and why the data still explode in size.

t: Optical Imaging in Brainsmatics
sum: This review coins “brainsmatics” for mapping the brain with careful 3D addresses, not just lists of connections. The authors argue that light microscopy is the practical way to see every neuron in a whole brain, and that the datasets will only work if labs share standard, automated pipelines.

t: Serial block face scanning electron microscopy in cell biology: Applications and technology.
sum: Serial block-face SEM lets biologists mill through a sample in the microscope and build 3D pictures of cells. This review explains how the method works, what it is good for—including brain wiring—and how the images are analyzed.

t: Serial-section electron microscopy using Automated Tape-Collecting Ultramicrotome (ATUM)
sum: ATUM is a gadget that catches ultrathin slices on tape so a scanning electron microscope can photograph thousands of them. This chapter is a practical how-to, from preparing the block to lining the pictures up.

t: Synaptic inputs from identified bipolar and amacrine cells to a sparsely branched ganglion cell in rabbit retina
sum: A rarely discussed rabbit ganglion cell has long, thin dendrites that look a bit like an amacrine cell. Electron-microscope wiring shows it only receives synapses, gets about a third of them from bipolar cells, and lots of inhibitory input from far-reaching amacrine cells.

t: Wide-field amacrine cell inputs to ON parasol ganglion cells in macaque retina
sum: Parasol cells in the monkey eye are good at noticing motion. This wiring study finds that about a fifth of their synapses come from bipolar cells and another slice from long-range inhibitory cells that can report motion outside the cell’s classic receptive field.

t: An Adversarial and Densely Dilated Network for Connectomes Segmentation
sum: Computers still struggle to outline neuron membranes in electron-microscope pictures. This paper trains a network that tries to fool a critic into thinking its outlines are human-drawn, and reports better, less blurry maps on two public EM sets.

t: Building a functional connectome of the Drosophila central complex
sum: The fly’s central complex is a compass-like brain region whose wiring was mostly guessed from which cells’ branches overlap. This study actually stimulates one cell type and records another, and finds fewer working connections than the pictures suggested, with a few bottleneck cells in the middle.

t: Connectomic Identification and Three-Dimensional Color Tuning of S-OFF Midget Ganglion Cells in the Primate Retina
sum: Blue-OFF color signals in monkeys were a wiring mystery. This paper shows that in the fovea, each blue cone has a private OFF midget pathway, and that some midget cells mix blue, green, and red inputs in ways that are not just the textbook color axes.

t: Flexible Learning-Free Segmentation and Reconstruction for Sparse Neuronal Circuit Tracing
sum: Machine-learning tracers often need lots of hand-drawn labels and still break on a new kind of microscope image. FLoRIN skips training, uses local brightness tricks, and the authors say it traces sparse labeled neurons in EM, X-ray, and confocal stacks much faster.

t: Functional Connectomics in C. elegans
sum: We have a complete wiring diagram of the worm, but that still does not tell us how it behaves. This review walks through new ways to watch, tickle, and simulate the whole nervous system, including light, ultrasound, and computer models.

t: Guided graph spectral embedding: Application to the C. elegans connectome
sum: Usual map-making of the worm’s wiring treats every neuron as equally important. This method lets you spotlight sensory cells, or motor cells, and the resulting 2D maps line up better with where those cells sit and what they do.

t: Mesoscale Connectomics
sum: Brains can be mapped as big fiber highways, as cell-type-to-cell-type routes, or as every synapse. This review focuses on the middle scale and the tracing tools used to chart how each cell class sends and receives long-range connections.

t: Methods for Mapping Neuronal Activity to Synaptic Connectivity: Lessons From Larval Zebrafish
sum: Baby zebrafish are see-through and small, so the same brain can be watched with a two-photon microscope and later taken apart in an electron microscope. This article explains how to do that and what the olfactory bulb’s wiring looked like when they tried.

t: Neuropeptides encoded by nlp-49 modulate locomotion, arousal and egg-laying behaviours in Caenorhabditis elegans via the receptor SEB-3
sum: Worms have a wireless chemical network of neuropeptides on top of their synapses. This study matches the peptide NLP-49 to the receptor SEB-3 and shows the pair helps control crawling, arousal, and egg-laying.

t: Sensorimotor integration in Caenorhabditis elegans: a reappraisal towards dynamic and distributed computations
sum: Textbooks draw the worm’s brain as senses feeding forward into motor commands. Whole-brain imaging instead shows that even early interneurons fire with the animal’s current movement, so sensing and acting look mixed from the start.

t: t-GRASP, a targeted GRASP for assessing neuronal connectivity
sum: To see whether two fly neurons touch at synapses, researchers can split a green fluorescent protein across the two cells so it lights up only where the halves meet. t-GRASP aims that signal at real contact sites and works with all the common fly genetic driver systems.

t: The effects of aging on neuropil structure in mouse somatosensory cortex—A 3D electron microscopy analysis of layer 1
sum: Old mouse cortex in this study has fewer synapses, but the ones that remain are bigger, so the total synaptic surface stays about the same. Inhibition drops more than excitation, which may make the remaining wiring stronger but less flexible.

t: The Feeding Connectome: Convergence of Monosynaptic and Polysynaptic Sensory Paths onto Common Motor Outputs
sum: This team traces feeding-related neurons in a fruit-fly larva brain from electron-microscope pictures. Direct sensory-to-motor shortcuts and longer multi-step paths both land on the same swallowing and hormone-output cells.

t: Complexity and Vulnerability Analysis of the C. Elegans Gap Junction Connectome
sum: The worm C. elegans has a complete map of electrical junctions among its neurons. This paper shows that a few command cells make that map far more complex than a random network with the same number of links, and that removing those links makes it simpler than random.

t: Methods to investigate the structure and connectivity of the nervous system
sum: This review surveys ways to figure out which brain cells connect to which. The authors say you should pick the method based on the question: electron microscopy is great for a wiring snapshot, not for watching synapses change.

t: Multi-stage Multi-recursive-input Fully Convolutional Networks for Neuronal Boundary Detection
sum: Computers that outline cell membranes in electron-microscope pictures often confuse inner clutter with real walls. This team stacks several network stages that look at the picture at different zoom levels and reports strong scores on two public contests.

t: Organization of the Drosophila larval visual circuit
sum: Fruit-fly larvae see with tiny eyes of about a dozen light sensors. This team maps every connection in that first visual hub and suggests one cell type tracks how bright it is while another tracks how brightness is changing.

t: A platform for brain-wide imaging and reconstruction of individual neurons
sum: Following a single neuron’s thin axon across a whole mouse brain is usually impractical. This team builds a fast two-photon microscope that shaves and images the brain in 3D and traces several motor-cortex cells all the way to their endings.

t: CONNECTOMICS, THE FINAL FRONTIER
sum: We still do not know which genes tell each worm neuron whom to connect to. This essay argues that comparing the full wiring diagram with where cell-adhesion proteins are expressed could crack that code.

t: Filling the gap: adding super-resolution to array tomography for correlated ultrastructural and molecular identification of electrical synapses at the C. elegans connectome
sum: Electrical synapses are tiny protein channels that are hard to name in electron-microscope pictures. This team images the same worm tissue with super-resolution light microscopy and electron microscopy so the channels can be both seen and molecularly labeled.

t: Gap junctions in C. elegans: Their roles in behavior and development
sum: Worms do not use the same gap-junction proteins that we do; they use innexins. This review explains that worms have many innexin genes, most cells use more than one, and that redundancy makes single-gene knockouts surprisingly mild.

t: ON Bipolar Cells in Macaque Retina: Type-Specific Synaptic Connectivity with Special Reference to OFF Counterparts
sum: In the monkey retina, bipolar cells sort cone and rod signals toward different ganglion cells. This electron-microscopy study lists how each ON bipolar type connects and matches it to an OFF partner.

t: Quantifying Mesoscale Neuroanatomy Using X-Ray Microtomography
sum: Cutting a brain into thousands of slices to photograph it is slow. This team uses synchrotron X-rays to scan thick pieces of mouse brain in 3D and automatically counts cells and blood vessels.

t: Species-specific wiring for direction selectivity in the mammalian retina
sum: Some retinal cells fire more when a bar moves one way than the other. This study maps mouse starburst-cell wiring, finds it differs from rabbit, and shows the difference may keep angular speed tuning similar despite different eye sizes.

t: An algorithm to predict the connectome of neural microcircuits
sum: Nobody can measure every synapse type in a piece of cortex. This team writes a computer recipe that starts from near-touches between axons and dendrites and prunes them down to a predicted wiring diagram, then checks it against the few types that have been measured.

t: An Iterative Convolutional Neural Network Algorithm Improves Electron Microscopy Image Segmentation
sum: A first-pass computer map of cell membranes in electron-microscope pictures is often gappy. This paper trains a second network to fill in missing membrane from the neighborhood and runs it several times, which improves how well neurons stay separated.

t: Flow-Based Network Analysis of the Caenorhabditis elegans Connectome
sum: This paper treats the worm’s directed wiring diagram like a traffic network. It groups neurons by how signals would flow, predicts which cell deletions would scramble that flow, and sorts cells into four flow roles.

t: The beginning of connectomics: a commentary on White et al. (1986) ‘The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans’
sum: This commentary retells how the first complete wiring diagram of an animal—the worm C. elegans—was published in 1986 and why that map still shapes neuroscience.

t: The connectomics of brain disorders
sum: Brain diseases often spread along the brain’s wiring rather than staying in one spot. This review argues that mapping those networks helps explain how damage travels and how the brain sometimes copes.

t: Topological organization of connectivity strength in the rat connectome
sum: This paper treats the rat brain as a network of 67 regions linked by traced axons of different strengths. Strong links tend to sit inside modules and between hub regions, not just anywhere.

t: What Properties are Desirable from an Electron Microscopy Segmentation Algorithm
sum: Computers that color in neurons on electron-microscope pictures still make mistakes, and gluing two cells together is worse than accidentally cutting one. This paper trains the computer with a few clicks and tries extra hard not to glue cells together.

t: Exploring the Connectome
sum: Electron-microscope brain pictures can be so large they will not fit in a graphics card. This team builds a viewer that only loads the piece you are looking at, even while the microscope is still scanning.

t: mGRASP enables mapping mammalian synaptic connectivity with light microscopy
sum: A trick from worms and flies makes a green glow only where two neurons actually touch at a synapse. This team redesigns that trick for mouse brains and uses it to map connections in hippocampus and thalamus-to-cortex pathways.

t: A Computational Framework for Ultrastructural Mapping of Neural Circuitry
sum: Stitching thousands of electron-microscope snapshots into a 3D brain map used to take a career. This team releases software and a molecular-labeling strategy so large retinal wiring volumes can be built in months and browsed like a map.

t: A technicolour approach to the connectome
sum: This review explains why it is so hard to draw a precise wiring diagram of the brain from microscope pictures and surveys new coloring and imaging tricks, including rainbow-like neuron labels, that might help.

t: Towards neural circuit reconstruction with volume electron microscopy techniques.
sum: Following every wire in a piece of brain needs electron microscopy, but cutting and aligning thousands of slices used to be crushing work. This 2006 review says new automated 3D electron-microscope methods were starting to make large wiring diagrams realistic.

t: Search for computational modules in the C. elegans brain
sum: The authors ask whether the worm’s wiring diagram contains small repeating circuit gadgets, like logic gates in electronics. They find some two-, three-, and four-cell patterns that show up more often than chance; five-cell patterns do not.

t: A central somatotopic map of the fly leg supports spatially targeted grooming
sum: A fly must scratch the exact spot that was touched. This preprint maps leg-touch neurons in the fly’s ventral nerve cord and shows a short chain of cells that turns a touch map into a well-aimed grooming movement.

t: A Systematic Study of Behavioral Cloning for Scientific Data Annotation
sum: People who correct brain maps or animal videos spend most of their time clicking through software, not drawing from scratch. This paper trains computers to copy those click-by-click habits on toy tasks, then tries the same idea on tracing neurons.

t: BioNIC: Biologically Inspired Neural Network for Image Classification Using Connectomics Principles
sum: This paper builds an image classifier whose wiring is copied from a piece of mouse visual cortex mapped by the MICrONS project. It performs about as well as a normal neural net at guessing facial emotions, which the authors take as a sign that real brain wiring can guide AI design.

t: DevoTG: Temporal Graph Neural Networks for Modeling C. elegans Developmental Connectomics
sum: This paper, according to its abstract, uses time-aware graph networks to follow how the worm’s neurons are born and how their connections change from hatchling to adult, and it finds that remembering history beats a static network model.

t: Hidden symmetries in network connectivity support ring attractor dynamics in the fly’s neural compass
sum: Textbook models of the fly’s internal compass assume neatly symmetric wiring, but real connectomes look messy. This preprint shows how copying cells into “clones” can hide the needed symmetry inside messy weights so the compass still works.

t: In silico neuronal morphology classification: A systematic review.
sum: Computers try to sort neurons by shape, but papers use many different recipes. This review of recent studies finds that neural networks and microscope pictures are now the usual tools, and that accuracy scores dominate how those tools are judged.

t: Inferring Active Neural Circuits Using Diffusion Scores
sum: Brain recordings show which cells light up, not who is driving whom a moment later. This team turns a machine-learning score of activity snapshots into statistical tests for directed, time-lagged links in the worm C. elegans.

t: Representational geometry as a fidelity metric for connectome-constrained networks: evidence from the Drosophila visual system
sum: A model can walk like a fly without thinking like a fly. This paper measures the shape of population responses in fruit-fly visual networks and finds that real wiring makes a cleaner circular map of motion direction than shuffled wiring.

t: Scalable Comparative Connectomics: Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Evolutionary Signatures and Reconstruction Artifacts
sum: Different animals’ neurons might have simple numerical fingerprints. Using three measurements—cable length, synapse count, and partner count—this study trains a classifier that mostly tells species apart, while warning that filling in missing values can fake a biological story.

t: Spatial synaptic regularization stabilizes learning across biological and artificial neural networks
sum: Learning has to add new memories without wiping old ones. This team finds a center-surround pattern of synapse strengths along human cortical dendrites and turns that pattern into a regularizer that helps artificial networks forget less.

t: The Cerebellar Connectome
sum: The cerebellum is more than a motor helper, but its wiring diagram is less mapped than the rest of the brain. This paper assembles thousands of rat tracing studies into a large directed network and looks for hubs and fragile links.

t: Uncovering the Basis of Human Connectome Complexity: The Role of Neuronal Morphology
sum: Human brain cells are bushier than rodent cells, not just bigger. This study uses those 3D shapes to guess where synapses could form and finds that the human shapes produce more complex local wiring.

t: Weight distributions in the fruit-fly and the mouse connectomes
sum: Lists of synapse strengths in fly and mouse visual systems look heavy-tailed. This paper argues the whole network follows one kind of tail, while the busiest cells follow a fatter one, and that incomplete proofreading can change the picture.

t: Learning and criticality in a self-organizing model of connectome growth
sum: Real brain networks have heavy-tailed connection strengths and bursty activity. This model lets pretend neurons avalanche on a modular web and strengthen links when they fire together, reproducing both kinds of statistics without hand-tuning a critical point.

t: The Drosophila Connectome as a Computational Reservoir for Time-Series Prediction
sum: Fruit-fly wiring can be used as a fixed computer network that only trains a thin readout. This study finds that real fly topology and synapse weights resist overfitting better than typical random reservoirs on chaotic time-series tasks.

t: A connectome manipulation framework for the systematic and reproducible study of structure–function relationships through simulations
sum: To learn what a wiring pattern does, you need to change it. This software rewires large simulated rat cortex models in a controlled way and shows that those changes shift which cell groups are driven from inside versus outside the network.

t: Functional imaging and connectome analyses reveal organizing principles of taste circuits in Drosophila
sum: Flies taste sugar, bitter, and more, but it has been unclear how that information is organized in the brain. Combining a wiring diagram with imaging, this team finds that taste types stay mostly separate in the first brain cells, with local neurons acting as hubs to later projection cells.

t: Homogenized $\textit{C. elegans}$ Neural Activity and Connectivity Data
sum: Worm brain data sit in many incompatible files. This project puts calcium recordings and wiring diagrams into one cleaned format so people can study how structure relates to activity.

t: Neurons Underlying Aggression-Like Actions That Are Shared by Both Males and Females in Drosophila
sum: Male and female fruit flies both threaten and fight, but most known aggression cells work in only one sex. Activating a small set of neurons called CL062 produces aggression-like movements in both sexes, even with no opponent nearby.

t: Perisomatic Features Enable Efficient and Dataset Wide Cell-Type Classifications Across Large-Scale Electron Microscopy Volumes
sum: In huge electron-microscope volumes, most neurons are only partly traced. This team shows that measurements around the cell body are often enough to guess the cell type, so rare cells can be found without finishing every axon.

t: Specific inhibition and disinhibition in the higher-order structure of a cortical connectome
sum: Brain cells are often described as teams that excite each other, with inhibition sprayed on everyone. In a piece of mouse visual cortex, inhibition instead aims at particular places in larger wiring patterns that you cannot see if you only look at pairs of cells.

t: Unambiguous identification of asymmetric and symmetric synapses using volume electron microscopy
sum: Inhibitory synapses are thin and easy to miss in 3D electron-microscope pictures, especially after a stain that makes membranes darker. This protocol uses a weaker stain so both excitatory and inhibitory synapses can still be told apart, and it checks the inhibitory ones with a GABA marker.

t: 3D Domain Adaptive Instance Segmentation via Cyclic Segmentation GANs
sum: A computer trained to outline cell nuclei in electron-microscope images may fail on a different kind of microscope. This method learns to both restyle the pictures and outline nuclei in one network, then throws away the restyling part when it is time to run.

t: Connecting Connectomes to Physiology
sum: A wiring diagram is not a movie of brain activity. This viewpoint explains simple math that can reveal hidden loops and slow timescales that come from how cells are connected, not from each cell’s membrane alone.

t: Current Progress and Challenges in Large-Scale 3D Mitochondria Instance Segmentation
sum: Finding every mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope block is harder than on the tiny test cubes used before. A community challenge on human and rat cortex shows that even the best methods still fail on tricky shapes, and that the original scorecard was too easy on false alarms.

t: High-resolution volumetric imaging constrains compartmental models to explore synaptic integration and temporal processing by cochlear nucleus globular bushy cells
sum: Some cochlear-nucleus cells lock spikes to sound timing. This study measures their 3D shape and nerve endings in electron-microscope volumes, then runs those measurements in a computer model to test how the cells add up inputs.

t: Multilevel visual motion opponency in Drosophila
sum: Fruit-fly motion cells are tuned to opposite directions and suppress each other. This paper shows that the same kind of push–pull happens at three successive circuit layers, and that a few strong inhibitory contacts can match many weak excitatory ones.

t: Regional and LTP-Dependent Variation of Synaptic Information Storage Capacity in Rat Hippocampus
sum: Memory may live in how large each dendritic spine is. By grouping spine sizes that do not overlap, this study counts how many distinct “volume notes” hippocampal synapses can play, and finds that a learning protocol increases that number in dentate gyrus.

t: The Intrinsic Similarity of Topological Structure in Biological Neural Networks
sum: Now that several tiny nervous systems have been mapped synapse by synapse, this paper checks whether they share the same kind of network shape. They mostly do: clustered small worlds, similar connection-strength tails, and similar little wiring motifs.

t: Automatic classification and neurotransmitter prediction of synapses in electron microscopy
sum: A complete wiring list still hides whether each connection is a “go” or “stop” signal. This study trains a computer on electron-microscope snapshots of sea-squirt synapses to guess both where synapses are and which chemical they likely use.

t: Circuit analysis of the Drosophila brain using connectivity-based neuronal classification reveals organization of key communication pathways
sum: Instead of sorting fruit-fly neurons only by brain region, this study groups cells that wire to others in the same statistical way. The groups highlight a dopamine-rich core that may stitch senses together, plus other candidate communication routes.

t: Mating-driven variability in olfactory local interneuron wiring
sum: Even a named fruit-fly neuron does not wire the same way in every animal. An inhibitory smell-circuit cell called TC-LN visits different odor maps depending on sex and whether a female has mated, which may change how food odors are treated.

t: RealNeuralNetworks.jl: An Integrated Julia Package for Skeletonization, Morphological Analysis, and Synaptic Connectivity Analysis of Terabyte-Scale 3D Neural Segmentations
sum: Computers that color in neurons still leave a blob, not a stick-figure skeleton. This Julia toolbox turns huge electron-microscope segmentations into skeletons you can measure and compare, shown on a zebrafish dataset in the cloud.

t: Taste quality and hunger interactions in a feeding sensorimotor circuit
sum: A fly starts eating only if food tastes good and the animal is hungry. This paper maps a short brain circuit from taste sensors to the muscles of the feeding snout, and shows hunger boosting an early step while bitter brakes a later step.

t: The brainstem connectome database
sum: The brainstem is a crowded junction of vital pathways, but its directed wiring has been scattered across decades of tracing papers. This database gathers those rat connections so researchers can measure the network and simulate what happens when links weaken, as in multiple sclerosis.

t: A whole-brain monosynaptic input connectome to neuron classes in mouse visual cortex
sum: This team uses a carefully tuned rabies virus to list the cells that talk to chosen neuron types in mouse visual cortex across the whole brain. Different visual areas, layers, and cell classes turn out to have distinct input maps, including a two-stream layout and a special role for layer 6 in linking the two hemispher

t: High-throughput segmentation of unmyelinated axons by deep learning
sum: Most nerve fibers lack myelin and are too numerous to count by hand on electron-microscope pictures. This team trains a computer to outline those fibers in rat nerves and reports that experts spend far less time when the computer drafts first.

t: Large-scale dendritic spine extraction and analysis through petascale computing
sum: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are huge, so computers that trace cells usually cannot keep up. This group runs those tracing programs on a supercomputer, then automatically pulls out dendritic spines so thousands of synapses can be measured together.

t: Mechanisms Underlying Target Selectivity for Cell Types and Subcellular Domains in Developing Neocortical Circuits
sum: Brain cells in the cortex must wire to particular partners and even to particular parts of those partners, but how they choose is still poorly understood. This review gathers the developmental rules that might explain that choice and notes that cortex is especially hard because many cell types sit mixed together.

t: Neurodevelopment: Comparative connectomics and the study of circuit assembly.
sum: A commentary explains a fly-larva study that changed one cell type and then remapped the circuit at synapse resolution. The lesson is that comparing wiring diagrams after a developmental tweak can reveal which rules actually build specific connections.

t: NucMM Dataset: 3D Neuronal Nuclei Instance Segmentation at Sub-Cubic Millimeter Scale
sum: Counting cell nuclei in three-dimensional brain images gets harder as the chunk of tissue gets bigger. This paper releases two large labeled volumes—one fish brain in electron microscopy and one piece of mouse cortex in micro-CT—and a computer method that outlines nuclei more accurately than earlier tools on those data

t: Prefrontal connectomics: from anatomy to human imaging
sum: Maps of the human prefrontal cortex from MRI may not match the actual one-synapse wiring known from monkey anatomy. This review puts those two kinds of map side by side so imaging hubs can be read more carefully.

t: Small brains for big science.
sum: Some insects are almost as small as single cells yet still have brains with thousands of neurons. This opinion piece argues that those tiny brains would be cheaper and faster to map completely than the usual laboratory animals.

t: The conserved core of the nereid brain: Circular CNS, apical nervous system and lhx6-arx-dlx neurons.
sum: A small marine worm’s young brain has now been mapped in unusual detail. This review uses that map to guess which parts of our distant ancestors’ first brain still show up in animals today.

t: Title: Multi-Scale LM/EM Neuronal Imaging from Brain to Synapse with a Tissue Clearing Method, ScaleSF
sum: Brain wiring has to be seen both as a whole-brain sketch and as tiny synapses. This team clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so they can zoom from a whole slice down to a chosen synapse in mouse and marmoset.

t: Where the genome meets the connectome: Understanding how genes shape human brain connectivity
sum: This review asks how genes help build the wiring and activity patterns of the human brain. It compares family studies, DNA-variant studies, and maps of gene activity in brain tissue, and it reports that physical wiring looks more heritable than functional coupling.

t: A Pathoconnectome of Early Neurodegeneration: Network changes in retinal degeneration
sum: When photoreceptors die, the remaining retinal circuit does not simply go quiet—it rewires. This team maps those new and broken connections in a rabbit model of retinitis pigmentosa at electron-microscope resolution.

t: A perspective on C. elegans neurodevelopment: from early visionaries to a booming neuroscience research
sum: The roundworm C. elegans was the first animal with a complete cell lineage, genome, and wiring diagram. This perspective retells how that toolkit still drives discoveries about how nervous systems develop.

t: FlyBrainLab: Accelerating the Discovery of the Functional Logic of the Drosophila Brain in the Connectomic/Synaptomic Era
sum: Fly brains now come with rich wiring and cell-type catalogs that are hard to use together. FlyBrainLab is a software workbench that lets researchers look at those maps in 3D and immediately run them as living circuit models.

t: Gap junctions: historical discoveries and new findings in the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system
sum: Worms use protein pores called gap junctions to let neighboring cells share signals quickly. This review collects what is known about those pores in C. elegans, including special wiring that appears only when the animal enters a stress-resistant dauer state.

t: Network topology of the marmoset connectome
sum: Researchers turned an open map of marmoset cortical wiring into a network sketch. The sketch shows clustered specialist areas plus a tightly linked core that can mix information, a pattern also seen in other animals.

t: Toward an Automated HPC Pipeline for Processing Large Scale Electron Microscopy Data
sum: Electron-microscope movies of brain slices create more data than a desktop can chew. This paper strings together existing tracing programs on a supercomputer so neurons can be reconstructed as the images come in.

t: A blueprint of mammalian cortical connectomes
sum: Four mammals’ cortical wiring diagrams are compared to see what is shared and what is species-specific. Cell-type architecture, not just distance, helps predict which areas connect, and the most central hubs sit in different kinds of cortex in different species.

t: A Cellular-Resolution Atlas of the Larval Zebrafish Brain.
sum: This atlas traces more than two thousand individually labeled neurons in a baby zebrafish brain and parks them in a shared 3D map. Researchers can look up cell shapes, genetic labels, and which brain regions talk to which.

t: A Drosophila larval premotor/motor neuron connectome generating two behaviors via distinct spatio-temporal muscle activity
sum: A crawling fly maggot uses the same motor neurons to walk forward or backward. This team maps the cells that drive those motor neurons and shows, with a model, that one premotor pool can produce both marching orders.

t: Diverse Community Structures in the Neuronal-Level Connectome of the Drosophila Brain
sum: Thousands of individually imaged fly neurons are turned into a brain-wide network sketch. The sketch splits into smell, vision, hearing, and motor neighborhoods, with a tightly linked club of cells in the central complex.

t: Iron-sequestering nanocompartments as multiplexed Electron Microscopy gene reporters
sum: Fluorescent proteins come in many colors, but electron microscopy has had few genetic labels that can be told apart. This team grows two sizes of iron-filled protein cages in cells so a computer can read out two gene reporters on ordinary EM pictures.

t: Neuronal cell types in the annelid Platynereis dumerilii.
sum: A small marine worm’s larva is clear enough that researchers can list its neuron types across the whole body. This review surveys those cell types and notes features, such as swimming with cilia, that fruit flies and roundworms do not have.

t: Synchronization Patterns in Modular Neuronal Networks: A Case Study of C. elegans
sum: This theory paper puts living worm wiring, including chemical “wireless” extrasynaptic links, into a simulation of oscillating neurons. Stronger wireless coupling makes the network less synchronized, while a different grouping of cells can produce split, chimera-like rhythms tied to motor neurons.

t: The head direction circuit of two insect species
sum: Flies and locusts both have a brain compass built from a ring of cells, but the wiring is not identical. This modeling study finds the locust version can still hold a heading, while the fly version updates faster and the locust version shrugs off noise better.

t: Analysis Tools for Large Connectomes
sum: Wiring diagrams of brains are getting so large that analyzing them is becoming harder than collecting them. This essay sorts the needed software into tools for tracing, tools for papers, and tools for simulations, and it argues for a shared public archive.

t: Caenorhabditis elegans and the network control framework—FAQs
sum: This FAQ explains a math framework that asks which worm neurons you must “drive” to control crawling muscles. Some predicted cells were surprising, such as a tail neuron that affects how the animal turns.

t: Connectomics of the zebrafish's lateral-line neuromast reveals wiring and miswiring in a simple microcircuit
sum: In a baby zebrafish’s lateral line, hair cells that point different ways plug into different nerve endings with striking precision. Mutants that scramble cell orientation still wire specifically, pointing to a molecular identity signal rather than to cells simply firing together.

t: Cross-Species Evidence of Interplay Between Neural Connectivity at the Micro- and Macroscale of Connectome Organization in Human, Mouse, and Rat Brain
sum: In humans, mice, and rats, brain areas whose neurons are larger or more complex also tend to send more long-range cables. This paper treats that micro-to-macro match as a shared design feature of mammalian cortex.

t: Geppetto: a reusable modular open platform for exploring neuroscience data and models
sum: Many neuroscience websites need the same 3D viewers and simulation knobs. Geppetto is shared plumbing so fly atlases, worm simulations, and NEURON interfaces do not each rebuild those pieces from scratch.

t: The importance of the whole: Topological data analysis for the network neuroscientist
sum: Ordinary brain-network maps only count pairwise links and can miss holes and loops in the wiring. This tutorial teaches a topological method that tracks those holes as connections are added, with examples from mouse, worm, and genome data.

t: Connectomic Analysis of Brain Networks: Novel Techniques and Future Directions
sum: To map who talks to whom in a brain, researchers must see individual cells and their synapses, which is hard because the wires are tiny and long. This review surveys new stains, tissue-clearing tricks, and microscopes that make those maps more practical.

t: Connectomics at cellular precision
sum: Seeing every connection in a piece of brain is still extremely hard because even a tiny cube contains huge numbers of cells and synapses. This short overview argues that such maps have already explained motion detection in the eye, while cortex-scale maps were not yet routine.

t: Eye-Trace: Segmentation of Volumetric Microscopy Images with Eyegaze
sum: Following a neuron through a stack of microscope pictures usually means slow mouse clicks. Here people steer with a gamepad and their eye gaze, so looking at a fiber is enough to trace it, at tens of sections per second.

t: Recent advancement in the challenges to connectomics.
sum: Brain-wiring maps now come from both light and electron microscopes, and the pictures are so complex that computers must help analyze them. This review argues that mixing those imaging methods is the way to learn how complete maps relate to brain function.

t: Rod-Cone Crossover Connectome of Mammalian Bipolar Cells
sum: Night vision and day vision compete so that one mode can dominate. This rabbit-retina wiring map shows many inhibitory side-paths between rod and cone bipolar cells that could flip that switch.

t: SANTIAGO: Spine Association for Neuron Topology Improvement and Graph Optimization
sum: Tiny dendritic spines often break off in computer traces of electron-microscope images, which hides real connections. This method glues spines back onto the right dendrites using biological rules about how spines attach.

t: Statistical Analysis of Tract-Tracing Experiments Demonstrates a Dense, Complex Cortical Network in the Mouse
sum: Many weak wires between mouse cortical areas are easy to miss in noisy tracer pictures. A statistical model that separates real signal from background finds the cortex is much more densely connected than earlier estimates, including extremely faint links.

t: High-performance probes for light and electron microscopy
sum: Standard fluorescent tags often fail to light up the tiniest bits of a neuron and run out of colors. These ‘spaghetti monster’ proteins display many antibody handles so weakly expressed molecules and several cell types can be seen at once, even in electron-microscope preparations.

t: Exploring the third dimension: volume electron microscopy comes of age.
sum: Electron microscopes can now grind or slice through a sample automatically to make 3D pictures of cells. This review explains those machines and how pairing them with light microscopy could become routine.

t: From Caenorhabditis elegans to the human connectome: a specific modular organization increases metabolic, functional and developmental efficiency
sum: Brain wiring is grouped into modules, but that grouping does not explain everything. Compared with shuffled networks that keep the same modules, real worm and human maps cluster more locally, take longer global paths, use less wire, and look simpler to specify.

t: Structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions.
sum: This study maps synapses between two hippocampal areas and finds they are not sprinkled evenly. Cells born around the same time cluster their connections, which may help dendrites process information.

t: Automated Transmission-Mode Scanning Electron Microscopy (tSEM) for Large Volume Analysis at Nanoscale Resolution
sum: Ordinary transmission electron microscopes see a very small patch of tissue at a time. This scanning-microscope setup photographs much larger patches at the same fine pixel size, so more of a circuit can be imaged automatically.

t: CoCoMac 2.0 and the future of tract-tracing databases
sum: Decades of monkey tracer studies live in a database called CoCoMac. This perspective relaunches that database with better search and downloadable wiring matrices, and asks how it should sit beside new imaging methods.

t: Functional specificity of local synaptic connections in neocortical networks
sum: Nearby cells in mouse visual cortex are not randomly wired. Cells that like the same visual patterns are more likely to be synaptically connected, including two-way links.

t: Q&A: What is the Open Connectome Project?
sum: Huge electron-microscope pictures of brain wiring used to sit on private disks. This Q&A explains a project that put such images on the web so anyone could browse them.

t: Segmentation fusion for connectomics
sum: Computers tracing neurons in a stack of electron-microscope slices often decide one picture at a time and then get stuck. This method lists many possible 2D cuts, then picks the combination that makes the whole 3D volume consistent.

t: Neurogeometry and potential synaptic connectivity.
sum: If you know the 3D shapes of axons and dendrites, you can count places where they come close enough that a synapse could form. This review calls those places potential synapses and uses them to think about wiring specificity and plasticity.

t: A Computational Perspective on the No-Strong-Loops Principle in Brain Networks
sum: Brain areas often send a strong signal forward and only a weaker signal back, avoiding tight loops. Computer models here suggest that pattern helps networks remember more, while strong two-way loops hurt memory capacity.

t: Brain-wide mapping of oligodendrocyte organization, oligodendrogenesis, and myelin injury
sum: The cells that wrap brain wires with myelin are mapped here across the whole mouse brain as animals age and in disease. Some regions stay resilient; others lose myelin, including near Alzheimer’s-like plaques.

t: Deep conservation of head direction circuits in bees, ants and flies
sum: Flies, bees, and ants appear to use the same compass cell types in a brain navigation center, a layout stable for hundreds of millions of years. The fine synaptic wiring still differs, which models say can retune the compass without replacing it.

t: FLYNN: Robust Neural Network for Robot Navigation using Fly Brain Topology
sum: Instead of inventing a robot brain from scratch, this work copies the fruit fly’s wiring diagram into a neural net that steers in simulation. The copied network kept working when the camera failed, unlike ordinary nets of similar size.

t: From homeostasis to credit assignment: a signed-XOR connectomic motif for local directional error signalling
sum: When a brain prediction is wrong, a synapse needs a local hint about whether to get stronger or weaker. The authors describe a small eight-cell wiring pattern that could send those two opposite messages, and they find it more often than chance in worm, fly, and mouse maps.

t: From local motifs to global dynamical stability in the mouse brain connectome
sum: Using a detailed but sparse map of mouse brain connections, this study finds two-way links everywhere and hubs that stitch modules together. Simulations suggest the wiring is built to stay stable rather than to maximize memory tricks.

t: Mapping brain-wide monosynaptic inputs to single neurons with ROInet-seq.
sum: A modified rabies virus tags each infected brain cell with a unique barcode so many cells’ incoming connections can be read out by sequencing. Applied in mouse cortex, a few thalamic cells fan out to many cortical cells, while cortical inputs often converge.

t: Mitotic lineage adds predictive information beyond cell type in the C. elegans connectome
sum: Worm neurons remember their family tree from cell divisions. Knowing that tree helps predict who synapses with whom, even after you already know each cell’s type.

t: Multisensory learning recruits visual neurons into an olfactory memory engram
sum: Flies remember better if a smell and a color are learned together, and later either cue can bring back the memory. The extra performance depends on visual mushroom-body cells and a serotonergic neuron that can link smell and color channels.

t: NeuroMArVL: An interactive and collaborative web-based tool for visualizing brain networks
sum: Brain-network figures in papers are usually one frozen picture. This free web tool lets you flip between a brain-shaped view and a blob-and-line graph view and send colleagues a link to the exact display.

t: Precise kinematic and muscle recording in freely behaving flies enabled by closed-loop tracking and annotation-free pose estimation
sum: Fruit flies are filmed walking freely while a camera chases them, capturing fine limb motion and glowing muscle activity. A computer trained on simulated flies estimates 3D pose without hand-labeling frames.

t: State-Dependent Organization of Microscale Functional Circuitry in Visual Cortex
sum: From calcium movies of tens of thousands of mouse visual-cortex cells, this study infers who influences whom, and checks those guesses against electron-microscope synapses. The directed map changes with arousal: different layers dominate when the pupil is small versus large.

t: Whole-Brain Connectomic Graph Model Enables Whole-Body Locomotion Control in Fruit Fly
sum: A fruit-fly wiring diagram is turned into the “brain” of a simulated fly that learns to walk and turn. The connectome-shaped controller learns more efficiently than generic networks and makes the flow of information easier to interpret.

t: Neuromorphic hierarchical modular reservoirs
sum: Brains are organized as nested clusters of clusters. This study builds artificial networks with that nested layout and shows they remember better, juggle more tasks, and produce more brain-like timing than flatter or random networks.

t: A circuit motif for color in the human foveal retina
sum: Color vision starts when the eye compares three kinds of cone cells. This team maps those comparisons in the human fovea and finds that the classic “red–green” and “blue–yellow” paths already mix in an excitatory circuit, which may help explain trichromatic color.

t: A recurrent neural circuit in Drosophila temporally sharpens visual inputs
sum: When a fly moves, the world blurs, yet it still needs sharp edges. This study shows that early visual cells use a feedback loop to sharpen contrast over time, and that the loop can be retuned when the fly is more active.

t: A scalable and modular computational pipeline for axonal connectomics: automated tracing and assembly of axons across serial sections
sum: Mapping single axons across a whole human brain is still out of reach for electron microscopy. This computational pipeline stitches serial light-microscope sections by following the axons themselves so long-range fibers can be traced at mesoscale.

t: A simulated annealing algorithm for randomizing weighted networks
sum: To tell whether a brain-network pattern is special, scientists scramble the network and look again. This paper’s scramble keeps each region’s total connection strength, which can change conclusions about hubs compared with older methods that only count links.

t: Cognitive limits of larval Drosophila: testing for conditioned inhibition, sensory preconditioning, and second-order conditioning
sum: Fruit-fly larvae can learn that a smell predicts no reward, a slightly more complex trick than simple pairing. They did not, in these tests, show two other forms of higher-order learning that adult flies and bees can do.

t: Connectome Projects and Mentality
sum: This commentary says wiring diagrams of synapses leave out the gel that wraps every neuron. The authors think memories may be stored as chemical complexes in that gel, so connectome maps alone cannot explain thoughts or feelings.

t: Descending control and regulation of spontaneous flight turns in Drosophila
sum: Flying fruit flies make quick body turns when searching locally and fly straight when traveling far. This team finds four descending neurons that command the turns and a large inhibitory cell that can silence them.

t: From Worms to Mice: Homeostasis Maybe All You Need
sum: This short commentary asks whether a tiny mix of “on” and “off” connections, like an XOR logic gate, is a repeated motif from worms to mice. Counting it in published wiring diagrams, the author suggests homeostasis alone might steer learning.

t: NeuroVerse: Immersive exploration of 3D ultrastructural brain reconstructions for education and collaborative analysis
sum: Electron-microscope reconstructions of brain cells are usually stuck on a scientist’s computer. This project puts those 3D models into a shared virtual-reality space so students and labs can walk around them together.

t: Somatotopic organization among parallel sensory pathways that promote a grooming sequence in Drosophila
sum: Flies wipe dust off their heads in a set order. This team maps almost all of the touch sensors on the fly head into the brain, showing that each patch of bristles has its own path and that together they can trigger the full wiping sequence.

t: Volume Electron Microscopy for Genetically and Molecularly Defined Neural Circuits.
sum: Electron-microscope wiring maps see shape but not always which genes a cell expresses. This review covers new labels and combined-microscope methods meant to put molecular identity into those 3D maps, including circuits that use dopamine.

t: What do the mushroom bodies do for the insect brain? Twenty-five years of progress
sum: Twenty-five years after a landmark journal issue, this editorial says the insect mushroom body is now a working circuit diagram for learning. Shared wiring maps and genetic tools, not only new molecules, made that possible.

t: Compression-based inference of network motif sets
sum: Instead of asking whether a little wiring pattern is “surprisingly common,” this method asks which set of patterns best compresses the network. That gives a fairer way to compare motifs in real brain wiring diagrams.

t: Dissecting the Functional Organization of the C. elegans Serotonergic System at Whole-Brain Scale
sum: Serotonin makes a worm slow down and eat more, but it hits many receptors across the brain. This study names the key receptors, watches the whole brain, and shows how the wiring diagram plus receptor locations predict which cells join in.

t: ElegansNet: a brief scientific report and initial experiments
sum: Researchers copy the worm’s wiring diagram into a deep network for image tasks. They report that this bio-shaped net beats randomly rewired copies and scores extremely high on standard vision benchmarks.

t: How Flies See Motion.
sum: Fruit flies are a showcase for how brains detect which way things move. This review gathers the cells, chemicals, and wiring that compute motion and explains why simply shutting off one input cell can be misleading.

t: Inferring Neuron-level Brain Circuit Connection via Graph Neural Network Amidst Small Established Connections
sum: Once some of a brain’s connections are known, a graph network tries to guess the rest from who is already linked to whom. The authors report high accuracy on fly and worm wiring diagrams using only a small fraction of known links.

t: Learning and memory using Drosophila melanogaster: a focus on advances made in the fifth decade of research
sum: This review tours a decade of fruit-fly memory research: new output cells from the learning center, how dopamine writes good versus bad memories, and how the brain also actively forgets. Wiring diagrams now sit underneath those stories.

t: Molecular logic of neuromodulatory systems in the zebrafish telencephalon
sum: Brain cells are not only wired by synapses; they are also bathed in chemical messengers. This zebrafish atlas shows each cell type listens to many messengers but really “turns up” only a few, and some types look related to those in other vertebrates.

t: Neuronal motifs reveal backbone structure and influential neurons of neural network in C. elegans
sum: Worm wiring is usually drawn as one kind of arrow, but chemical synapses and electrical gap junctions are different. Splitting them reveals new repeating triangles and a “backbone” the authors say is important for movement, plus a ranked list of influential cells.

t: Postsynaptic cell type and synaptic distance do not determine efficiency of monosynaptic rabies virus spread measured at synaptic resolution
sum: A popular virus that hops one synapse backward does not label every input. In mouse visual cortex, under typical conditions, it marked about two in five excitatory contacts, and that fraction did not depend on cell type or how far the synapse sat from the cell body.

t: Presynaptic inhibition selectively suppresses leg proprioception in behaving Drosophila
sum: When a fly walks, it still needs to know where its legs are, but it may not want a flood of movement signals. This study finds a spinal-cord-like circuit that turns down movement sensors during self-made steps, using a prediction from the brain.

t: The cellular architecture of memory modules in Drosophila supports stochastic input integration
sum: A fly memory-output cell receives almost a thousand input wires. A detailed model says those inputs count roughly equally no matter where they sit on the tree, so the circuit can use messy, random connections and still learn many smells.

t: X-Ray2EM: Uncertainty-Aware Cross-Modality Image Reconstruction from X-Ray to Electron Microscopy in Connectomics
sum: X-rays can scan thick brain tissue faster than slicing it for electron microscopy, but the pictures are blurrier. This model tries to paint EM-like membranes onto X-ray volumes so computers can trace cells more easily.

t: Connectomic analysis of thalamus-driven disinhibition in cortical layer 4
sum: When a whisker signal hits cortex, it does not only excite cells; it also turns selected inhibitory cells on in a precise pattern. Mapping those connections in a mouse barrel, the authors find a disinhibitory loop that could open different time windows for two kinds of excitatory neurons.

t: Connectomics: Relating synaptic connectivity to physiology.
sum: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing how the circuit computes. This short commentary explains a fly study that links synapses to physiology and sketches how modelers might use that link.

t: Instance Segmentation of Unlabeled Modalities via Cyclic Segmentation GAN
sum: Labeling every nucleus in a new kind of microscope image is slow. This method learns to both paint one image type into another and find each nucleus, using unlabeled examples of the new type, and it beats doing those two steps separately.

t: Neural model generating klinotaxis behavior accompanied by a random walk based on C. elegans connectome
sum: Worms climb salt gradients while still wandering. This simulation uses the worm’s wiring, a more realistic nose cell, and noisy synapses to get both steering and random walking from the network instead of adding wandering by hand.

t: Reconstructing neural circuits using multiresolution correlated light and electron microscopy
sum: Light microscopy can show which cells are active or labeled, but electron microscopy is needed to see their synapses. This team images the same mouse tissue at several zoom levels so they only spend high-resolution EM time on the cells they already know from light.

t: Scale matters: The nested human connectome
sum: Human brain wiring can be mapped with MRI of the whole brain or with microscopes that see single axons, but those views live at very different zoom levels. This Science piece argues we need ways to combine them, and to show how sure we are about each pathway.

t: A Novel and Functionally Diverse Class of Acetylcholine-Gated Ion Channels
sum: In the worm, acetylcholine is not only an on-switch: some newly characterized channels prefer choline and can turn cells down instead of up. The authors use those receptors to guess which connections in the wiring diagram are excitatory or inhibitory.

t: A specialized spinal circuit for command amplification and directionality during escape behavior
sum: When a fish must dart left or right to escape, the spinal cord—not only the brain—helps choose the side. This study finds a repeating class of spinal cells that amplify the brain’s escape command and send it straight to motor neurons via axon-to-axon synapses.

t: Architectures of Neuronal Circuits
sum: Brain cells do not work alone: they are wired into repeating patterns, like feedforward loops and maps of neighboring cells. This review collects those patterns and asks how they are built in development and evolution.

t: Ascaris suum Informs Extrasynaptic Volume Transmission in Nematodes
sum: Worm wiring diagrams show synapses, but chemical messages can also travel in the body fluid. This study finds a peptide in the pig-parasite worm’s body fluid that can reach reproductive muscle even without a direct synaptic connection.

t: Conserved Circuits for Direction Selectivity in the Primate Retina
sum: Other mammals compute motion direction in the retina; primates were thought to wait until visual cortex. This preprint reconstructs macaque retinal wiring and finds a conserved circuit that could compute direction much earlier than expected.

t: Forward and backward locomotion patterns in C. elegans generated by a connectome-based model simulation
sum: The tiny worm walks forward and backward with a small set of motor neurons. This team trains a wiring-based computer model until the virtual muscles oscillate in both directions and can switch when a command-like input flips.

t: Model-based Comparison of Current Flow in Rod Bipolar Cells of Healthy and Early-Stage Degenerated Retina
sum: When the retina starts to degenerate, rod bipolar cells still look similar but they receive input from fewer rods. Computer models built from electron-microscope wiring diagrams predict those cells sit at a lower voltage, which matters for designing retinal implants.

t: Origins of direction selectivity in the primate retina
sum: Textbooks often say primates compute visual motion in cortex, not in the eye. This study records from macaque retina and traces its wiring, and finds cells that already prefer motion in particular directions.

t: Promisomics and the Short-Circuiting of Mind
sum: Some neuroscientists talk as if a complete map of every synapse would explain a mouse’s mind. This commentary says a wiring diagram is still just a map of one level, not a theory of thought or behavior.

t: The Drosophila Larval Locomotor Circuit Provides a Model to Understand Neural Circuit Development and Function
sum: Fruit-fly maggots crawl using a small, well-mapped set of nerve cells. This review explains why that crawling circuit is a good stand-in for studying how any motor circuit is built and how it can differ between individuals.

t: Wired For Insight- Recent Advance in C. elegans Neural Circuits
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram is famous, but it is still being updated, and new genetic tools let researchers turn single cells on and off in a crawling animal. This short review collects those advances, including signals between gut and brain.

t: Geometric framework to predict structure from function in neural networks
sum: Lots of different wiring diagrams can make a network behave the same way. This theory paper describes a geometric test for when a synapse must exist if the network is to produce a given set of responses.

t: Latent Feature Representation via Unsupervised Learning for Pattern Discovery in Massive Electron Microscopy Image Volumes
sum: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are too big to browse by hand. This method teaches a computer to group similar-looking bits of image so a scientist can click an interesting blob and find more like it.

t: Microtubule Tracking in Electron Microscopy Volumes
sum: Tiny tubes inside neurons are visible in electron-microscope pictures and can help check whether a cell was traced correctly. This paper teaches a computer to follow those tubes much faster and more accurately than earlier software.

t: Multiscale ATUM-FIB Microscopy Enables Targeted Ultrastructural Analysis at Isotropic Resolution
sum: Researchers often must choose between seeing a large piece of tissue coarsely or a tiny piece in fine 3D. This hybrid method slices the tissue into thick-ish sheets, finds the rare spot of interest, then zooms in with ion-beam electron microscopy.

t: The connectome
sum: A connectome is a map of how parts of the nervous system are linked, whether those parts are single cells or whole brain areas. This textbook chapter explains the idea and how it is used in human brain research.

t: The Mixture Graph-A Data Structure for Compressing, Rendering, and Querying Segmentation Histograms
sum: When a 3D scan is labeled with many cell IDs, zooming out mixes those labels and the picture can flicker or lie. This data structure stores those mixes compactly so you can still render and ask “what labels are in this box?” quickly.

t: Towards a functional connectome in Drosophila
sum: Complete fruit-fly brain wiring diagrams were on the way, building on the worm’s famous map. This perspective says those maps will help, but they will also show that brain parts are more mixed together than textbook circuits suggest.

t: Connectome verification: inter-rater and connection reliability of tract-tracing-based intrinsic hypothalamic connectivity
sum: When scientists copy wiring information out of old tracing papers, they may not all copy the same links. This study has several experts read the same hypothalamus papers and measures how much their connection lists disagree.

t: Deciphering neural circuits for Caenorhabditis elegans behavior by computations and perturbations to genome and connectome
sum: The worm is the only animal with a full wiring diagram, a mapped genome, and simple measurable behaviors. This review asks how far computer models and genetic or cell perturbations have gone toward explaining how that animal moves.

t: Dynamic Computational Model of the Human Spinal Cord Connectome
sum: Most wiring maps are of the brain, not the spinal cord. This paper builds a first-draft computer model of human spinal circuits from published anatomy and uses it to think about spinal stimulation for pain.

t: MagC, magnetic collection of ultrathin sections for volumetric correlative light and electron microscopy
sum: Picking up thousands of extremely thin tissue slices by hand is slow and easy to ruin. This method adds a magnetic bit of plastic so a magnet can gather the slices onto a wafer for both light and electron microscopy.

t: Multiplexed peroxidase-based electron microscopy labeling enables simultaneous visualization of multiple cell types
sum: Electron microscopy shows synapses clearly but usually cannot tell which genetic cell types they belong to. This team stains different cell classes with a darker enzyme targeted to different parts of the cell so several types can be seen at once.

t: Novel Technological Advances in Functional Connectomics in C. elegans
sum: We know every synapse in the worm, but that still does not tell us how it behaves. This review covers tools that watch, turn on, or turn off cells in the living animal, and computer models that try to put those measurements together.

t: Reconstruction of 1,000 projection neurons reveals new cell types and organization of long-range connectivity in the mouse brain
sum: A neuron’s long-distance cable can wander through much of the mouse brain, but those cables are rarely traced from end to end. This project images and draws more than a thousand complete cells and puts them in an online atlas.

t: Spectral peculiarity and criticality of a human connectome.
sum: Researchers compared the “sound” of brain-network graphs across animals by looking at their mathematical spectra. The human map stood out, and its spacing of graph frequencies looked like a physical system sitting at a critical point.

t: CDeep3M - Plug-and-Play cloud based deep learning for image segmentation
sum: Powerful image-segmentation networks often stay locked in expert labs because the software is hard to install. This team puts a ready-made deep-learning segmenter in the cloud so other groups can train it on their microscope pictures.

t: Domain Adaptive Segmentation In Volume Electron Microscopy Imaging
sum: A computer trained to outline mitochondria in one kind of electron-microscope image often fails on another lab’s images. This paper adds a reconstruction task so the network learns features that transfer, needing fewer new hand labels.

t: Neuronal Identity: The neuron types of a simple chordate sibling, the tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis.
sum: A tiny sea-squirt larva has a complete wiring diagram of its small nervous system. This review catalogs the cell types in that map and warns that they are not just miniature vertebrate neurons.

t: Rewiring the connectome: Evidence and effects
sum: Brain maps often assume the wires stay put after they form. This review argues that local circuits do rewire during learning, which could matter for treating brain disease.

t: Schaffer Collateral Inputs to CA1 Excitatory and Inhibitory Neurons Follow Different Connectivity Rules
sum: The same incoming axons in mouse hippocampus wire onto excitatory and inhibitory cells in different ways. Excitatory cells get a patterned map; a major inhibitory class looks more random.

t: The Worm Connectome: Back to the Future.
sum: The first complete animal wiring diagram was the worm, finished in 1986 by hand. This essay says that map still teaches both the power and the limits of connectomics.

t: Volume EM Reconstruction of Spinal Cord Reveals Wiring Specificity in Speed-Related Motor Circuits.
sum: Fish swim by turning on bigger motor cells as they go faster. This study maps every local wire onto those cells in a stretch of larval zebrafish spinal cord and finds that some interneurons pick their motor targets on purpose.

t: Volumetric reconstruction of main Caenorhabditis elegans neuropil at two different time points
sum: In the worm’s nerve ring, being next to another cell is not enough to predict a synapse. This preprint rebuilds the 3D shapes of those processes at two ages and finds extra, non-spatial rules are needed.

t: Connectomics of synaptic microcircuits: lessons from the outer retina
sum: Rod and cone pathways in the eye were thought to meet later in the circuit. This review of a 3D electron-microscope map of mouse outer retina finds they already mix at the first synapse, with several exceptions to the textbook wiring.

t: Deep Learning Improves Template Matching by Normalized Cross Correlation
sum: Stitching electron-microscope slices into a 3D brain volume depends on matching image patches. A neural net that pre-cleans those patches makes the classic matching method much less error-prone.

t: Guiding network analysis using graph slepians: an illustration for the C. Elegans connectome
sum: Network maps can be viewed through a mathematical lens that zooms in on one group of cells while still remembering the whole worm. The authors illustrate that trick on the C. elegans wiring diagram.

t: Multichannel activity propagation across an engineered axon network
sum: Instead of mapping a whole brain, this team grows two clumps of cortex linked by a long bundle of axons. They then watch how patterns of activity change as they travel from one clump to the other.

t: Semiparametric spectral modeling of the Drosophila connectome
sum: Statisticians take the wiring diagram of a larval fruit-fly learning center and draw a compact map of each cell. The map is meant to show hidden structure, not just the four textbook cell classes.

t: Synaptic organization of visual space in primary visual cortex
sum: A visual-cortex cell sees a small patch of the world, but its dendrites also listen to other patches. This study maps those listening posts on individual spines and finds they prefer partners that line up with the cell’s favorite orientation.

t: Reconstruction of Neural Circuits Using Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy
sum: This methods report shows how to reconstruct synapses in a piece of rat hippocampus by shaving the sample inside a scanning electron microscope. The pictures come out already aligned, which saves a lot of stitching work.

t: Toward Whole-Body Connectomics
sum: Most connectome projects map only the brain. This lecture-based essay says we also need the nerves of the rest of the body if we want to explain real behavior.

t: Specification of synaptic connectivity by cell surface interactions
sum: Neurons may choose their partners using families of sticky surface proteins. This review discusses several of those protein families and how they might help build precise circuits.

t: Automatic discovery of cell types and microcircuitry from neural connectomics
sum: Instead of naming cell types by hand, this method lets a statistical model group neurons from their wiring and positions. It works on retina and worm data, and even on the transistors of an old computer chip.

t: Motif-Role-Fingerprints: The Building-Blocks of Motifs, Clustering-Coefficients and Transitivities in Directed Networks
sum: When scientists count little wiring triangles in a brain graph, they are really counting how each cell sits inside those triangles. This math paper shows those cell-level counts are the building blocks of several popular network scores.

t: Polarity-specific high-level information propagation in neural networks
sum: Brain networks have an in door, a middle, and an out door. Measuring how signals travel along those directions, not just along shortest shortcuts, shows worm and fly circuits mix and route information more efficiently than simple small-world models.

t: The AII amacrine cell connectome: a dense network hub
sum: A famous retinal cell that helps you see in dim light turns out to talk to at least 28 kinds of partners. Far from a simple relay, it sits at the center of several rod and cone networks.

t: Deconstructing Complexity: Serial Block-Face Electron Microscopic Analysis of the Hippocampal Mossy Fiber Synapse
sum: The giant mossy-fiber synapse in hippocampus is built in stages after birth. Volume electron microscopy shows early contacts on the dendritic shaft, a messy exploratory phase, then a cleaned-up adult structure.

t: ON Cone Bipolar Cell Axonal Synapses in the OFF Inner Plexiform Layer of the Rabbit Retina
sum: Textbooks split the inner retina into ON and OFF layers. A rabbit connectome shows ON bipolar axons still making synapses in the so-called OFF layer, creating extra mixing and crossover circuits.

t: From functional architecture to functional connectomics
