sum: A classic 1962 vision paper taught us that cortex is organized in columns. This essay explains how that idea splits into ‘where a cell sits,’ ‘what type it is,’ and ‘what it encodes,’ and why the last piece was still the hardest to map in 2012.

t: Graph Theoretical Model of a Sensorimotor Connectome in Zebrafish
sum: Researchers built a detailed wiring model of how a larval zebrafish feels water flow and turns its body. The model looks small-world, and cutting out three famous command cells shortens the easy paths from sensors to muscles.

t: Interactive Volume Exploration of Petascale Microscopy Data Streams Using a Visualization-Driven Virtual Memory Approach
sum: Electron microscopes can pour out more pictures than a computer can store as a finished 3D pyramid. This paper describes a viewer that builds only the pieces of the volume you are actually looking at.

t: Visualizing Neuromodulation In Vivo: TANGO-Mapping of Dopamine Signaling Reveals Appeptite Control of Sugar Sensing
sum: A connectome list of synapses cannot tell you how a hungry fly will act, because chemicals such as dopamine retune the circuit. This paper introduces a genetic map of where dopamine lands and shows it turns up sugar sensors when the fly is hungry.

t: Large-scale automated histology in the pursuit of connectomes
sum: To understand how brains compute and how they are fueled, we need maps of both synapses and blood vessels. This 2011 survey sketches the microscopes and software then being built to draw those maps automatically.

t: Multiscale Exploration of Mouse Brain Microstructures Using the Knife-Edge Scanning Microscope Brain Atlas
sum: A special microscope can photograph an entire mouse brain in fine detail, but the files are huge. This paper describes a web atlas so researchers can zoom from the whole brain down toward cells and vessels.

t: Specificity and randomness: structure-function relationships in neural circuits
sum: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing what the circuit computes. This review explains new ways to match each cell’s sensory responses to its synapses in the eye and in visual cortex.

t: From the Connectome to the Synaptome: An Epic Love Story
sum: Listing every human brain synapse is probably impossible. This essay says we should instead build statistical models of synapses that still connect to larger-scale brain maps.

t: Ssecrett and NeuroTrace: Interactive Visualization and Analysis Tools for Large-Scale Neuroscience Data Sets
sum: Modern electron microscopes create brain-image files so large that ordinary viewers choke. This paper introduces two tools meant to let scientists browse and analyze those volumes while tracing neurons.

t: Scalable and Interactive Segmentation and Visualization of Neural Processes in EM Datasets
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are huge and hard to trace by hand. NeuroTrace is an early interactive computer tool that helps people follow nerve fibers through those pictures in 3D.

t: The Interscutularis Muscle Connectome
sum: Only the worm had a complete wiring diagram of a circuit. This team maps every motor nerve and muscle fiber in a small mouse ear muscle and finds the wiring is variable, not a neat shortest-path plan.

t: Gene Expression of Caenorhabditis elegans Neurons Carries Information on Their Synaptic Connectivity
sum: In the worm, scientists already know both the wiring diagram and which genes many neurons express. This study asks whether a cell’s gene list can predict who it connects to, and finds that it can, at least in part.

t: Three-Dimensional Structure and Composition of CA3→CA1 Axons in Rat Hippocampal Slices: Implications for Presynaptic Connectivity and Compartmentalization
sum: In the hippocampus, the axons that carry messages from CA3 to CA1 are not a string of identical beads. Serial electron microscopy shows boutons of many sizes, many without mitochondria, and thin necks that could keep each bouton chemically private.

t: A High-Performance Computing Portal Applied to 3D Electron Microscopy
sum: Three-dimensional electron-microscope volumes are now so large they need supercomputers. This paper describes a website, 3dem.org, that lets microscopy labs run that computing in a browser.

t: Caenorhabditis elegans in neuroscience: from neural communication to neurodegenerative disease modeling
sum: The roundworm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram and genes that often match ours. This review explains how scientists use that simple nervous system to study aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s.

t: Connectomic analysis reveals the axial circuit for self-righting posture control in Drosophila
sum: When a fruit-fly maggot is flipped on its back, it rights itself with a stereotyped twist. This preprint maps the nerve cells for that maneuver along the body and shows the circuit shares parts with rolling and crawling.

t: Diffusion Model-Based Data Augmentation for Enhanced Neuron Segmentation
sum: Teaching computers to trace neurons in electron-microscope images usually needs lots of hand-drawn labels. This team uses a diffusion model to invent extra realistic training images so the tracer can learn from fewer real labels.

t: Digging Deep into Alzheimer Disease: How Electron Microscopy Helps Elucidating Its Pathogenesis
sum: Alzheimer disease changes cells in ways too small for ordinary microscopes. This review traces how electron microscopy, from the 1960s to modern 3D and cryo methods, has shown plaques, tangles, and damaged organelles up close.

t: Evidence for a Functional Proximity Law in Multilayer Networks
sum: This preprint argues that important hubs in one layer of a network stay important in other, similar layers. One of the tests uses the fruit-fly larva wiring diagram.

t: From small brains to smart machines: translating Caenorhabditis elegans neural circuits into artificial intelligence
sum: The worm’s tiny, fully mapped nervous system still produces flexible behavior. This short review asks what artificial intelligence could learn from that efficient wiring.

t: Impact of Aii Amacrine Cell Rewiring in a Pathoconnectome-Based Computational Model of Early Retinal Degeneration
sum: In a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration, the inner retina rewires as rods die. This preprint models how changes onto Aii amacrine cells can make ganglion cells fire in abnormal rhythms.

t: Imprecision in Vision: Lessons From Neural Circuits in the Fly
sum: Fly eyes look like a repeating grid of identical units, which should make vision the same everywhere. This essay uses wiring diagrams to argue that cells of one named type still differ in who they connect to.

t: Perfusion quality does not necessarily predict ultrastructural preservation after hyperosmotic brain perfusion
sum: Flushing a brain with fixative can look successful from the outside or on a scan and still ruin the fine structure needed for wiring diagrams. This technical report shows that extra dehydrating chemicals can cause that mismatch.

t: Probing molecular diversity and ultrastructure of brain cells with fluorescent aptamers
sum: Wiring diagrams from electron microscopy usually cannot tell you a cell’s molecular type. This method uses small DNA-like aptamer labels that glow under light microscopy without soap that would wreck the membranes needed for EM.

t: RAEM: random-access electron microscopy for revisitable 3D imaging
sum: Electron microscopy at full detail is too slow for whole large samples. RAEM first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the microscope back only to the spots that matter, like selected synapses or mitochondria.

t: Sexual dimorphism in the nervous system: Three principles from the nematode C. elegans
sum: Male and hermaphrodite worms do not have identical nervous systems. This review sorts the differences into three ideas: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different physiological ‘mode’.

t: A lightweight data-driven spiking neuronal network model of Drosophila olfactory nervous system with dedicated hardware support
sum: Fruit-fly smell circuits are small enough to simulate neuron by neuron. This team built a lightweight spiking model from the fly connectome and ran it in real time on a small custom chip.

t: Compensatory enhancement of input maintains aversive dopaminergic reinforcement in hungry Drosophila
sum: Hungry flies still need to learn what to avoid, even while hunger quiets some dopamine neurons so they will seek food. This study finds a hormone pathway that turns up incoming signals to keep punishment learning working.

t: Connectome-based prediction of functional impairment in experimental stroke models
sum: A stroke in one place can silence far-away brain areas that were never directly damaged. This rat study uses a whole-brain connection map to predict those remote effects, especially in the hippocampus.

t: Discriminating neural ensemble patterns through dendritic computations in randomly connected feedforward networks
sum: Brain cells might read combinations of incoming messages if those inputs land close together on a dendrite. This modeling paper argues that even random wiring is often enough to create those clusters.

t: Dynamic encoding of temperature in the central circadian circuit coordinates physiological activities
sum: Fruit flies change walking and sleep when the temperature changes, on top of their daily clock. This study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and then push one downstream path for evening movement and another for nighttime sleep.

t: FISBe: A Real-World Benchmark Dataset for Instance Segmentation of Long-Range thin Filamentous Structures
sum: Computers still struggle to separate individual neurons in 3D light-microscope images, where thin branches tangle together. This paper releases a fruit-fly brain dataset with careful labels so algorithms can be scored fairly.

t: Generating brain-wide connectome using synthetic axonal morphologies
sum: We can map tiny local wiring with electron microscopy, but not every long-distance axon in a mammal. This paper grows realistic computer copies of those long axons from a smaller set of real reconstructions to estimate whole-brain connections.

t: Geometric Scaling Law in Real Neuronal Networks.
sum: In fruit-fly brains mapped down to synapses, neurons that sit closer together are more likely to connect, following a regular geometric rule. This paper argues that rule is not just packing, but part of how the network balances mixing and separating information.

t: Gossamer: Scaling Image Processing and Reconstruction to Whole Brains
sum: A whole mouse brain scanned with lightsheet microscopy is too big for older tracing programs. Gossamer is software that rebuilds neurons as 3D stick figures using far less computer memory, so one machine can handle a full brain.

t: Modular segmentation, spatial analysis and visualization of volume electron microscopy datasets
sum: Volume electron microscopy produces huge 3D pictures of cells, but turning them into labeled organelles is hard for non-programmers. This protocol strings together free tools so a lab computer can segment, measure, and display those structures.

t: Morphology and synapse topography optimize linear encoding of synapse numbers in Drosophila looming responsive descending neurons
sum: In the fly, looming-sensitive cells dump synapses onto big descending neurons that drive escape. This preprint finds those synapses sit in type-specific neighborhoods but are shuffled inside them, which helps the cell add up synapse numbers linearly.

t: Neuproofreader: An Interactive Proofreading System with Suggestive Prompts for Connectomics
sum: Computers chop electron-microscope neurons into too many pieces, and people must glue them back. NeuProofreader suggests which pieces likely belong together so proofreaders spend less time searching.

t: On human nanoscale synaptome: Morphology modeling and storage estimation
sum: If we listed every human synapse, how much disk space would that take? This paper estimates petabytes—more than most neuroscience supercomputers can hold—depending on how many cells and how much detail you store.

t: Rabies virus-based barcoded neuroanatomy resolved by single-cell RNA and in situ sequencing
sum: Researchers tag mouse brain cells with barcoded rabies virus, then read both the tags and the cells’ gene activity. That pairing shows which cell types send long-range projections or share synaptic partners.

t: Self-organized emergence of modularity, hierarchy, and mirror reversals from competitive synaptic growth in a developmental model of the visual pathway
sum: A computer model grows visual-cortex wiring from simple competition among synapses. Areas, a hierarchy, and flipped maps appear without a detailed genetic blueprint for those flips.

t: The emergence of multiscale connectomics-based approaches in stroke recovery.
sum: Stroke recovery is a problem of brain networks at many zoom levels, not only of a single damaged spot. This review argues that wiring-diagram ideas from the synapse up to whole-brain scans could better track how the brain remaps.

t: vEMstitch: an algorithm for fully automatic image stitching of volume electron microscopy
sum: Volume electron microscopes take many overlapping snapshots that must be sewn together. This algorithm aims to join those tiles without blurry double images, even when the tissue itself is a bit warped.

t: Whole-brain spatial organization of hippocampal single-neuron projectomes
sum: Researchers traced the full axon trees of more than ten thousand individual mouse hippocampal neurons. The maps show that where a cell’s body sits in the hippocampus predicts where its axon goes in the brain.

t: Wrapped up: advancements in volume electron microscopy and application in myelin research
sum: Myelin is a tightly wrapped insulation that is hard to see in three dimensions with ordinary electron microscopy. This review explains how volume EM and computer segmentation now measure those wraps and their diseases.

t: Connectomes: from a sparsity of networks to large-scale databases
sum: Thirty years ago almost no whole-brain wiring diagrams existed. This review surveys the flood of maps now available, from worms and flies to a planned 100,000 human scans.

t: Converting Biological Neural Networks to DAGs: Evaluation of Customized Algorithms on C. Elegans
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram has loops. This student paper tries two algorithms that cut loops so the network becomes a one-way flowchart, and reports that one method keeps the original shape better.

t: Impact of Retinal Degeneration on Response of ON and OFF Cone Bipolar Cells to Electrical Stimulation
sum: Eye implants usually wait until photoreceptors are gone. This study models how remaining bipolar cells in a degenerating rabbit retina respond to electrical pulses, and finds ON and OFF cells do not change in the same way.

t: Insights into vision from interpretation of a neuronal wiring diagram
sum: A wiring diagram of the fruit-fly optic lobe is used to guess how flies see shapes, not just motion or color. Some cells look built to prefer lines at particular angles, a trick also discussed for mammalian visual cortex.

t: MCMC sampling of directed flag complexes with fixed undirected graphs
sum: Fancy shape statistics on brain wiring diagrams can look impressive just because there are many little cliques. This paper builds a fair random comparison and finds the worm and some simulated cortical networks are still unusual.

t: Molecular organization of neuronal cell types and neuromodulatory systems in the zebrafish telencephalon
sum: In the adult zebrafish forebrain, every neuron type seems to listen to several chemical broadcast systems at once, but a few receptors are much louder than the rest.

t: Neural-circuit basis of song preference learning in fruit flies
sum: Female fruit flies learn which courtship songs to prefer. This paper finds a tiny pair of cell types in the brain that inhibit each other and need both GABA and dopamine for that learning.

t: Organization of an Ascending Circuit that Conveys Flight Motor State
sum: When a fly beats its wings, its own sensors are flooded with self-made signals. Two pairs of histaminergic cells carry a copy of flight motor commands up to the brain so sensory circuits can tell self from world.

t: Overlap and divergence of neural circuits mediating distinct behavioral responses to sugar
sum: Sugar makes flies eat, slow down, linger, and remember places. This study asks whether those reactions share one circuit or split apart, and finds the split starts a synapse or two downstream of the sensors.

t: Self-Organized Criticality in C. Elegans Neural Network
sum: Big brains are sometimes said to hover at a knife-edge between quiet and chaos. This conference paper asks whether the tiny worm nervous system sits at that same edge, using a simple activity-spreading number instead of large avalanches.

t: Synaptic gradients transform object location to action
sum: To jump away from a threat, a fly must turn retinal location into a body-centered escape. This Nature paper shows that the mapping is written as graded synapse strengths, not as a second picture in the axons.

t: The evolution of Big Data in neuroscience and neurology
sum: Neurology is gathering huge piles of scans and records, but this survey says much of that work is not truly ‘big data’ yet. Better sharing, faster home measures, and clearer standards could change patient care.

t: Translating single-neuron axonal reconstructions into meso-scale connectivity statistics in the mouse somatosensory thalamus
sum: Thousands of traced mouse neurons sit in public databases. This team turns 257 sensory-thalamus cells into a simple map: where the cell body sits predicts the shape of its axon and which cortical patches it hits.

t: Anatomical and Functional Differences in the Sex-Shared Neurons of the Nematode C. elegans
sum: Male and female worms share most of the same neurons, yet those shared cells can grow extra branches, make different synapses, or simply work differently. This short review collects those tricks and the genes behind them.

t: CELR: Cloud Enhanced Local Reconstruction from low-dose sparse Scanning Electron Microscopy images
sum: Electron microscopes can scan faster if they skip most pixels and use a faint beam, but then a computer must fill in the picture. This system splits the work: a local neural net reconstructs live, while the cloud keeps training the net.

t: Classifying Drosophila olfactory projection neuron boutons by quantitative analysis of electron microscopic reconstruction
sum: Olfactory neurons in the fly dump smell information into the learning center at swollen axon endings. Electron-microscope reconstructions split those endings into three shapes, and the most elaborate ones look best equipped to release both fast transmitters and slower chemical modulators.

t: Complex topological features of reservoirs shape learning performances in bio-inspired recurrent neural networks
sum: Some machine-learning networks keep a frozen tangle of loops and only train the readout. This study asks whether using real brain wiring diagrams as that tangle helps prediction, and finds that community structure and connection density matter.

t: Connectome of the lamina reveals the circuit for early color processing in the visual pathway of a butterfly.
sum: Swallowtail butterflies see color in finer steps than people do. This paper maps the first waystation of that visual system and finds photoreceptors talking to each other in ways fruit flies lack.

t: Deep neural network automated segmentation of cellular structures in volume electron microscopy
sum: Cell biologists can now mill and scan an entire cell in an electron microscope, but painting every organelle by hand is impractical. This pipeline trains a neural net on a little bit of human labeling and then finds mitochondria, Golgi, ER, pores, and coated vesicles automatically.

t: From Photons to Behaviors: Neural Implementations of Visual Behaviors in Drosophila
sum: Fruit flies turn what they see into walks, turns, chases, and memories. This review walks through the known neural paths from the eye to those actions, now sharpened by wiring diagrams.

t: Research trends and hotspots on connectomes from 2005 to 2021: A bibliometric and latent Dirichlet allocation application study
sum: This paper counts two decades of ‘connectome’ publications instead of dissecting one experiment. Imaging journals and U.S. institutions lead, and computer methods plus disease studies are the two big themes.

t: Saturated reconstruction of living brain tissue
sum: Wiring diagrams from electron microscopes are snapshots of dead tissue. This preprint shows a super-resolution light method that reconstructs living brain tissue down to synapses while cells still fire.

t: Sequential addition of neuronal stem cell temporal cohorts generates a feed-forward circuit in the Drosophila larval nerve cord
sum: Nerve-cord circuits in the fly larva are built in birth-order batches. In the vibration-onset circuit studied here, the cells that send the answer are born before the cells that bring the news—the opposite of a simple old-wires-to-old-wires rule.

t: Systems neuroscience: Auditory processing at synaptic resolution.
sum: Hearing pathways deep in the brain have never been fully wired in any animal. This short commentary highlights a fly study that pairs a song-circuit wiring diagram with how the cells actually fire.

t: Uncovering brain tissue architecture across scales with super-resolution light microscopy
sum: Super-resolution light microscopy usually sees labeled cells, not the whole dense neighborhood. This preprint introduces CATS, which stains the spaces around cells so researchers can map brain tissue from large regions down to individual synapses, including in human samples.

t: A quick and versatile protocol for the 3D visualization of transgene expression across the whole body of larval Drosophila
sum: Fruit-fly larvae are easy to genetically label, but published pictures usually show only one organ. This paper gives a fast, relatively non-toxic way to make the whole larva clear so many fluorescent labels can be seen at once.

t: A Transcriptome Community-and-Module Approach of the Human Mesoconnectome
sum: This paper tries to guess how human brain regions group into circuits by looking at which genes turn on together, not by tracing axons. The authors say some of those gene-based groups look like networks already known from imaging, such as the default mode network.

t: Analyzing neural degeneration of the retina with connectomics
sum: Electron microscopy can show every connection and organelle in a piece of retina, which matters in diseases that destroy photoreceptors. This short perspective explains how large serial-section volumes are used to study macular telangiectasia, including a border zone where damage is still spreading.

t: Dense Circuit Reconstruction to Understand Neuronal Computation: Focus on Zebrafish.
sum: Complete wiring diagrams from electron microscopy are most useful when they can be matched to how neurons fire and how the animal behaves. This review argues that larval and adult zebrafish are well suited to that combination, and it walks through examples in brainstem, spinal cord, and olfactory bulb.

t: NeuroConstruct: 3D Reconstruction and Visualization of Neurites in Optical Microscopy Brain Images
sum: Wide-field microscopes can photograph large pieces of brain quickly, but tracing thin nerve fibers across cut slices is still hard. NeuroConstruct is a software suite meant to help people label those fibers, have a network finish the tracing, and glue the slices back into one 3D picture.

t: Neuropeptides and Behaviors: How Small Peptides Regulate Nervous System Function and Behavioral Outputs
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram is famous, but much of behavior is also shaped by small signaling peptides that are not ordinary fast synapses. This review collects how those peptides change feeding, mating, sleep, learning, and movement.

t: Normative and mechanistic model of an adaptive circuit for efficient encoding and feature extraction
sum: Fly-larva smell neurons send overlapping messages that are hard to tell apart. This theory paper argues that local inhibitory neurons learn those overlaps from activity, match the wiring in the connectome, and clean up the smell code before it goes deeper into the brain.

t: Sex-specific topology of the nociceptive circuit shapes dimorphic behavior in C. elegans
sum: Male and hermaphrodite worms can use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, which changes how they avoid danger. This preprint shows that small rewiring can switch one sex’s behavior toward the other, and that making males more avoidant can hurt mating.

t: Symmetry-driven network reconstruction through pseudobalanced coloring optimization
sum: Real wiring diagrams are missing some connections, which can hide repeating patterns in the network. This methods paper looks for almost-symmetries in the worm connectome and adds or deletes the fewest links needed to make those patterns complete.

t: SynCoPa: Visualizing Connectivity Paths and Synapses Over Detailed Morphologies
sum: A wiring list does not show where synapses sit on a neuron’s branches. SynCoPa is visualization software that draws those synapses and the paths between cells on detailed 3D neuron shapes so a circuit can be inspected by eye.

t: The role of spatial embedding in mouse brain networks constructed from diffusion tractography and tracer injections
sum: MRI can estimate brain wiring in living humans, but long fibers are easy to lose or mis-trace. By comparing mouse MRI maps with gold-standard tracer maps, this study shows that MRI networks look more like ‘nearby regions stick together’ geometry than the tracer networks do.

t: Activity regulates brain development in the fly.
sum: People used to think fruit-fly brains are wired by genes alone, like a fixed blueprint. This review says electrical activity during development also helps build fly circuits, so flies can be used to study that process.

t: An ultrastructural connectomic analysis of a higher‐order thalamocortical circuit in the mouse
sum: We know a lot about how first-order sensory thalamus talks to primary cortex, and much less about ‘higher-order’ thalamic messages. This study uses genetic labels plus electron microscopy in mouse to look at those higher-order synapses.

t: Automatic whole cell organelle segmentation in volumetric electron microscopy
sum: Cells are packed with many kinds of organelles that are hard to count in 3D. This Janelia preprint uses fine-scale electron microscopy and machine learning to draw 35 kinds of structures inside whole cells and shares the data as OpenOrganelle.

t: CEM500K, a large-scale heterogeneous unlabeled cellular electron microscopy image dataset for deep learning
sum: Computer programs that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures usually fail on a new lab’s images. This paper releases a large mixed set of unlabeled EM snapshots so programs can practice first, then fine-tune on a specific job.

t: Computational synthesis of cortical dendritic morphologies
sum: There are not enough manually traced neurons to fill a realistic digital cortex. This Blue Brain preprint grows artificial dendrites that statistically match real ones and then asks how diseased-looking branches would change the wiring of a column.

t: Connectomic analysis reveals an interneuron with an integral role in the retinal circuit for night vision
sum: Night vision in mammals funnels through a well-known chain of retinal cells, but it was unclear who applies most of the brakes on a key cell in that chain. This study finds one wide-field inhibitory cell type does most of that job.

t: Electrophysiological validation of premotor interneurons monosynaptically connected to the aCC motoneuron in the Drosophila larval CNS
sum: A wiring diagram can say two fly-larva neurons touch, but that is not the same as proving a working synapse. This paper uses electrical recordings, including a drug that blocks most network spikes, to confirm four premotor cells really talk directly to a named motor neuron.

t: Extrasynaptic volume transmission: A novel route for neuropeptide signaling in nematodes
sum: Worm wiring diagrams show synapses, but peptides might also travel in the body fluid and act at a distance. This preprint finds such peptides in the body cavity of a parasitic nematode and shows they can drive muscle and worm behavior without needing a direct synapse.

t: Graphical-model framework for automated annotation of cell identities in dense cellular images
sum: In worm whole-brain recordings, each glowing cell needs a name before experiments can be compared. This paper offers an automated naming method that looks at shapes and neighbor relationships instead of forcing every brain onto one template.

t: Network Architecture of Gap Junctional Coupling among Parallel Processing Channels in the Mammalian Retina
sum: Retinal cells share not only chemical synapses but also electrical pores. Mapping those pores in a rabbit retina, this study finds that ON bipolar cells are far more electrically networked with each other than the textbook Aii pathway alone would suggest.

t: Neuronal circuits in barrel cortex for whisker sensory perception.
sum: Mice and rats feel the world with whiskers, and each whisker has its own patch of cortex. This review gathers how those patches are built from different excitatory and inhibitory cells and how that may support touch-guided choices.

t: Prediction of a Cell-Class-Specific Mouse Mesoconnectome Using Gene Expression Data
sum: If you know which genes are on in each mouse brain region, how well can you guess the long-range wiring? This study trains models on public maps and finds gene patterns, especially ones tied to synapses, predict quite a lot of the projection pattern.

t: Sparse Scanning Electron Microscopy Data Acquisition and Deep Neural Networks for Automated Segmentation in Connectomics
sum: Electron microscopes can waste time parking the beam on every pixel. This methods paper tests skipping many pixels, filling the picture back in with algorithms, and still automatically tracing neurons—claiming a two- to three-fold time or dose saving.

t: Statistical analysis of unidirectional and reciprocal chemical connections in the C. elegans connectome
sum: In the worm, some cell pairs send chemical synapses both ways and some only one way. Counting those patterns in males and hermaphrodites, this paper finds two-way links are unusually synapse-rich and that males wire shared cells less reciprocally than hermaphrodites.

t: Testing biological network motif significance with exponential random graph models
sum: Biologists often ask whether a small wiring pattern appears more often than chance, but the usual chance models can mislead. This paper uses a more careful statistical family and finds that feed-forward loops really are extra common in some gene networks, while missing feedback loops may just follow from other network

t: Unsupervised learning of control signals and their encodings in Caenorhabditis elegans whole-brain recordings
sum: Worm whole-brain recordings look like a high-dimensional movie of cell activity. This paper finds a few brief ‘control’ events that help explain switches between behaviors, and it points to neurons that could generate those events.

t: A null model of the mouse whole-neocortex micro-connectome
sum: We have coarse maps of which mouse cortical areas talk to which, and a smaller set of individually traced axons. This paper combines those ingredients into a first statistical guess at every neuron-to-neuron long-range connection in neocortex, meant as a baseline for simulations.

t: Connection strength of the macaque connectome augments topological and functional network attributes
sum: A map that only says whether two brain areas are connected ignores how strong those pathways are. In the macaque, this paper finds that the strong pathways are not randomly assigned: they boost local grouping and the tightly linked hub core, and they make simulated activity more synchronized in those groups.

t: Correlative three-dimensional super-resolution and block face electron microscopy of whole vitreously frozen cells
sum: Seeing a named protein and the cell’s fine structure in the same whole cell is usually a compromise. This team freezes cells, images fluorescent labels, then mills the same cells with an electron microscope and finds several unexpected layouts, including a web of contacts between cultured brain cells.

t: Culling for Extreme-Scale Segmentation Volumes: A Hybrid Deterministic and Probabilistic Approach
sum: Once every voxel in a huge brain image is given a label, even asking which objects sit where becomes slow. This paper stores those labels in a hybrid tree so viewers can skip empty space and run spatial queries over millions of segments.

t: Hierarchies & Lower Bounds in Theoretical Connectomics
sum: A wiring diagram does not automatically tell you what a circuit computes. This theory paper asks which timed spike computations a network could possibly perform, no matter how each neuron is tuned.

t: Modality-specific circuits for skylight orientation in the fly visual system
sum: Flies use a strip of eye at the top of the head to sense the sky’s polarized light. This study shows that those specialized pixels wire to their own partner cells in the next brain layer, separate from the cells that handle color.

t: Multilevel feedback architecture for adaptive regulation of learning in the insect brain
sum: Learning signals in the fly larva’s memory center are not a simple one-way drip of dopamine. This team maps every incoming synapse onto those signal cells and finds a large web of feedback that lets old memories of good and bad change what is learned next.

t: Pathoconnectome Analysis of Müller Cells in Early Retinal Remodeling
sum: When the retina starts to degenerate, support cells called Müller glia change first. This short study reconstructs one such cell in a diseased-retina wiring volume and shows mixed chemistry and tangled endfeet even at an early stage.

t: TeraVR empowers precise reconstruction of complete 3-D neuronal morphology in the whole brain
sum: Tracing a neuron across an entire mouse brain is like following a thread through a warehouse of images. This team puts the volume in virtual reality so people can walk the branches together and finish complete 3-D shapes.

t: Architecture of the Mouse Brain Synaptome
sum: Brain maps usually count cells or cables, not the molecular flavors of individual synapses. This mouse atlas labels excitatory synapses across the whole brain and finds that each region has its own mix, which disease mutations can scramble.

t: Caenorhabditis elegans excitatory ventral cord motor neurons derive rhythm for body undulation
sum: The worm’s crawling wave has to start somewhere in its tiny nervous system. This review argues that the motor neurons themselves keep time, while stretch sensing and a few command cells keep the wave traveling the right way.

t: Clues to basis of exploratory behaviour of the C. elegans snout from head somatotropy
sum: A worm crawls by bending in one plane, but the tip of its head can poke around in all directions. This essay reads the head’s wiring diagram as an eight-sided steering system for exploring soil.

t: Eigenvector-based community detection for identifying information hubs in neuronal networks
sum: Some brain regions are hubs that gather or send lots of signals. This methods preprint uses the math of network eigenvectors to find those hubs and their neighborhoods in worm, monkey, and human connection maps.

t: Fast Mitochondria Segmentation for Connectomics
sum: Mitochondria in electron-microscope brain images are clues to cell health, but there are far too many to outline by hand. This detector outlines them as fast as the microscope can scan, using a compact neural net.

t: Functional connectomics from neural dynamics: probabilistic graphical models for neuronal network of Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram is known, but activity still has to travel along it. This paper turns simulated neuron traces into a probability map of who depends on whom when a stimulus arrives.

t: Mitochondria at the neuronal presynapse in health and disease
sum: Nerve terminals need energy and tight calcium control, jobs mitochondria are good at, yet many terminals have none. This review asks what mitochondria do at the sending side of a synapse and how their failure might lead to disease.

t: Spatiotemporal ontogeny of brain wiring
sum: Brains of flies and humans look different but share cheap, cliquey wiring and a few hubs. This model grows those patterns from staggered developmental clocks and spatial position, without needing learning or chemical trail maps.

t: Three-dimensional simulation of the Caenorhabditis elegans body and muscle cells in liquid and gel environments for behavioural analysis
sum: To know whether a worm’s nerve cells explain crawling, you need a virtual body that can bend in water or on gel. This simulation gives the animal a physical skin and muscles copied from anatomy.

t: A connectomic approach to the lateral geniculate nucleus
sum: The brain’s visual relay station is small enough that a modern electron-microscope volume could hold hundreds of its neurons. This short review explains why mapping every synapse there would settle old arguments about how vision is wired.

t: FIJI Macro 3D ART VeSElecT: 3D Automated Reconstruction Tool for Vesicle Structures of Electron Tomograms
sum: Counting synaptic bubbles in 3-D electron-microscope movies by hand is painfully slow. This Fiji toolkit finds the bubbles automatically, with an optional human cleanup step, and is used on fish and worm synapses.

t: Identified Serotonergic Modulatory Neurons Have Heterogeneous Synaptic Connectivity within the Olfactory System of Drosophila
sum: Brain chemicals that change mood-like states are often imagined as a sprinkler system. In the fly nose, two serotonin cells both listen to and speak to specific odor channels, not uniformly.

t: Inferring Functional Neural Connectivity with Deep Residual Convolutional Networks
sum: Watching neurons fire together is cheaper than photographing every synapse, but it is easy to mistake coincidence for a real connection. This preprint trains a deep net on fake circuits to get better at guessing the real wires.

t: Mapping and Analysis of the Connectome of Sympathetic Premotor Neurons in the Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla of the Rat Using a Volumetric Brain Atlas
sum: The brainstem cells that keep blood pressure up were thought to hear from the whole brain. A viral map in the rat finds that almost all of their direct incoming wires stay in the brainstem.

t: Mechanisms of Connectome Development.
sum: Brain wiring is not a finished photograph; it grows. This review asks what spatial and timing rules build healthy connection maps and how those rules fail in disease.

t: Neural Interactome: Interactive Simulation of a Neuronal System
sum: A wiring diagram sits still; the interesting part is watching it run. This software shows the worm’s nerve net as a live graph you can stimulate or snip, the way an experimenter would.

t: Pavlovian Conditioning of Larval Drosophila: An Illustrated, Multilingual, Hands-On Manual for Odor-Taste Associative Learning in Maggots
sum: Fruit-fly maggots can learn that a smell predicts a taste reward, using a setup simple enough for a classroom. This paper is the how-to guide, in several languages, so more people can run the experiment.

t: Simulating extracted connectomes
sum: Once a fly neuron’s shape is traced from electron microscopy, you can try to run it as a simulation. This preprint shows that a simple blob model, not a full 3-D tree, is enough for a famous motion-detecting cell.

t: Statistical Inference on Random Dot Product Graphs: a Survey
sum: A brain wiring diagram is a giant network, and networks need statistics just as tables of numbers do. This survey explains a model that turns a network into points in space so you can test and cluster them.

t: Further Insight into the Brain's Rich-Club Architecture
sum: Some brain regions are like busy train stations that also have extra tracks to each other. This short student/postdoc commentary explains a study that found the same ‘rich club’ among individual neurons and argues most messages travel through it.

t: Microscopy Image Browser: A Platform for Segmentation and Analysis of Multidimensional Datasets
sum: 3-D microscope movies pile up faster than people can outline the objects inside them. This free program gives biologists a workbench to paint, interpolate, and measure cells and organelles in those volumes.

t: Synapse biology in the 'circuit-age' - paths towards molecular connectomics
sum: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecular Velcro made that contact. This review sketches how protein-labeling chemistry could catalog the ingredients of specific synapses.

t: Aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation.
sum: Brain maps need tissue that can sit on a shelf without ice damage and still show clean synapses. This paper’s abstract describes fixing rabbit and pig brains, filling them with antifreeze, and glassifying them for long-term storage.

t: Connectome of the fly visual circuitry.
sum: Fruit flies detect motion with a small, well-studied visual system, but seeing every synapse requires electron microscopy. This review says those wiring maps finally named the cells that compute motion.

t: Control of synaptic connectivity by a network of Drosophila IgSF cell surface proteins
sum: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins as name tags when they choose synaptic partners. Breaking one matched pair scrambles wiring at a muscle synapse and in the eye.

t: neuTube 1.0: A New Design for Efficient Neuron Reconstruction Software Based on the SWC Format
sum: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure trees is still slow, even with computers. neuTube is free software that lets you trace and edit those trees in 2D and 3D at the same time.

t: Three-dimensional volume imaging with electron microscopy toward connectome.
sum: Electron microscopes can now take 3D pictures of brain tissue instead of one thin slice at a time. This review explains those scanning-EM methods and warns that analyzing the pictures is still the hard part.

t: Automatic Neuron Type Identification by Neurite Localization in the Drosophila Medulla
sum: A fly’s visual brain repeats similar cell shapes in each column. This paper groups reconstructed neurons by shape and location so computers can name cell types and catch incomplete tracings.

t: Common Connectome Constraints: From C. elegans and Drosophila to Homo sapiens
sum: Brains from worms to people can be drawn as networks of nodes and wires. This primer says those networks are built in modules and layers, and that we still do not know how that layering relates to thought.

t: From cosmos to connectomes: the evolution of data-intensive science.
sum: Astronomy already had to store sky maps in giant computer centers instead of on one lab machine. This Neuron piece says brain-wiring images now face the same problem and can reuse those tools.

t: Post-acquisition image based compensation for thickness variation in microscopy section series
sum: When you slice a brain for electron microscopy, the slices are not all the same thickness. This method looks at how much the pictures change from slice to slice and puts each slice back at a more realistic depth.

t: Volumetric Exploitation of Synaptic Information using Context Localization and Evaluation
sum: Finding tiny synapses in electron-microscope pictures of mammalian brain is hard, especially when the slices are thick and unstained. VESICLE is computer vision that hunts those contacts using biological context and can run on very large volumes.

t: A modeling framework for deriving the structural and functional architecture of a short-term memory microcircuit
sum: Some brain circuits keep a memory by staying active after a cue. This team fits a model of an eye-movement memory circuit to many kinds of data at once, instead of building a cartoon and hoping it matches.

t: DP2: Distributed 3D image segmentation using micro-labor workforce
sum: Computers still struggle to outline cells in 3D electron-microscope stacks. This tool pays online workers a penny to say whether two dots sit on the same cell, and many such yes/no answers build the outlines.

t: Functional allocation of synaptic contacts in microcircuits from rods via rod bipolar to AII amacrine cells in the mouse retina
sum: Seeing in near-darkness means catching a single photon in a rod and getting that whisper to the rest of the retina. This mouse EM study counts how rod, rod-bipolar, and AII cells share synapses so the signal is copied locally instead of smeared.

t: Graph analysis of the human connectome: Promise, progress, and pitfalls
sum: Human brain maps are often turned into networks of regions and links so they can be measured with graph math. This review says that approach is powerful but easy to misuse.

t: VolRoverN: Enhancing surface and volumetric reconstruction for realistic dynamical simulation of cellular and subcellular function
sum: Pretty 3D pictures of cells are not the same as shapes a physics simulator can trust. VolRoverN turns traced outlines into sealed, well-behaved surfaces for modeling how ions move in real cell geometry.

t: WATERSHED MERGE FOREST CLASSIFICATION FOR ELECTRON MICROSCOPY IMAGE STACK SEGMENTATION
sum: Electron-microscope brain slices are easier to outline if you peek at the slices next door. This method builds a family tree of region merges in each slice and uses neighbors to pick better outlines.

t: Analyzing Self-Similar and Fractal Properties of the C. elegans Neural Network
sum: The worm’s 300-cell nervous system is a complete wiring list. Mathematicians here test whether that network looks like a fractal, a random scribble, or a small world, and they find order without true fractal structure.

t: Beyond counts and shapes: Studying pathology of dendritic spines in the context of the surrounding neuropil through serial section electron microscopy
sum: Counting how many dendritic spines look stubby or long is not enough to understand brain disease. This review says you need 3D electron microscopy to see each spine with its partner axon and nearby support cells.

t: Combining collation and annotation efforts toward completion of the rat and mouse connectomes in BAMS
sum: Rat and mouse brain maps use many different names for the same regions, so connection lists cannot simply be pasted together. BAMS is a public database that translates those names and builds large wiring tables from published tracing studies.

t: The Intrinsic Connectome of the Rat Amygdala
sum: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei that traffic emotion and memory signals. This team gathered published rat tracing studies into one directed network and asked which nuclei sit at the center.

t: Cell Type–Specific Three-Dimensional Structure of Thalamocortical Circuits in a Column of Rat Vibrissal Cortex
sum: Each whisker on a rat’s snout maps to a cortical column. This study rebuilds the 3D wiring from thalamus onto nine kinds of excitatory cells in one column and asks which cells that thalamic input can actually explain.

t: Dense, Unspecific Connectivity of Neocortical Parvalbumin-Positive Interneurons: A Canonical Microcircuit for Inhibition?
sum: A major class of inhibitory cells in mouse cortex appears to connect to essentially all nearby excitatory cells, not to a hand-picked few. The authors suggest local inhibition is more like a dense mesh than a precise wiring diagram.

t: Neuronal Tracing for Connectomic Studies
sum: To map every wire in a circuit you must follow each branch through a mountain of microscope images. This review covers computer programs that try to do that tracing in light and electron microscopy.

t: Reconstruction of complete connectivity matrix for connectomics by sampling neural connectivity with fluorescent synaptic markers.
sum: Instead of photographing every synapse with electron microscopy, this paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring with compressive sensing. Simulations on the worm map suggest a much faster path, if the method works in real tissue.

t: Reconstruction of the neuromuscular junction connectome
sum: At the junction between nerve and muscle, you can see whole wiring diagrams in the light microscope, but following each axon by hand is painful. AxonTracker-3D is software to trace those axons in 3D with a person in the loop.

t: Computational inference of the molecular logic for synaptic connectivity in C. elegans
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram can be lined up with which genes each neuron turns on. This paper’s math looks for groups of genes that together predict who connects to whom.

t: Synaptic connectivity in the midget‐parvocellular pathway of primate central retina
sum: In the center of a primate eye, midget cells carry fine detail toward color vision. This study counts synapses from OFF midget bipolar cells in marmosets and macaques and finds similar numbers whether the marmoset has two or three cone types.

t: Nervous system-wide single-cell morphology atlas of excitatory and inhibitory neurons in larval zebrafish
sum: This team traces more than twenty thousand larval zebrafish neurons, marks them as excitatory or inhibitory, and lines them up in one standard fish brain. From how axons sit next to dendrites they sketch who might talk to whom, with the caveat that nearby is not the same as a synapse.

t: Topological Origin of the Diversity of Timescales in Recurrent Neural Circuits
sum: Some neurons in cortex are social hubs with many incoming wires, and some are slow thinkers. This theory says those facts are linked: hub wiring plus partly symmetric synapses naturally creates a mix of fast and slow cells, matching mouse connectome recordings.

t: A gut-brain-gut interoceptive circuit loop gates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
sum: Flies decide how much sugar to swallow using sensors in the food tube that talk to brain cells, which then relax the crop—the fly’s stretchy storage stomach. It is a gut–brain–gut loop, not only a later metabolic aftertaste.

t: Decomposing cortical activity through neuronal tracing connectome-eigenmodes in marmosets
sum: A marmoset brain’s tracing-based wiring diagram can be turned into vibration-like patterns (eigenmodes) that predict how resting activity is allowed to spread. Those same patterns also help guess activity in matching parts of the human brain.

t: Hue selectivity from recurrent circuitry in Drosophila
sum: Fruit flies have cells in their visual system that care about hue, not just raw wavelength. A wiring-based model plus genetic tests says the key is looping connections, not a one-way chain from the eye.

t: Self-Supervised Edge Detection Reconstruction for Topology-Informed 3D Axon Segmentation and Centerline Detection
sum: Tracing axons through huge 3D brain images usually needs experts to paint labels. Teaching the network first to redraw edges, without those labels, made axon maps and centerlines more accurate and better connected.

t: Structure, biophysics, and circuit function of a “giant” cortical presynaptic terminal
sum: A giant synapse in the hippocampus is famous as a possible detonator for memory circuits. This review gathers new nanoscale anatomy and physiology of that connection and asks how its physics shapes learning and disease.

t: The effects of axonal beading and undulation on axonal diameter estimation from diffusion MRI: Insights from simulations in human axons segmented from three-dimensional electron microscopy
sum: MRI can try to guess axon thickness from how water wiggles. Simulations in real human axons from electron microscopy show that bumps and wiggles in the axon itself can make those guesses too small, which matters when reading disease scans.

t: Anatomical restructuring of a lateralized neural circuit during associative learning by asymmetric insulin signaling
sum: Worms remember the salt level they ate at by physically adding synapses and flipping which side of a paired circuit talks louder. Insulin signals from one cell to another drive that rewiring.

t: Ancient origin of the rod bipolar cell pathway in the vertebrate retina
sum: Night vision in mammals was thought to use a special retinal circuit invented in our lineage. A zebrafish study finds two rod bipolar cell types, one wired much like the mammalian night pathway, so that design is probably ancient.

t: Flexible circuit mechanisms for context-dependent song sequencing
sum: A male fruit fly sings simple notes from far away and mixed songs up close. The same descending pathway does both: extra brain cells unlock a more flexible spinal-like circuit only when the female is near.

t: Learning Multiscale Consistency for Self-Supervised Electron Microscopy Instance Segmentation
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of neurons are hard to outline because labels are scarce and the shapes are fiddly. This method first teaches a network to agree with itself at many zoom levels on unlabeled volumes, then uses that skill to segment cells and mitochondria.

t: Linking neural circuits to the mechanics of animal behavior in Drosophila larval locomotion
sum: A crawling maggot is both a wiring diagram and a soft machine. This review says you need the nerves and the physics of the body together if you want to explain how the animal actually moves.

t: Mapping of Neuronal and Glial Primary Cilia Contactome and Connectome in the Human Cerebral Cortex
sum: Tiny antennae on brain cells, called primary cilia, reach into the space around neurons and glia. A human cortex wiring volume shows they touch different partners by layer and cell type, and some even sit in the synapse itself.

t: Neural dynamics and architecture of the heading direction circuit in zebrafish
sum: Larval zebrafish keep an internal compass of which way they are pointing. Imaging and electron microscopy find a small hindbrain circuit whose activity bump rotates with turns and is held in place by cells inhibiting each other.

t: Neural mechanisms of dopamine function in learning and memory in Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: Dopamine helps animals learn, but in people it comes from huge groups of cells. This review says the worm’s tiny, fully mapped nervous system is a place to watch dopamine neuron by neuron as memories form and fade.

t: Online citizen science with the Zooniverse for analysis of biological volumetric data
sum: Huge 3D microscope volumes need more eyes than a lab has. This how-to explains how research teams have used the Zooniverse website so volunteers can help outline structures in those volumes.

t: Sleep benefits different stages of memory in Drosophila
sum: Sleep helps fruit flies learn and lock in memories, but not always in the same way. This review gathers how fly sleep interacts with different memory stages and notes that hungry flies can switch to a sleep-independent route.

t: Technical report: surgical preparation of human brain tissue for clinical and basic research
sum: During brain surgery, a small piece of cortex is often in the way. This technical note tells surgeons how to lift that piece quickly and gently so scientists can still record from it or look at it with electron microscopy.

t: A single-cell resolution gene expression atlas of the larval zebrafish brain
sum: Researchers painted 200 genes onto a standard map of the baby zebrafish brain. Overlaying those colors with cell tracings and a hunger-related activity gene revealed a new class of cerebellar cells that talk to the hypothalamus after a meal.

t: EMPIAR: the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive
sum: Electron-microscope movies and huge 3D cell images need a public library, not only the pretty reconstructed maps. EMPIAR is that library, already past a thousand datasets and two petabytes.

t: Imposing Connectome-Derived Topology on an Echo State Network
sum: A machine-learning reservoir is usually a random net. These authors drop in the fruit fly’s actual connection pattern instead and find it predicts a chaotic time series as well or more stably than the random version.

t: Ordering in heterogeneous connectome weights for visual information processing
sum: Mouse visual cortex wiring looks messy if you only list synapses. This short commentary explains a companion study that fits a simple excitatory–inhibitory network to real visual responses and reads ordered connection rules out of that fit.

t: Percolation may explain efficiency, robustness, and economy of the brain
sum: Turn up the fraction of excitatory synapses on a fly brain map and, at a sharp point, the network suddenly becomes good at sending signals, surviving damage, and staying cheap to wire. That physics idea is called percolation.

t: Semi-Supervised Neuron Segmentation via Reinforced Consistency Learning
sum: Drawing every neuron in an electron-microscope stack takes forever. This paper shows a network can learn from a handful of labels plus lots of unlabeled pictures, by insisting that slightly messed-up copies get the same answer.

t: Brain research challenges supercomputing
sum: Mapping the human brain in fine detail creates more data than ordinary computers can handle. This short Science piece says that challenge may force new supercomputing ideas, using the tiny worm connectome as the completeness benchmark we do not yet have for humans.

t: Cross-modal coherent registration of whole mouse brains
sum: Mouse brains imaged with different microscopes do not line up on the standard atlas by themselves. This method, mBrainAligner, uses landmarks and neural nets to warp whole brains into the Allen map so cells and axons can be compared.

t: Dopamine Neurons That Cotransmit Glutamate, From Synapses to Circuits to Behavior
sum: Some dopamine cells also spit out glutamate. This review traces that double signal from synapses to circuits to behavior and asks whether it could be a more precise drug target than dopamine alone.

t: FIB-SEM as a Volume Electron Microscopy Approach to Study Cellular Architectures in SARS-CoV-2 and Other Viral Infections: A Practical Primer for a Virologist
sum: A focused ion beam can peel a cell like a 3D onion inside an electron microscope. This primer shows virologists how that works and finds SARS-CoV-2 particles sitting on outward-bulging bits of the cell membrane.

t: High-precision targeting workflow for volume electron microscopy
sum: Finding one glowing cell inside a big chunk of tissue, then milling only that cell in an electron microscope, is hard. This workflow keeps the glow, marks the block, and aims the ion beam with micrometre aim.

t: Local and long-distance organization of prefrontal cortex circuits in the marmoset brain
sum: Marmoset prefrontal cortex sends two kinds of long-range wires: tight columns and a wide spray. The columnar style is much clearer in this primate than in the mouse, hinting at how primate frontal circuits are tiled.

t: Model simulations unveil the structure-function-dynamics relationship of the cerebellar cortical microcircuit
sum: The cerebellum looks like a crystal, but the exact numbers of wires are still argued. A detailed computer reconstruction of mouse cerebellar cortex lets mossy-fiber bursts play through realistic cells and predicts how activity climbs toward Purkinje cells.

t: Sequential Semi-supervised Segmentation for Serial Electron Microscopy Image with Small Number of Labels.
sum: If you only labeled a few slices in a stack of electron-microscope pictures, you still want the rest filled in. This methods paper walks a network along the stack, using each slice to help the next, instead of pretending it must work on brand-new samples.

t: The mouse cortico–basal ganglia–thalamic network
sum: Textbook diagrams give the basal ganglia three channels. A mouse whole-system map finds six parallel loops, each returning to the same cortical starting point, with much finer neighborhoods in striatum, pallidum, nigra, and thalamus.

t: The nonhuman primate neuroimaging and neuroanatomy project
sum: Human brain scans cannot be checked with dye tracers. This project scans macaque and marmoset monkeys with the same MRI methods used in people, then compares those maps with gold-standard anatomical tracing.

t: An interactive ImageJ plugin for semi-automated image denoising in electron microscopy
sum: Electron-microscope stacks get noisy if you scan them faster. This team ships an ImageJ plugin that denoises the pictures on a graphics card so labs can collect data more quickly without wrecking later tracing.

t: BAcTrace, a tool for retrograde tracing of neuronal circuits in Drosophila
sum: Fruit-fly geneticists can already light up chosen neurons, but not always the cells that talk to them. This paper engineers a Botox-based tracer that jumps backward across synapses and checks it against an electron-microscope wiring map.

t: Cellular and circuit mechanisms of olfactory associative learning in Drosophila
sum: Fruit flies can learn to link odors with reward or punishment. This review explains how that short-term memory is built from genes, single cells, and circuits, and why new wiring diagrams will speed the next experiments.

t: EM-net: Deep learning for electron microscopy image segmentation
sum: Electron-microscope pictures of cells are low-contrast and expensive to outline by hand. This paper trains a neural net that needs fewer labels and combines several versions of the model to pick out mitochondria more cleanly.

t: Estimation of the number of synapses in the hippocampus and brain-wide by volume electron microscopy and genetic labeling
sum: Counting every synapse in a whole brain with an electron microscope is impractical. This team measures real 3D synapse density in a bit of mouse hippocampus, then uses that as a ruler to turn fluorescent synapse snapshots from many other regions into estimated densities.

t: Evolution of neuronal anatomy and circuitry in two highly divergent nematode species
sum: Two nematode worms split about 100 million years ago. This paper matches their nose-sensor neurons one-for-one and finds that cell number and positions stayed put while the fine sensory endings and who synapses with whom changed.

t: Expression profiling of the mature C. elegans nervous system by single-cell RNA-Sequencing
sum: The worm’s wiring diagram names every neuron type, but not which genes each type uses. This preprint profiles tens of thousands of single neurons and matches most of those types, with extra splits often marked by different neuropeptides.

t: Fluorescence-Based Quantitative Synapse Analysis for Cell Type-Specific Connectomics
sum: It is hard to count which inhibitory cells synapse onto a cortical pyramid. This paper paints the pyramid’s synapses one color and the inhibitory axons another, then shows parvalbumin cells dominate while VIP contacts are scarce.

t: Gotta Trace ‘em All: A Mini-Review on Tools and Procedures for Segmenting Single Neurons Toward Deciphering the Structural Connectome
sum: Tracing every neuron in a mammal brain by hand is too slow. This short review surveys computer tools for carving single cells out of 3D images, plus clearing and super-resolution methods that will make those tools even more necessary.

t: Inhibiting mGluR5 activity by AFQ056/Mavoglurant rescues circuit‐specific functional connectivity in Fmr1 knockout mice
sum: A mouse model of Fragile X has odd brain-network coupling on MRI. This study asks whether an mGluR5 drug puts those networks back, and finds that some circuits improve on the scan even when social behavior and white matter do not.

t: Mapping brain asymmetry in health and disease through the ENIGMA consortium
sum: People’s left and right brain halves differ a little, and psychiatry has long wondered if those differences change in illness. This consortium paper pools thousands of MRI scans to map typical asymmetry and test a few diagnoses at a much larger scale.

t: Perfusion fixation in brain banking: a systematic review
sum: Animal brains are usually fixed by pumping chemical through blood vessels; human banked brains are usually soaked. This review gathers decades of human perfusion attempts and concludes the pictures often look as good or better, and not slower.

t: Synaptic Specializations of Melanopsin-Retinal Ganglion Cells in Multiple Brain Regions Revealed by Genetic Label for Light and Electron Microscopy
sum: A special class of retinal cells tells the brain about overall light for clocks and pupils. This study tags those cells for both light and electron microscopy and finds that their endings look different in each brain target, including an unusual dendrite-to-dendrite network in the clock nucleus.

t: A Disinhibitory Circuit Motif and Flexible Information Routing in the Brain
sum: Your cortex has too many incoming cables to listen to all of them at once. This review argues that a three-part inhibitory circuit can open one pathway and close another, and that this motif is stronger in association areas than in early sensory areas.

t: Increasing Electrical Stimulation Efficacy in Degenerated Retina: Stimulus Waveform Design in a Multiscale Computational Model
sum: When the retina degenerates, leftover cells fire noisily and prosthetic electrodes struggle to talk to them. This modeling paper tests shock waveforms and proposes an uneven two-phase pulse that quiets that noise so timing is easier to control.

t: Neural Circuits of Sexual Behavior in Caenorhabditis elegans.
sum: Male and hermaphrodite roundworms share most of their neurons but not all of their wiring. This review uses both complete maps to explain how shared and sex-only cells together run mating and egg-laying.

t: Neural Mechanisms of Motion Processing in the Mammalian Retina.
sum: When something moves on the eye, many types of retinal cells fire in parallel. This review explains how the famous direction-selective circuit works, and why other motion detectors in the retina still need better tools and more natural movies.

t: Segregated Subnetworks of Intracortical Projection Neurons in Primary Visual Cortex.
sum: Cells in visual cortex that send axons to different next-stage areas often see the world similarly. This paper finds they still avoid linking to each other locally, which may keep those output pipelines from mixing.

t: Synaptic transfer between rod and cone pathways mediated by AII amacrine cells in the mouse retina
sum: In dim light, a specialized interneuron hands rod signals to both ON and OFF cone pathways. This paper maps those contacts in mouse retina and shows the cell does not copy the same message to every partner.

t: The Mouse Cortical Connectome Characterized by an Ultra Dense Cortical Graph Maintains Specificity by Distinct Connectivity Profiles
sum: Mouse cortical areas might be either sparsely or almost fully interconnected. This tracing study finds nearly every possible link exists, but the strengths of those links still give each area a unique fingerprint.

t: Visual physiology of the layer 4 cortical circuit in silico
sum: A huge computer model of one layer of mouse visual cortex is shown movies and compared with real recordings. Wiring rules between cells matter most; even a stripped-down version still gets many qualitative facts right.

t: Predictive Model of Spread of Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Using Directional Network Diffusion
sum: Some brain diseases seem to walk along the wires of the connectome. This study tests that idea in progressive supranuclear palsy and finds that keeping the direction of those wires in the model improves the match to real atrophy patterns.

t: Proximodistal heterogeneity of hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neuron intrinsic properties, connectivity and reactivation during memory recall
sum: The hippocampal area CA3 is often drawn as one uniform loop. This paper shows a smooth gradient: mossy-fiber input is stronger at one end, cortex input at the other, and memory-trace replay peaks in the middle.

t: Role of Graph Architecture in Controlling Dynamical Networks with Applications to Neural Systems
sum: Steering a network takes energy that depends on how the “driver” nodes plug into the rest. Applied to fly, mouse, and human wiring diagrams, this theory suggests more complex brains are built to be cheaper to control and fairly robust if one connection is lost.

t: Structural and functional, empirical and modeled connectivity in the cerebral cortex of the rat
sum: In rats, the team compares a wiring diagram built from published tracer studies with resting-state MRI. Stronger anatomical links and certain dense motifs go with stronger functional coupling, and a simple simulation on the wiring partly recreates the MRI pattern.

t: Using high-throughput barcode sequencing to efficiently map connectomes
sum: Instead of photographing every synapse, this method tries to read connections as paired DNA barcodes. The biochemistry mostly works, but stitching the two barcodes together is still far too inefficient to map a real circuit.

t: Cliques of Neurons Bound into Cavities Provide a Missing Link between Structure and Function
sum: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.

t: Community detection in networks: A user guide
sum: Finding clusters in a network sounds simple until you notice nobody agrees what a cluster is. This long guide walks through the definitions, tests, and algorithms so you can pick a method without treating it as magic.

t: Sex-specific pruning of neuronal synapses in Caenorhabditis elegans
sum: Male and hermaphrodite worms share most neurons but not all of their synapses. This paper shows many connections are wired both ways at first, then each sex prunes the extras, under the control of the cell’s sexual identity and a conserved transcription factor.

t: Chimera-like States in Modular Neural Networks
sum: In a computer model inspired by the worm’s wiring, some groups of cells fire together while others fire out of step. That mixed pattern, called a chimera-like state, appears when local electrical coupling and longer-range chemical coupling are balanced just so.

t: Comparison of diffusion tractography and tract‐tracing measures of connectivity strength in rhesus macaque connectome
sum: MRI maps of brain cables are cheaper than injecting tracers, but it is hard to know whether more reconstructed fibers really mean a stronger connection. In macaques, streamline counts from diffusion MRI do rise with classic tracer measures of pathway strength.

t: Glial Regulation of the Neuronal Connectome through Local and Long-Distant Communication
sum: A wiring diagram of the brain is usually a map of neurons. This essay argues that support cells—glia—also shape those wires, from whole-brain pathways down to single synapses, so they belong in the connectome too.

t: Neuroinformatics of the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas.
sum: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas is a public 3D map of which mouse brain areas send axons where. This methods paper explains the computer pipeline that turns injection images into that quantitative atlas.

t: Identification of Important Nodes in Directed Biological Networks: A Network Motif Approach
sum: Not every important cell in a directed biological network is a hub with many links. This paper scores nodes by the wiring triangles they sit in, and reports that the score finds command neurons and key regulators better than simpler rankings.

t: Multilayer Analysis and Visualization of Networks
sum: Some networks have more than one kind of link between the same players, like different synapse types. This paper releases muxViz, a free tool to analyze and draw those multilayer maps, including a worm nervous-system example.

t: NeuroMorph: A Toolset for the Morphometric Analysis and Visualization of 3D Models Derived from Electron Microscopy Image Stacks
sum: Electron-microscope stacks can be turned into 3D cell shapes, but measuring those shapes is still tedious. NeuroMorph is a free add-on to the Blender 3D program that lets you inspect and measure spines and boutons on those models.

t: The Budapest Reference Connectome Server v2.0.
sum: No two human brain maps are identical, but many cables show up again and again. This web server lets you download a consensus wiring diagram built from 96 MRI scans, with sliders for how common an edge must be.

t: The Stimulus Selectivity and Connectivity of Layer Six Principal Cells Reveals Cortical Microcircuits Underlying Visual Processing
sum: Deep in mouse visual cortex, two kinds of output cells do different jobs. One talks mostly to other cortical cells and is loosely tuned; the other talks to thalamus, fires very rarely, and is extremely picky about orientation and direction.

t: Wiring patterns in the mouse retina: collecting evidence across the connectome, physiology and light microscopy
sum: The eye’s retina was thought to send visual features down separate private cables. This review of the mouse retina says the channels share parts, and that electron microscopy, physiology, and light microscopy must be combined before we trust a wiring diagram.

t: Connectomic approaches before the connectome
sum: People have been drawing maps of brain connections for centuries. This history essay says modern imaging is powerful, but a true complete map of the human brain is still a long way off, and many of today’s pictures are only rough stand-ins.

t: Large-scale network organization in the avian forebrain: a connectivity matrix and theoretical analysis
sum: Bird brains look different from ours—they are built of clumps, not layers—yet some birds are strikingly smart. A wiring diagram of the pigeon forebrain is reported to follow the same high-level network rules as mammal brains: modules, short paths, and a core of hub regions.

t: Computational Methods and Challenges for Large-Scale Circuit Mapping
sum: Photographing even a small piece of brain at synapse scale creates enormous computer files. This 2012 review explains why tracing those pictures still needed people as well as algorithms, and what the software problems were.

t: A tutorial in connectome analysis: Topological and spatial features of brain networks
sum: Once you have a map of brain connections, you still need to know how to score it. This tutorial walks through common network measurements, from single nodes up to the whole graph, and reminds readers that real brains also have a physical length cost.

t: Anterograde or retrograde transsynaptic labeling of CNS neurons with vesicular stomatitis virus vectors
sum: To draw a circuit diagram you need a way to see which cells actually talk to which. This team retunes a livestock virus so it hops synapses forward, backward, or just one step from a chosen starting cell in the mouse brain.

t: Beyond the wiring diagram: signalling through complex neuromodulator networks
sum: A list of synapses is not a complete recipe for behavior, because chemical modulators constantly retune those synapses. This essay explains that extra chemical network and why it makes brains harder to read from wiring alone.

t: Ultrastructural preservation of a whole large mammal brain with a protocol compatible with human physician-assisted death
sum: To keep a whole large brain looking intact under an electron microscope after death, blood has to be washed out very quickly. In pigs, this team reports a preservation protocol meant to match a human medically assisted death, with a roughly 14-minute window after the heart stops.

t: Cell type-specific connectome predicts distributed working memory activity in the mouse brain
sum: Working memory is the brain’s scratchpad. A computer model of the mouse brain that includes which cell types project where predicts that memory traces live across many regions, not in one spot, and that inhibitory cell density helps set the pattern.

t: Centralized brain networks underlie body part coordination during grooming
sum: When a fly grooms its antennae, the head, antennae, and front legs move together on purpose. Mapping the responsible neurons in the fly connectome points to a central controller, not a chain of reflexes that wait on each body part to feel the others.

t: Combinatorial expression of γ-protocadherins regulates synaptic connectivity in the mouse neocortex
sum: Brain cells need a way to avoid wiring to the wrong neighbors. In mouse cortex, cells that wear more similar combinations of γ-protocadherin surface proteins are less likely to synapse, like a molecular ‘do not connect if we match’ rule.

t: Creating Efficient Workflows for Electron Microscopy Laboratories with Automated Specimen Preparation
sum: Getting tissue ready for electron microscopy usually takes days of timed chemical baths. This lab-practice article describes machines that automate those baths, cutting the wait and the hands-on time for ordinary TEM and for 3D volume EM.

t: Directed and acyclic synaptic connectivity in the human layer 2-3 cortical microcircuit
sum: Most of what we know about how cortical cells wire to their neighbors comes from rodents. Recordings from human surgical tissue suggest a different pattern: connections run mostly one way, with few loops, which models say may help the network compute in higher dimensions.

t: Disrupted basolateral amygdala circuits supports negative valence bias in depressive states
sum: Depression often makes the world look more threatening. In mice given a stress hormone, and in people with bipolar depression, smells are valued more negatively, and the study traces that shift to a split in amygdala output paths—one toward reward circuits, one toward fear circuits.

t: Geometry and dynamics of representations in a precisely balanced memory network related to olfactory cortex
sum: Memory is often imagined as a set of on/off basins in a network. A model based on a fish brain area like olfactory cortex instead keeps excitation and inhibition co-tuned, so memories look like smooth shapes in activity space rather than a few rigid attractors.

t: Neural Control of Naturalistic Behavior Choices.
sum: Lab studies of decisions often use unnatural trials, while real animals keep choosing what to do next in a messy world. This review proposes studying those natural choices in genetically tractable animals such as flies, using connectomes as a map.

t: OsO2 as the Contrast‐Generating Chemical Species of Osmium‐Stained Biological Tissues in Electron Microscopy
sum: Brain tissue is stained with osmium so electron microscopes can see membranes. This chemistry paper reports that the dark contrast comes from metallic osmium dioxide specks in the lipids, which also help the sample conduct electrons.

t: Perineuronal Net Microscopy: From Brain Pathology to Artificial Intelligence
sum: Many brain cells wear a lattice of sugars and proteins, a perineuronal net, around their synapses. This review explains how that lattice looks under the microscope in disease, and it introduces a machine-learning helper for tracing the lattice’s outlines.
