t: Synaptic connectome of a neurosecretory network in the Drosophila brain
sum: Flies, like us, use brain hormones to run the body. This preprint charts who synapses onto the fly’s hormone cells and finds that gut-related neurons are especially influential, while the hormone cells themselves make few conventional synapses—except a corazonin pathway tied to egg-laying.

t: A cerebellar disinhibitory circuit supports synaptic plasticity
sum: The cerebellum learns by weakening some synapses when an error signal arrives, but nearby inhibitory cells can block that weakening. An electron-microscope wiring map suggests the error fibres also turn off those inhibitors at the right moment, giving learning a clear shot.

t: Axonal energy metabolism, and the effects in aging and neurodegenerative diseases
sum: The long cables of the brain are energy-hungry, and in aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s they often fail first. This review explains how axons make and use fuel, and why the most connected brain regions may be the most metabolically at risk.

t: Development and circuitry of the tunicate larval Motor Ganglion, a putative hindbrain/spinal cord homolog
sum: A sea-squirt larva swims with a tiny cluster of motor neurons at the base of its tail. This review explains how that cluster develops and is wired, and why it may be a miniature version of the vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.

t: Gap junctions desynchronize a neural circuit to stabilize insect flight
sum: Flies beat their wings with a tiny motor circuit. This Nature paper shows that the electrical synapses in that circuit do not lock the cells together; they stagger them, which helps keep flight stable.

t: Hunger- and thirst-sensing neurons modulate a neuroendocrine network to coordinate sugar and water ingestion
sum: Flies decide whether to drink sugar or water using a few brain cells that sense hunger and thirst. This preprint follows those cells into a hormone-releasing network that pushes the two choices in opposite directions.

t: Network inference from short, noisy, low time-resolution, partial measurements: Application to C. elegans neuronal calcium dynamics
sum: Can you guess which neurons are wired together just from how their calcium signals wiggle? This paper tests three guessing methods on worm data and on toy chaotic networks, and shows why messy, short recordings make the job hard.

t: Re-formation of synaptic connectivity in dissociated human stem cell-derived retinal organoid cultures
sum: Lab-grown human retinal cells only help if they can plug back into a circuit. This study uses a tracing virus to show that after the cells are pulled apart, photoreceptors and ganglion cells do form new synapses.

t: Regional and cell-type-specific afferent and efferent projections of the mouse claustrum
sum: The claustrum is a thin sheet of cells tucked beside cortex and wired to much of the brain. This mouse map shows which cortical cell types talk to it and how its own cells send axons back to matching sets of areas.

t: Brain-wide analysis of the supraspinal connectome reveals anatomical correlates to functional recovery after spinal injury
sum: Many brain regions send axons into the spinal cord, not just the famous motor pathway. This mouse study labels those cells brain-wide after injury and asks which leftover groups go with better recovery.

t: Differences in the critical dynamics underlying the human and fruit-fly connectome
sum: Some theories say brains hover near a tipping point between quiet and fully locked-together activity. This physics paper compares a fly wiring diagram with a human one and finds the fly’s tipping point is sharper.

t: Glassy phase in dynamically-balanced neuronal networks
sum: Brain models often assume random wiring that keeps excitation and inhibition in a tight tug-of-war. This theory paper shows that when connections are a bit symmetric, the network can freeze into a glassy landscape of many almost-stable states.

t: PointNeuron: 3D Neuron Reconstruction via Geometry and Topology Learning of Point Clouds
sum: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure traces usually means slicing a huge 3D grid. This computer-vision paper treats the neuron as a cloud of points instead, which is lighter and can follow thin branches through gaps.

t: Imaging Three-Dimensional Brain Organoid Architecture from Meso- to Nanoscale across Development
sum: Mini-brains grown from stem cells are too big and cloudy for ordinary microscopes to see both the whole lump and single synapses. This preprint swells the tissue and uses a light-sheet microscope to zoom from the whole organoid down toward synaptic scale.

t: Integration of signals from different cortical areas in higher order thalamic neurons
sum: Messages from touch cortex and movement cortex were thought to stay on separate lines through the thalamus. This electron-microscope study finds that many thalamic cells in the mouse actually collect both.

t: Petabyte-Scale Multi-Morphometry of Single Neurons for Whole Brains
sum: A mouse brain imaged in fine 3D detail fills petabytes. This platform helps teams mark cell bodies, trace dendrites and long axons, and flag likely synapses across dozens of whole brains.

t: Small, correlated changes in synaptic connectivity may facilitate rapid motor learning
sum: When you quickly adjust a reaching movement, motor-cortex activity shifts. This modelling paper asks whether that means the local wires changed, and finds that small, structured weight tweaks—or changes in incoming signals—can both look a lot like the recordings.

t: Synaptic recognition molecules in development and disease
sum: Wiring diagrams show which neurons touch, but not which molecular nametags told them to. This book chapter reviews the sticky and repulsive proteins that help vertebrate neurons pick, reject, specify, and later prune synapses.

t: The organization of the zebrafish pallium from a hodological perspective
sum: The roof of the adult zebrafish forebrain is divided into several neighborhoods. This tracing study, as summarized from the catalog abstract, finds those neighborhoods are only weakly wired to each other, as if they were separate workstations.

t: Untangling the cortico-thalamo-cortical loop: cellular pieces of a knotty circuit puzzle
sum: Cortex and thalamus are locked in a two-way conversation. This review sorts which cell types talk to which, and how those loops chain together across the brain.

t: An efficient analytical reduction of detailed nonlinear neuron models
sum: Detailed digital neurons are slow to simulate because every twig is a tiny electrical compartment. This method folds the tree into a simpler shape that still behaves like the original at the cell body, so big networks become computable.

t: Analysis of Synaptic Microcircuits in the Mushroom Bodies of the Honeybee
sum: A honeybee’s learning centers are packed with tiny synaptic knots that change as the bee grows up, leaves the hive, and forms memories. This review gathers what those knots look like and how they rewire.

t: Determinants of seeding and spreading of α-synuclein pathology in the brain
sum: Parkinson’s protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, this team seeds the clumps in one brainstem region and finds that cell type decides who takes them up, while the wiring map only loosely predicts how bad the spread looks.

t: DIP/Dpr interactions and the evolutionary design of specificity in protein families
sum: Fly neurons use families of look-alike surface proteins to choose partners. This paper shows that what often matters is not a special ‘on’ switch but many small ‘don’t bind them’ features scattered over the same handshake surface.

t: Drifting assemblies for persistent memory: Neuron transitions and unsupervised compensation
sum: We often picture a memory as a fixed club of neurons. This theory paper says the club’s membership can turn over completely, while unsupervised plasticity keeps the memory itself intact.

t: Macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation and inhibition in the neocortex
sum: Every patch of cortex looks a bit like every other, yet they do different jobs. This review argues that excitation and inhibition change smoothly from sensory areas to association areas, and those slopes can flip circuits into new kinds of behavior.

t: Rapid mesoscale volumetric imaging of neural activity with synaptic resolution
sum: Watching synapses fire across a wide stretch of mouse cortex is usually a choice between zooming in or seeing the big picture. This team shapes the laser into a long thin focus so they can do both, even across two hemispheres.

t: SEQUIN multiscale imaging of mammalian central synapses reveals loss of synaptic connectivity resulting from diffuse traumatic brain injury
sum: Synapses are tiny and packed like sand, so counting them in a chunk of brain is hard. This paper offers a practical super-resolution recipe and uses it to show that diffuse head injury, like some Alzheimer models, quietly deletes cortical connections.

t: Ubiquitin-dependent regulation of a conserved DMRT protein controls sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity and behavior
sum: Male and female worms share many of the same neurons but wire some of them differently. This paper finds a switch protein that is kept stable only in hermaphrodites, and that stability is enough to build the female-like connections.

t: Correlated states in balanced neuronal networks.
sum: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper, summarized from the catalog abstract, says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.

t: Expansion Microscopy of Lipid Membranes
sum: Expansion microscopy usually lights up proteins or DNA, not the fatty membranes of cells. This preprint adds a membrane stain and a gentler expansion recipe so lipids and proteins can be seen together at nanoscale with a light microscope.

t: Impact of higher order network structure on emergent cortical activity
sum: A wiring diagram is more than who connects to whom on average; clumps of all-to-all connected cells also matter. This modelling study keeps the simple connection rules the same but removes those clumps, and some firing patterns change.

t: Methods for analysis of brain connectivity: An IFCN-sponsored review.
sum: Doctors and scientists map human brain networks with electrical recordings, magnetic stimulation, and scanners. This IFCN review, summarized from the catalog abstract, surveys those tools and how to combine them.

t: Microstructure-Informed Connectomics: Enriching Large-Scale Descriptions of Healthy and Diseased Brains
sum: Whole-brain wiring maps are useful, but they often treat regions as simple dots. This review argues that adding tissue texture and local cell biology to those maps would better explain healthy brains and diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, and autism.

t: Molecular basis of synaptic specificity by immunoglobulin superfamily receptors in Drosophila
sum: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins to choose synaptic partners. This team solves several of those protein structures and redesigns them to show how the matches help wire a muscle circuit.

t: Neural mechanisms of contextual modulation in the retinal direction selective circuit
sum: Some retinal cells that report motion direction also notice whether a moving edge is continuous or broken. This study finds separate inner-retina circuits for bright and dark edges that create that extra sensitivity.

t: A macaque connectome for large-scale network simulations in TheVirtualBrain
sum: This team builds a macaque brain wiring map for a whole-brain simulator and shows that the simulated resting activity resembles real fMRI, including familiar frontal, auditory, and visual networks.

t: A Survey of Methods for 3D Histology Reconstruction
sum: Slicing tissue for a microscope flattens a 3D object into a stack of 2D pictures. This review surveys decades of computer methods that restack those slices, sometimes using MRI as a shape guide.

t: NeuroMorphoVis: a collaborative framework for analysis and visualization of neuronal morphology skeletons reconstructed from microscopy stacks
sum: Neuron tracings from microscopes often need cleanup before they can be turned into 3D models. This paper releases a free toolkit that repairs those tracings and builds meshes for visualization and simulation.

t: Sexually dimorphic unc-6/Netrin expression controls sex-specific maintenance of synaptic connectivity
sum: Male and female roundworms keep different synapses between the same named cells. This study shows that a well-known guidance cue, Netrin, is left on in one male cell to preserve a male-specific connection.

t: Whole Mouse Brain Structural Connectomics using Magnetic Resonance Histology
sum: High-detail MRI of a whole mouse brain usually takes too long. This team uses compressed sensing so they can scan finer and still keep the wiring-map numbers close to a full slow scan.

t: An intersectional gene regulatory strategy defines subclass diversity of C. elegans motor neurons
sum: Motor neurons that look like one type still differ along a worm’s head-to-tail axis. This study shows a general identity gene working together with position genes to create those subtypes.

t: Cell biology of astrocyte-synapse interactions
sum: Star-shaped brain cells called astrocytes help build and adjust synapses. This review gathers what is known about how they do that and lists what is still missing.

t: Efferents of anterior cingulate areas 24a and 24b and midcingulate areas 24aʹ and 24bʹ in the mouse
sum: This paper traces outgoing wires from mouse cingulate cortex and reports that neighboring cingulate patches share many targets but differ in how strongly and exactly they project.

t: Pyramidal cell-interneuron circuit architecture and dynamics in hippocampal networks
sum: This team infers which hippocampal cells talk to which inhibitory cells from the tiny delays between spikes, then checks the guesses by forcing single cells to fire in mice that are behaving.

t: Scalable volumetric imaging for ultrahigh-speed brain mapping at synaptic resolution
sum: This microscope scans a whole cleared mouse brain in about two hours, sharp enough to see dendritic spines, and is used to compare which cells turned on after a stressful swim.

t: Sparse synaptic connectivity is required for decorrelation and pattern separation in feedforward networks
sum: Brain networks that pull similar patterns apart often use very few synapses per cell. Models of the cerebellum’s input layer here show that those sparse wires, not just quiet firing, are what make the patterns separable.

t: Suggestive Annotation: A Deep Active Learning Framework for Biomedical Image Segmentation
sum: Labeling biomedical images for a computer is slow and needs experts. This method asks which regions to label next so that half as much drawing still matches a fully labeled training set.

t: Toward a neurocentric view of learning
sum: Learning is often explained as stronger synapses. This review argues that neurons can also join a memory by becoming easier to fire, even without rewriting their connections first.

t: Cell type-specific long-range connections of basal forebrain circuit
sum: The basal forebrain has several cell types mixed together. This mouse study maps who talks to each type and finds similar incoming wires but very different outgoing wires.

t: Functional complexity emerging from anatomical constraints in the brain: the significance of network modularity and rich-clubs
sum: Brain wiring is grouped into modules and a club of busy hubs. This study shows that both ingredients help the network produce rich activity patterns, and it offers a simple score of that richness.

t: Sexually dimorphic differentiation of a C. elegans hub neuron is cell-autonomously controlled by a conserved transcription factor
sum: A sensory neuron present in both worm sexes becomes a busy hub only in males. One conserved sex-determining gene, acting inside that cell, is enough to flip on the male wiring program.

t: Super-Resolution Mapping of Neuronal Circuitry With an Index-Optimized Clearing Agent.
sum: Seeing synapses with a light microscope deep inside tissue is usually blurry. This paper introduces a clearing recipe that matches oil-immersion lenses so super-resolution can go more than ten times deeper.

t: Community Detection and Classification in Hierarchical Stochastic Blockmodels
sum: This statistics paper finds groups inside a network, then asks which groups are built the same way, repeating the process to reveal a hierarchy—illustrated on a fly brain graph and a social network.

t: Connectomics and graph theory analyses: Novel insights into network abnormalities in epilepsy
sum: Epilepsy often involves whole-brain networks, not just one damaged spot. This review explains how mapping a person’s brain connections with network math might eventually guide diagnosis and treatment.

t: Diverse coupling of neurons to populations in sensory cortex
sum: Even neighboring visual-cortex cells differ: some fire with the crowd (“choristers”) and some do not (“soloists”). That simple difference predicts extra synapses, sensitivity to movement, and much of the pairwise correlation structure.

t: Fast Approximate Quadratic Programming for Graph Matching
sum: Lining up two wiring diagrams is a hard matching problem. This algorithm does it faster and, on a standard test set, better than the previous champion, including on worm brain graphs.

t: The Secreted Protein C1QL1 and Its Receptor BAI3 Control the Synaptic Connectivity of Excitatory Inputs Converging on Cerebellar Purkinje Cells.
sum: Two kinds of excitatory input land on cerebellar Purkinje cells in tidy, separate zones. This paper identifies a secreted protein and its receptor that help set those territories.

t: Frustrated hierarchical synchronization and emergent complexity in the human connectome network
sum: When simple oscillator models run on a map of human white-matter connections, they do not just lock together or fall apart. A messy in-between regime appears, with parts of the network aligning while others drift.

t: Rapid Golgi Analysis Method for Efficient and Unbiased Classification of Dendritic Spines
sum: Sorting dendritic spines into shapes by eye is slow and disagreeable. This paper uses simple length and width rules in a spreadsheet so the typing is faster and less subjective.

t: Visualizing the human connectome
sum: Maps of human brain connections are only as useful as the pictures that show them. This review walks through how those pictures evolved and why they still get cluttered or misleading.

t: Morphology and Physiology of Excitatory Neurons in Layer 6b of the Somatosensory Rat Barrel Cortex
sum: A deep, overlooked cortical layer contains mixed excitatory cell shapes. This rat study sorts them into three main groups using both their anatomy and their electrical properties.

t: Spatial profile of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connectivity in mouse primary auditory cortex
sum: In mouse auditory cortex, excitatory and inhibitory cells connect over similar short distances. Depending on the incoming pattern, that layout can either sharpen tuning or keep excitation and inhibition balanced.

t: Statistical Inference on Errorfully Observed Graphs
sum: Wiring maps are built from noisy guesses about which cells touch. This paper asks how carefully you should check each possible connection if the real goal is to label the cells, not to get every edge perfect.

t: Challenges and Opportunities in Mining Neuroscience Data
sum: Brain research produces huge piles of different kinds of data. This Science essay argues that sharing, standard labels, and computer-readable tables are needed if anyone is going to put those piles together.

t: The Retrosplenial Cortex: Intrinsic Connectivity and Connections with the (Para)Hippocampal Region in the Rat. An Interactive Connectome
sum: Researchers gathered published tracing studies of a memory-and-navigation region in the rat and turned them into a searchable wiring map, including how that region talks to the hippocampus.

t: Transfection via whole-cell recording in vivo: bridging single-cell physiology, genetics and connectomics
sum: The team records from a living mouse neuron through a tiny pipette, then uses that same pipette to insert DNA so the cell can later be genetically labeled and its input partners traced.

t: Specificity of Sensory-Motor Connections Encoded by Sema3e-PlexinD1 Recognition
sum: Some spinal sensory neurons should wire only to particular motor neurons. This mouse study finds a molecular “keep away” signal that sets those fine connections without changing which muscle each motor pool belongs to.

t: Characterization and synaptic connectivity of melanopsin‐containing ganglion cells in the primate retina
sum: Some primate retinal cells contain the pigment melanopsin and also receive ordinary photoreceptor input. This study maps those cells in marmoset and counts likely synapses on their inner versus outer dendrites.

t: Brain Network Fingerprints of Alzheimer’s Disease Risk Factors in Mouse Models with Humanized APOE Alleles
sum: Mice carrying human Alzheimer’s risk genes, but not plaques, still show distinctive brain-network patterns for diet, sex, immunity, and APOE type. A small shared bundle of connections is hit by several of those risks at once.

t: Experience-dependent glial pruning of synaptic glomeruli during the critical period
sum: In young fruit flies, a burst of odor experience makes support cells eat away part of a smell circuit. The authors trace the molecular steps inside those glial cells that carry out the pruning.

t: Molecular patterns of evolutionary changes throughout the whole nervous system of multiple nematode species
sum: Three worm species kept the same neuron types for tens of millions of years, but many cells changed which chemical messages they can hear. Identity stayed put; the listening equipment evolved.

t: New rabies viral resources for multi-scale neural circuit mapping
sum: Rabies viruses can jump one synapse so scientists can see which cells talk to which. This team built twenty new versions that glow better, mark tiny parts of cells, or show up in both light and electron microscopes.

t: Relation of connectome topology to brain volume across 103 mammalian species
sum: Bigger mammal brains are not just scaled-up small ones. This study of more than a hundred species finds that large brains pack modules more tightly and rely more on spreading signals than on shortest-path routing.

t: Updates on mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease
sum: Not every Alzheimer’s mouse is the same. This review compares older overexpression lines with newer gene-edited models so labs can pick an animal that actually matches the question they want to ask.

t: A Personalized Longitudinal Strategy in Low-Grade Glioma Patients: Predicting Oncological and Neural Interindividual Variability and Its Changes over Years to Think One Step Ahead
sum: Slow-growing brain tumors in young adults invade wiring, not just a lump. This neurosurgeon argues for planning years of surgery around each patient’s changing brain networks, instead of a one-size protocol.

t: Identifying vulnerable brain networks associated with Alzheimer's disease risk.
sum: People who carry Alzheimer’s risk genes were scanned before most of them were ill. The study picks out brain-network patterns that track genotype, family risk, and age, aiming someday to flag individuals, not just groups.

t: Neuroimaging and thalamic connectomics in epilepsy neuromodulation.
sum: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures do not respond to drugs. This review discusses how brain scans of thalamic connections might guide where to place those stimulators.

t: Olfactory Evaluation in Alzheimer’s Disease Model Mice
sum: Smell often fades before memory in Alzheimer’s. This review gathers how scientists test smell in Alzheimer’s mice and what those tests have found so far.

t: The Concept of «Peritumoral Zone» in Diffuse Low-Grade Gliomas: Oncological and Functional Implications for a Connectome-Guided Therapeutic Attitude
sum: Slow gliomas do not stop at the bright blob on the scan. This review treats the rim of mixed tumor and healthy wiring as its own zone, and argues for removing or treating that rim using brain-network maps.

t: The Developing Human Connectome Project Neonatal Data Release
sum: A large public set of baby brain scans, taken with methods that tolerate wriggling, is now available so researchers can study how human brain wiring develops around birth.

t: Altered synaptic connectivity and brain function in mice lacking microglial adapter protein Iba1
sum: The stain everyone uses for brain immune cells turns out to matter for the cells’ job. Mice missing Iba1 have sluggish microglia, fewer excitatory synapses, and later problems with memory and social behavior.

t: An Open MRI Dataset For Multiscale Neuroscience
sum: A public MRI collection gives both the raw scans and ready-made brain-network matrices from several types of images, so other labs can ask how tissue structure lines up with wiring and activity.

t: Connectomic Deep Brain Stimulation for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.
sum: Brain stimulation for severe OCD may work by hitting a whole circuit, not one tiny spot. This review tries to draw that circuit from imaging and stimulation studies.

t: Quantitative skills in undergraduate neuroscience education in the age of big data.
sum: Neuroscience students still take old-style math while the field now runs on huge datasets and network graphs. This commentary says they need data-science training, even if faculty have to learn alongside them.

t: BRAIN Initiative: Cutting-Edge Tools and Resources for the Community
sum: Inventing a new brain tool is not enough; people have to be able to get it and use it. This BRAIN Initiative mini-symposium paper showcases projects that are trying to share connectomics and recording methods with the wider community.

t: Holographic Reconstruction of Axonal Pathways in the Human Brain
sum: Instead of trusting computer-drawn water-diffusion “wires,” expert anatomists stood in a hologram of the human brain and drew the real axonal paths, especially around a deep target used for Parkinson’s stimulation.

t: The hippocampus of birds in a view of evolutionary connectomics.
sum: Bird brains do not look like mammal brains, but their hippocampus still has specialized wiring along its length. This pigeon imaging study adds that pattern to the evolutionary comparison.

t: Comparative Primate Connectomics
sum: This review compares wiring maps among primates and asks what is unusual about human long-range connections, especially in language and tool-use areas.

t: Deficit of corpus callosum axons, reduced axon diameter and decreased area are markers of abnormal development of interhemispheric connections in autistic subjects
sum: The big cable between the two halves of the brain has fewer and thinner axons in the autistic cases studied here, especially the large, fast-conducting fibers.

t: Exploring early human brain development with structural and physiological neuroimaging
sum: A baby’s brain is not a miniature adult brain. This review explains what MRI and related tools can and cannot show about how human brain structure and function grow before and just after birth.

t: Lead-DBS v2: Towards a comprehensive pipeline for deep brain stimulation imaging
sum: To know whether a deep-brain stimulator is in the right spot, and which networks it is ticking, labs need shared software. This paper updates the open Lead-DBS toolbox to a full imaging-and-connectome pipeline.

t: Neuron-specific signatures in the chromosomal connectome associated with schizophrenia risk
sum: Schizophrenia risk DNA often sits far from the genes it may control. By folding maps of chromosomes in developing human brain cells, this study finds extra genes that physically touch those risk regions, especially in neurons.

t: A Semiparametric Two-Sample Hypothesis Testing Problem for Random Graphs
sum: Scientists often want to know whether two brain wiring diagrams really come from the same kind of network. This statistics paper gives a test for that question and uses it to tell people apart from their connectome scans and to tell chemical from electrical wiring in the worm.

t: Q&A: Why use synchrotron x-ray tomography for multi-scale connectome mapping?
sum: Mapping a whole brain at every zoom level is still too slow with today’s main imaging tools. This Q&A argues that synchrotron x-ray tomography could scan an entire animal at many scales and line up with living optical images.

t: Skull optical clearing window for in vivo imaging of the mouse cortex at synaptic resolution
sum: Looking at living mouse cortex usually means cutting or grinding the skull. This team paints clearing chemicals on the bone instead, and can watch synapses, immune cells, and tiny blood vessels through it.

t: 2015 Brainhack Proceedings
sum: This is not one experiment. It is a stack of short reports from 2015 Brainhack events, where people spent a few days building shared brain-imaging tools and then wrote up what they made.

t: Structural Plasticity, Effectual Connectivity, and Memory in Cortex
sum: Memories may depend not only on stronger synapses but on growing new ones in the right places. This theory paper defines how completely a memory’s neurons are wired to each other and uses that idea to explain why spaced practice can help learning.

t: The rhesus monkey connectome predicts disrupted functional networks resulting from pharmacogenetic inactivation of the amygdala
sum: Turning off one brain region can change conversations among many others. In monkeys, silencing the amygdala scrambled widespread fMRI coupling, and a wiring map of the monkey brain helped predict those distant effects.

t: Vision and Locomotion Shape the Interactions between Neuron Types in Mouse Visual Cortex
sum: Running changes how mouse visual cortex responds to what the eyes see. This study finds that the popular “VIP cells shut off SST cells, which frees excitatory cells” story is too simple: which inhibitory cells speed up depends on whether the visual stimulus is large or small.

t: ConnectomeDB – Sharing Human Brain Connectivity Data
sum: The Human Connectome Project needed a public warehouse for huge brain-scan files and the tests that go with them. ConnectomeDB is that warehouse: a website, fast downloads, and even mailed hard drives.

t: Resting-state functional connectivity in major depressive disorder: A review.
sum: Depression is not only a chemical story; it also shows up as changed conversations among large brain networks at rest. This review gathers those imaging studies and highlights a few patterns that keep appearing.

t: Graph Matching: Relax at Your Own Risk
sum: Matching two networks so that the same nodes line up is a notoriously hard puzzle. This paper shows that a popular “make it convex so it is easy” shortcut usually misses the right alignment, and a less tidy relaxation does better.

t: The huge plastic potential of adult brain and the role of connectomics: new insights provided by serial mappings in glioma surgery.
sum: Adult brains can reroute function after injury more than old modular maps suggest. This surgical review argues that glioma operations done awake show that plasticity, not a fixed list of “untouchable” spots, often keeps language and thought going—until key white-matter cables are cut.

t: Analyzing the structure and function of neuronal circuits in zebrafish
sum: Some brains are small enough that scientists can watch almost every cell fire and, in principle, draw almost every wire. This review explains why zebrafish are a leading animal for that kind of complete circuit work, especially in the smell center.

t: BrainNet Viewer: A Network Visualization Tool for Human Brain Connectomics
sum: Brain-network papers are full of abstract graphs that are hard to look at. BrainNet Viewer is a free MATLAB program that draws those networks as balls and sticks on a 3-D brain so the anatomy is obvious.

t: Conditional Ablation of Neuroprogenitor Cells in Adult Mice Impedes Recovery of Poststroke Cognitive Function and Reduces Synaptic Connectivity in the Perforant Pathway
sum: After a stroke, the brain makes extra new neurons, but do they help thinking come back? In mice, wiping out those progenitor cells made spatial memory recover worse, and a key memory pathway looked less well connected, while walking was not clearly worse.

t: Connectomics and epilepsy
sum: Epilepsy is a problem of how brain cells and regions are wired, not only of single molecules. This review surveys new ways to map those bad connections in the whole brain and in small circuits, with an eye toward better surgery and treatment.

t: Human Connectome Project Informatics: quality control, database services, and data visualization
sum: The Human Connectome Project is as much a software and quality-control operation as a scanner project. This paper describes how the team checks data, stores it, shares it, and looks at it on a 3-D brain workbench.

t: Comprehensive connectivity of the mouse main olfactory bulb: analysis and online digital atlas
sum: The mouse smell bulb sends and receives many cables, but those maps used to live in scattered papers. This team injects pairs of tracers, posts the pictures online, and shows that different parts of the bulb follow a topographic road map into smell cortex.

t: From simple graphs to the connectome: Networks in neuroimaging
sum: Brain science borrowed the idea of networks from other fields so it could talk about wiring, not only about single regions. This essay looks back at how that way of thinking entered neuroimaging.

t: Large scale brain models of epilepsy: dynamics meets connectomics
sum: We know many facts about epilepsy but still not why a seizure suddenly starts and stops. This review says the way forward is to put computer models of brain dynamics onto maps of whole-brain wiring.

t: Meeting the Memory Challenges of Brain-Scale Network Simulation
sum: Simulating a whole brain hits a wall when each computer chip runs out of memory. This paper measures that wall in the NEST simulator and changes how wiring is stored so much larger networks can fit on a supercomputer.

t: The UCLA multimodal connectivity database: a web-based platform for brain connectivity matrix sharing and analysis
sum: Many labs end up with a spreadsheet of how strongly every brain region connects to every other. This website lets them post those spreadsheets, run standard network measurements, and compare results across studies.

t: Specificity of Synaptic Connectivity between Layer 1 Inhibitory Interneurons and Layer 2/3 Pyramidal Neurons in the Rat Neocortex
sum: The top layer of rat cortex has several kinds of inhibitory cells, and they do not all plug into the excitatory cells below in the same way. One type (neurogliaform) strongly shuts those cells down but does not get the same return excitation the other types get.

t: Automated Reconstruction of Neuronal Morphology: An Overview
sum: Turning a microscope picture of a neuron into a digital stick figure is still mostly done by hand. This review explains why automatic tracing has been slow to take over and what a community contest revealed about the remaining gaps.

t: Geometry and structural plasticity of synaptic connectivity.
sum: A dendrite is surrounded by many axons it could touch with a short spine, but it only makes synapses with some of them. This theory paper estimates that leftover “empty slots” are common, so rewiring spines could change circuits a lot without growing new branches.
